Practice Analytical Text Response Topics Section A topics on Picnic at Hanging Rock tend to take one of three shapes. Learn to recognise them in reading time, because each asks you to do something slightly different. Task type What it asks Typical wording Construction How Weir builds an idea through the film: framing, sound, costume, setting, structure. Background and Context

Overview Peter Weir’s Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975) opens with a title card dating its events to St Valentine’s Day, 1900: a party of schoolgirls from Appleyard College picnics at Hanging Rock, near Mount Macedon in Victoria, and several members of the party disappear without trace. The film never explains what happened. Instead, it studies how a rigid, ordered colonial society reacts when something happens that its rules, clocks and explanations cannot contain. Knowing where the story comes from, when it is set and how it was made will help you write about Weir’s choices rather than just the plot.

Joan Lindsay’s Novel The film is adapted from Joan Lindsay’s 1967 novel of the same name. Lindsay deliberately blurred fact and fiction, presenting the disappearance as if it might have happened and declining to say whether it did. That ambiguity became part of the story’s legend: many readers and viewers came to believe the events were real. A final chapter that Lindsay cut from the novel, offering a strange, quasi-supernatural resolution, was published after her death; it plays no part in the film.

Analysis You are studying the film, not the novel. Weir keeps Lindsay’s refusal to resolve the mystery and makes it the centre of the viewing experience: the audience, like the characters, is left wanting an answer that never arrives. When you write about ‘unresolved mysteries’, remember that this is a deliberate construction, not a gap.

t: Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave
b: Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave Picnic at Hanging Rock was one of the defining films of the Australian New Wave, a revival of local filmmaking in the 1970s supported by new government film funding. Directed by Peter Weir from a screenplay by Cliff Green, it was a major critical and commercial success and helped bring Australian cinema to international audiences. Appleyard College was filmed at Martindale Hall in South Australia, while the picnic and search scenes were shot at Hanging Rock itself.

t: Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave - Analysis
b: Analysis The New Wave was partly about Australians telling stories about their own landscape and history. Weir’s film looks back at colonial society with a mixture of beauty and unease: the European culture of the college looks lovely but out of place against the ancient Australian bush. This tension between imported civilisation and the land is at the heart of most essay topics.

Victoria in 1900 In 1900 Victoria was still a British colony; Federation would come on 1 January 1901. Wealthy colonial society modelled itself on Britain: its schools taught deportment, French, poetry and the accomplishments expected of young ladies, and its social life was governed by strict rules about class, dress and behaviour. Girls were laced into corsets, gloved and hatted outdoors, and expected to be decorative, obedient and chaste. Class divisions were sharp. The Fitzhuberts are landed gentry; Albert, their groom, is a working man who grew up in an orphanage; Sara, his sister, is a ward whose fees go unpaid. Mrs Appleyard’s college depends on wealthy parents’ money and on its reputation for respectability.

Analysis The rules of this society explain much of what we see: the gloves Mrs Appleyard allows the girls to remove only ‘once the drag has passed through Woodend’, the horror at Miss McCraw being seen without her skirt, the police assumption that the explanation must be a man. Weir shows how fragile these conventions are once they meet something beyond them.

Hanging Rock Hanging Rock is a volcanic formation in the Macedon Ranges, north-west of Melbourne, and lies on the traditional lands of the Dja Dja Wurrung, Taungurung and Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung peoples. Geologically it is relatively young, a point Miss McCraw makes in the film, but in human terms it is ancient. Its jagged pinnacles, narrow passages and balanced boulders give it the maze-like quality Weir’s camera exploits.

Analysis The colonial characters treat the Rock as a picnic spot and a curiosity to be measured. The film suggests that it existed long before them and will outlast them. The settlers’ lack of any real relationship with the land, including the Indigenous history they overlook, is part of what makes it seem so alien and threatening to them.

The Film Script A transcript of the film’s dialogue is available online: Picnic at Hanging Rock film transcript (script-o-rama) . Use it to check the exact wording of quotes, which can differ from the published screenplay. The transcript leaves out numbers (times and dates), so check those against the film. The full script is also available to read online at ScriptSlug: Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975) .

t: The Look and Sound of the Film
b: The Look and Sound of the Film Cinematographer Russell Boyd gave the film its dreamy, soft-focus look, with diffused light, slow motion and lingering shots of the landscape. The soundtrack mixes Gheorghe Zamfir’s haunting pan flute, original music by Bruce Smeaton, European classical pieces such as the slow movement of Beethoven’s Fifth Piano Concerto, and an unsettling low rumble associated with the Rock.

t: The Look and Sound of the Film - Analysis
b: Analysis These choices create the film’s central tension between beauty and menace. The images are lovely, almost like paintings, but the sound and pacing keep the viewer uneasy. See the Film Techniques section for how to use them in essays.

The Novel and the Film Your set text is Peter Weir’s 1975 film, not Joan Lindsay’s 1967 novel. The film follows the novel closely, but the novel contains events and explanations that never appear on screen. Anything that exists only in the novel cannot be used as evidence in your essay, and using it tells the assessor you are not writing about the film.

t: What Happens Differently in the Novel
b: What Happens Differently in the Novel Sara’s death. In the novel, Sara is found days later beneath the school’s tower, apparently a suicide. In the film, the head gardener finds her body in the greenhouse; how she died is never shown. Mrs Appleyard’s death. In the novel, she jumps from a peak on the Rock. In the film, a closing voice-over reports that her body was found at the base of the Rock and that ‘it is believed she fell while attempting to climb the rock’. Miss Lumley. In the novel, she leaves with her brother Reg, and both die in a hotel fire. In the film, she simply resigns. Mademoiselle. In the novel, she announces she is getting married and leaves the college. In the film, she is still there at the end, dining with Mrs Appleyard. Miss McCraw. In the novel, a frill of calico thought to be from her dress is found in 1903. The film gives no such clue.

The Missing Final Chapter Lindsay cut the novel’s final chapter before publication. It was published after her death, in 1987, as The Secret of Hanging Rock . In it, the girls and a woman who seems to be Miss McCraw throw off their corsets and pass through a ‘hole in space’ in the Rock, while Irma is shut out when the hanging boulder tilts. This chapter has nothing to do with the film. Weir deliberately leaves the disappearance unexplained, and that refusal to explain is one of the most important things to analyse. Never use the missing chapter as an ‘answer’.

t: How to Stay on the Film
b: How to Stay on the Film Name the director, not the author: ‘Weir suggests’, not ‘Lindsay suggests’. Use film evidence: shots, framing, sound, music, costume, setting and editing, as well as dialogue. If you have read the novel, check every detail you plan to use against the film. If you cannot point to the moment on screen, leave it out. Use the novel only as context, and only in passing: for example, that Lindsay blurred fact and fiction, and that Weir keeps the mystery unresolved.

t: Social Values - Order, Rules and Respectability
g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Order, Rules and Respectability Appleyard College values discipline, punctuality and propriety above all. Mrs Appleyard’s instructions before the picnic about gloves, ‘tomboy foolishness’, snakes and returning ‘at about 8’ show a world that tries to anticipate and control every risk. The film questions whether these rules create real order or only the appearance of it: when the girls vanish, the rules offer no answer, and the institution begins to collapse.

t: Social Values - Class and Social Hierarchy
g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Class and Social Hierarchy Wealth and status decide who belongs. Sara, an orphan whose fees are ‘impossibly overdue’, is excluded from the picnic and treated harshly; Mrs Appleyard insists the college is not a ‘charitable institution’. Michael and Albert’s friendship across the class divide stands out as a rare challenge to these values.

g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Femininity and Restraint The girls are dressed in white, corseted and gloved, praised for beauty and refinement. The film links this ideal of femininity to repression: the girls who climb the Rock shed their shoes, stockings and gloves, and the community’s reaction to the disappearance focuses obsessively on bodies and sexual danger.

g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Cultural Values

g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Rationality and Science The characters trust measurement, investigation and explanation. Miss McCraw studies geometry and geology; Sergeant Bumpher interviews witnesses and organises searches; the doctor examines Irma. The film presents a world that does not yield to these methods, suggesting the limits of a purely rational worldview.

t: Cultural Values - European Culture in the Australian Landscape
g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: European Culture in the Australian Landscape The college is a piece of England transplanted to the bush: Botticelli prints, Valentine’s poetry, cultivated flowers, high tea and classical music. Weir sets this imported culture against an ancient landscape it does not understand, revealing the colonists’ sense of being outsiders in the land they occupy.

t: Cultural Values - Romanticism and the Sublime
g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Romanticism and the Sublime Some characters, especially Miranda and Michael, are drawn to nature as something beautiful, spiritual and liberating. This Romantic longing for connection with nature coexists with fear: the Rock is both enchanting and terrifying.

g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Key Ideas and Vocabulary Weir’s film can feel strange on first viewing, so it helps to go in knowing the ideas it keeps returning to. At its centre is a collision: on one side an ancient landscape that is vast and beyond explanation, on the other a colonial society that runs on clocks, rules and categories. The disappearance at the Rock tests every one of those systems, and none of them holds. The word lists below give you precise language for each idea.

t: Key Ideas and Vocabulary - Nature as a Fundamental Force
g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Nature as a Fundamental Force The film opens on the Rock before it shows a single person, and Weir keeps returning to it as a looming, brooding presence. He also fills the frame with smaller life: ants swarming over the picnic cake, a lizard on a boulder, birds calling, the Rock’s surface in close-up. Together these shots build a living world that exists entirely on its own terms. Characters split in how they respond. Edith finds the bush threatening and wants to stay put, while Miranda moves deeper into it, shedding her shoes and stockings as she goes. Because the other ideas in the film are all defined against the natural world, an essay on Picnic at Hanging Rock will almost always need to say something about it. Nature: natural environment, landscape, wilderness, Australian bush, surrounding landscape, untamed world, world of nature, natural realm, surrounding wilderness. Nature as a mysterious force: elemental forces of nature, impenetrability of the wilderness, untameable power of nature, overwhelming nature of the wilderness, primordial landscape, inscrutable forces of nature, unknowable dimensions of the wilderness, enigmatic world of the Australian landscape, ancient and indifferent landscape.

t: Key Ideas and Vocabulary - The Human Need for Rationality and Control
g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: The Human Need for Rationality and Control Faced with a world they cannot fully grasp, the characters reach for numbers, rules and explanations. Miss McCraw calculates and explains the Rock’s volcanic origin; Marion talks about people as if they were figures in a sum; Mr Hussey checks his watch; Sergeant Bumpher asks whether there was a man. After the disappearance the whole community wants an account that makes sense, and the film refuses to supply one. Notice how often a character offers a fact, a date or a theory as if it could tame what has happened. Order: structure, stability, certainty, predictability, clarity, understanding, balance, control, rationality, coherence. Chaos: disorder, uncertainty, unpredictability, confusion, mystery, wilderness, irrationality. Desire for knowledge: need to understand, the importance of learning, feeling of expertise, prioritisation of education, promotion of intellect, the search for reason, accumulation of information, desire to comprehend, need to make sense. Measurement: quantification, imposition of order, reduction of data, transforming the unknowable, a means of establishing order, faith in mathematical understanding.

t: Key Ideas and Vocabulary - Class and Civilisation
g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Class and Civilisation Colonial society sets itself up as the opposite of the bush. Appleyard College is the clearest example: a grand building with clipped lawns, placed in the middle of the Victorian countryside as if it could hold the landscape at bay. Inside, even nature is managed, from the plants in the glasshouse to the flowers arranged in vases. The same idea runs through costume and hierarchy: the girls in stockings and gloves, the police in polished buttons, Mrs Appleyard’s elaborately dressed hair, the maids and grooms who serve the gentry. Each layer of rules gives people the sense that the world has been tamed. The disappearance shows how thin that sense is. The ordered world of Appleyard College: the college’s routines and regulations, an institution built on discipline, the timetabled life of the boarders, a manicured enclave in the bush, the college as an outpost of empire, the rule-bound world of the school, the protective walls of the institution, the headmistress’s regime. The social structure of Edwardian society: a fixed class hierarchy, the manners of respectable society, colonial propriety, the codes of gentility, inherited rank and privilege, the expectations placed on young ladies, the divide between masters and servants, the imported values of Britain.

g: Values in Picnic at Hanging Rock
b: Time Time could sit under rationality and control, since a clock is just another way of measuring, but the film gives it so much attention that it is worth treating on its own. The picnic happens on a precise date, watches and clocks appear again and again, and their stopping at the Rock disturbs everyone who notices. Against these human hours the Rock offers geological time, measured in millions of years. Weir also bends the audience’s own experience of time, using slow motion, dissolves and long, drifting shots so that the climb feels suspended outside ordinary hours. Human-scale time: clock time, timetables and appointments, punctuality, the calendar, time as something to be counted and owned, deadlines and routines, the brief span of a human life, the steady march of the school day. Time in the natural world: geological ages, deep time, stillness, suspended or frozen time, time that loops or stops, an ancient and enduring landscape, timelessness, rhythms older than human history.
Thematic Quote Bank

Nature as a Fundamental Force Miranda (voice-over): ‘What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.’ Mrs Appleyard : ‘The vicinity is renowned for its venomous snakes and poisonous ants of various species.’ Mrs Appleyard : ‘The Rock is extremely dangerous, and you are therefore forbidden any tomboy foolishness in the matter of exploration.’ Irma , as the Rock comes into view: ‘Waiting a million years, just for us.’ Edith : ‘Why can’t we just sit on this log and look at the ugly old rock from here?’ Edith : ‘It’s nasty here.’ Edith (remembering the Rock): ‘It was a cloud... it was red.’ Michael , of the Rock: ‘It comes back at night in dreams.’ Sara , in Albert’s dream: ‘I’ve come a long way to see ya, and now I must go.’ Sara , after the disappearance: Miranda had many ‘secrets’; ‘she knew she wouldn’t come back.’

t: The Human Need for Rationality and Control
b: The Human Need for Rationality and Control Mr Hussey : ‘No one knows. No one saw her leave. We were asleep.’ Sergeant Bumpher (to Edith): ‘Was there a man?’ Mrs Bumpher , reporting local gossip: ‘It couldn’t be local... No one around here would do a thing like that.’ Mrs Bumpher , to her husband: ‘People just don’t disappear, my dear. Not without good reason.’ A townsman outside the police station: ‘We’ve got a bloody right to know.’ The doctor , examining Irma: her unmarked feet are ‘very strange’. The doctor , on Irma’s survival: ‘Remarkable.’ Mrs Appleyard , of Miss McCraw: how could her ‘masculine intellect’ be ‘spirited away... like a silly schoolgirl’? The head gardener : ‘There’s some questions got answers and some haven’t.’ Mrs Appleyard , on Irma being the only girl found: ‘This makes it worse.’ Michael , to Albert: ‘I wake up every night in a cold sweat. Just wondering if they’re still alive.’ Michael , insisting on searching the Rock himself: the girls ‘may be out there dying of thirst.’ Miss Lumley , rebuked by Mrs Appleyard: Irma’s discovery is ‘wonderful news.’

Can’t stand the ticking above my heart.’ Irma , of Miranda’s watch: she would wear it ‘always... even in the bath.’ Mr Hussey : ‘Blowed if me watch hasn’t stopped. I promised Mrs Appleyard I’d have you lot back at the college by eight.’ Marion : ‘I should like to make a few measurements of the rock if we have time.’ Irma : ‘We’ll be back long before tea.’ Miranda : ‘Everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place.’ Edith : ‘When are we going home?’ Miranda , to Mademoiselle: ‘We shall only be gone a little while.’ Mrs Appleyard , remembering Bournemouth: ‘Nothing changed – ever.’

You just think ’em.’ Edith , of the Fitzhuberts: they ‘might be the only living creatures in the whole world.’ Mrs Appleyard , to Sara: ‘You will be returned to the orphanage.’ Sara , repeating Mrs Appleyard’s words to herself: ‘This is not a charitable institution.’ Miss Lumley , to Sara: Sara is ‘not to go on the picnic.’

Character Quote Bank

Miranda Miranda leads the girls up the Rock and does not return. Beautiful, serene and drawn to the natural world, she is idealised by almost everyone around her. ‘What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.’ – the film’s opening voice-over. ‘Don’t wear it anymore. Can’t stand the ticking above my heart.’ – rejecting her jewelled watch at the picnic. ‘Everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place.’ – on top of the Rock, just before she disappears. ‘Someday, Sara, you shall have to come home with me to the station... meet my sweet, funny family for yourself.’ – to Sara on the morning of the picnic. ‘You must learn to love someone else, apart from me.’ – to Sara, as if anticipating her own absence. ‘We shall only be gone a little while.’ – reassuring Mademoiselle as the girls set off to explore.

Marion Marion is intellectual and detached, taking measurements on the Rock with a protractor. She does not return. ‘I should like to make a few measurements of the rock if we have time.’ – asking permission to explore. ‘I do wish you’d stop talking for once.’ – to Edith during the climb. ‘Whatever can those people be doing down there? Like a lot of ants. Surprising the number of human beings are without purpose.’ – looking down on the picnickers from the Rock.

Irma Irma is the heiress of the group and the only climbing girl who comes back, with no memory of what happened. She would wear Miranda’s watch ‘always... even in the bath.’ – at the picnic. ‘Waiting a million years, just for us.’ – awed by the Rock on the journey. ‘We’ll be back long before tea.’ – before the climb. ‘If only we could stay out all night and watch the moon rise.’ – on the Rock. ‘Poor Edith. We’ll go back soon.’ – to Edith before the girls disappear.

Edith Edith is plump, complaining and frightened. She keeps her hat, gloves, shoes and stockings on, and runs screaming from the Rock. ‘Why can’t we just sit on this log and look at the ugly old rock from here?’ – during the climb. ‘It’s nasty here.’ – as the others are drawn further in. ‘When are we going home?’ – repeatedly, during the climb. ‘It was a cloud... it was red.’ – remembering, when she returns to the Rock with Sergeant Bumpher. Miss McCraw ‘was funny’ – explaining that she was climbing without her skirt. The Fitzhuberts ‘might be the only living creatures in the whole world.’ – after the picnic meal.

Mrs Appleyard The headmistress embodies authority, convention and institutional control. As events slip beyond her control, she unravels. ‘You may remove your gloves once the drag has passed through Woodend.’ – instructions before the picnic. ‘The Rock is extremely dangerous, and you are therefore forbidden any tomboy foolishness in the matter of exploration.’ – warning the girls. ‘Mr Hussey! I shall expect you back, Miss McCraw and Mademoiselle, at about 8.’ – as the drag departs. ‘This makes it worse.’ – chiding Miss Lumley for calling Irma’s discovery ‘wonderful news’. ‘There are several sets of tuition fees impossibly overdue... Sara Waybourne, for instance.’ – as the college faces financial pressure. ‘We shall have to make other arrangements.’ – to Sara, about her unpaid fees. ‘You will be returned to the orphanage.’ – in her final meeting with Sara. Bournemouth was ‘a delightful place’ where ‘nothing changed – ever.’ – reminiscing with Mademoiselle at dinner. She had come to ‘depend so much on Greta McCraw’ and her ‘masculine intellect’: ‘How could she allow herself to be spirited away?’ – at the same dinner.

Sara Waybourne An orphan and ward of the college, Sara is forbidden from the picnic and devoted to Miranda. She is later found dead. Miranda had many ‘secrets’: ‘she knew she wouldn’t come back.’ – after the disappearance. At the orphanage she had her head shaved for telling the matron she wanted to be a ‘circus rider’. – confiding in Minnie. ‘This is not a charitable institution.’ – repeating Mrs Appleyard’s words to herself, beneath a painting of a woman holding two babies. ‘I’ve come a long way to see ya, and now I must go.’ – to Albert, in his dream on the night of her death.

Miss McCraw The mathematics mistress, admired by Mrs Appleyard for her ‘masculine intellect’. She climbs the Rock alone and does not return. ‘Stopped at twelve. Never stopped before. Must be something magnetic.’ – when the watches are found stopped. The Rock is ‘quite young, geologically speaking.’ – explaining its volcanic origin at the picnic. ‘How foolish can human creatures be.’ – reflecting that the picnickers have come for pleasure to a place of ‘venomous snakes and poisonous ants’.

Mademoiselle de Poitiers The French mistress is warm, romantic and admired by the students, but increasingly anxious for answers. ‘Now I know... Miranda is a Botticelli angel.’ – watching Miranda. Irma is ‘prettier than ever.’ – embracing Irma, before questioning her about what she told the police.

Miss Lumley The junior mistress is timid and fearful of Mrs Appleyard. She eventually resigns. Irma’s discovery is ‘wonderful news.’ – rebuked by Mrs Appleyard. Sara is ‘not to go on the picnic.’ – reminding Sara, though she is not going either. Strapping Sara to the wall is ‘for her own good’, to cure her ‘terrible stooping’. – in the gymnasium.

Michael Fitzhubert A young English aristocrat visiting his uncle and aunt. He watches the girls cross the stream and becomes obsessed with finding them. ‘I wake up every night in a cold sweat. Just wondering if they’re still alive.’ – to Albert. The girls ‘may be out there dying of thirst.’ – insisting on searching the Rock himself. ‘It comes back at night in dreams.’ – telling Albert he can’t stop thinking about the Rock.

Albert Crundall The Fitzhuberts’ groom: earthy, practical and loyal. He finds Irma and, without knowing it, is Sara’s brother. If ‘the bloody cop and the bloody... tracker and the bloody dog can’t find ’em, well, no one bloody can.’ – trying to talk Michael out of searching. He dreams of his ‘kid sister’ on the night of Sara’s death. – telling Michael about the dream. ‘I say the crude things. You just think ’em.’ – to Michael, at the stream.

The Investigators and the Town Mr Hussey: ‘No one knows. No one saw her leave. We were asleep.’ – reporting to Mrs Appleyard and Sergeant Bumpher. Sergeant Bumpher: ‘Was there a man?’ – questioning Edith. Sergeant Bumpher: ‘As the girls were jumping the creek, what were you thinking of?’ – interviewing Michael, who answers by pointing to a swan vase. Mrs Bumpher: ‘It couldn’t be local... No one around here would do a thing like that.’ – repeating the town’s gossip. Mrs Bumpher: ‘People just don’t disappear, my dear. Not without good reason.’ – to her husband, who has no answers. A townsman: ‘We’ve got a bloody right to know.’ – outside Bumpher’s house after Irma is found. The doctor: Irma’s unmarked feet are ‘very strange’. – listing her injuries. The doctor: ‘Remarkable.’ – on Irma surviving a week on the Rock. Mr Hussey: ‘Well after two, I’d say. We’d better be careful.’ – after his watch stops at the picnic. The head gardener: ‘There’s some questions got answers and some haven’t.’ – one of the film’s few direct statements of its idea.
Character Relationships

Mrs Appleyard and Sara Waybourne The film’s most painful relationship is one of power. Mrs Appleyard is upright, ornately dressed and usually framed above other characters or behind her desk; Sara is small, plain, stooped and often seated or diminished in the frame. Sara loves poetry and feeling; Mrs Appleyard values rules and fees. As the college comes under pressure, Mrs Appleyard turns her frustration on Sara, the one person with no family or money to protect her.

t: Mrs Appleyard and Sara Waybourne - Key Quotes
b: Key Quotes Mrs Appleyard: ‘There are several sets of tuition fees impossibly overdue... Sara Waybourne, for instance.’ Mrs Appleyard: ‘We shall have to make other arrangements.’ Mrs Appleyard: Appleyard College is not a ‘charitable institution’.

t: Mrs Appleyard and Sara Waybourne - Key Ideas
b: Key Ideas Class and social hierarchy Authority and cruelty Reason versus emotion Victim or agent of her own fate?

t: Mrs Appleyard and Sara Waybourne - Sara Waybourne: Victim of Fate or Author of Her Own Demise?
b: Sara Waybourne: Victim of Fate or Author of Her Own Demise? Sara is only a minor character, but she matters enormously. She adores Miranda: early on we see her watching Miranda wash and giving her a Valentine’s card. From the start she is set apart. She is kept back from the picnic to learn a poem, which she refuses to do because she thinks her own poetry is better. Mrs Appleyard keeps correcting her posture, an apt image of a girl who cannot, or will not, be made to fit. Later we learn that her guardian has stopped paying her fees. Irma calls her ‘doomed’, and the film bears this out. Sara is hard to pin down. Her defiance of Mrs Appleyard makes her easy to sympathise with, yet the film also shows how precarious her position is. As an orphan in 1900 she sits near the bottom of the social order: her brother Albert works as a groom, and without a guardian’s money she could just as easily be working beside Minnie in the kitchen. For now she lives among the daughters of wealthy families, reading and writing poems, but that comfort depends entirely on fees that are not being paid. Meanwhile she is singled out by Mrs Appleyard and strapped to the gymnasium wall by Miss Lumley. One side of Sara’s story On the other hand Miranda: ‘Someday, Sara, you shall have to come home with me to the station... meet my sweet, funny family for yourself.’ Sara says Miranda had many ‘secrets... she knew she wouldn’t come back’. Miranda: ‘You must learn to love someone else, apart from me.’ Sara shakes her head at this advice, but she has a brother she apparently doesn’t keep in touch with. Miss Lumley reminds Sara that she is ‘not to go on the picnic’. But Miss Lumley is sympathetic, because she is not allowed to go on the picnic either. Mrs Appleyard: ‘There are several sets of tuition fees impossibly overdue... Sara Waybourne, for instance.’ Mrs Appleyard: ‘This is not a charitable institution.’ Sara shakes her head when Mrs Appleyard says, ‘We shall have to make other arrangements.’ Sara was raised in an orphanage alongside Albert, so she would know exactly what being sent back would mean. Sara tells Minnie she had her head shaved at the orphanage for telling the matron she wanted to be a ‘circus rider’. She also bit the matron’s arm hard enough to draw blood. Miss Lumley straps Sara to the gymnasium wall to ‘cure her terrible stooping’. Mademoiselle is willing to confront Mrs Appleyard; Miss Lumley stays silent until she resigns. Just before Sara dies, Weir focuses on her photograph of Miranda, suggesting that Sara is all alone. Albert dreams of his ‘kid sister’ on the night of her death. The head gardener finds Sara’s body in the greenhouse. Mrs Appleyard claims that Sara’s guardian took her away. Question to answer: Does Sara’s fate come from outside her, or does she help bring it about?

t: Mrs Appleyard and Sara Waybourne - Control and the Natural World: a Spectrum
b: Control and the Natural World: a Spectrum Sara’s surname is symbolic: ‘Waybourne’ sounds like ‘wayward’, or contrary. Sara does not fit the rigid hierarchy of Appleyard College and is the complete antithesis of Mrs Appleyard. Try placing the characters (Sara, Mrs Appleyard, Miranda, Miss McCraw, Michael, Albert, Mademoiselle, Miss Lumley, Irma) on a spectrum from control (logic and hierarchy) to untamed forces (nature and mystery), and label each with a phrase: Towards control: faith in rules, reliance on logic, deference to authority, a need for explanation, comfort in routine, respect for rank, the urge to measure and record, anxiety about the unknown, belief that discipline makes people safe, loyalty to the institution. Towards untamed forces: the pull of the bush, instinct over reason, openness to mystery, indifference to rank, a dreamlike or spiritual sense of the world, acceptance of the unexplained, attraction to the wild, freedom from convention, trust in intuition.

Miranda and Sara Sara adores Miranda, who is kind to her and seems to offer belonging. Miranda’s gentle advice that Sara ‘must learn to love someone else’ reads, in hindsight, like a farewell. With Miranda gone, Sara is completely alone; just before Sara’s death, Weir focuses on her photograph of Miranda.

Key Quotes Miranda: ‘Someday, Sara, you shall have to come home with me to the station... meet my sweet, funny family for yourself.’ Miranda: ‘You must learn to love someone else, apart from me.’ Sara: Miranda had many ‘secrets... she knew she wouldn’t come back.’
Key Ideas Love and isolation Foreshadowing The cost of the disappearance for those left behind

Michael and Albert Michael is a privileged young Englishman; Albert is the Fitzhuberts’ groom, raised in an orphanage. At the picnic Albert makes crude remarks about the girls while Michael watches them in silence. The search draws them together: Albert rescues Michael from the Rock, and their conversations grow into a genuine friendship that ignores the social hierarchy around them. In their final scene Albert tells Michael about his dream of his ‘kid sister’, a connection to Sara that neither fully understands.

Key Quotes Albert: If ‘the bloody cop and the bloody... tracker and the bloody dog can’t find ’em, well, no one bloody can.’ Michael: The girls ‘may be out there dying of thirst.’ Michael: ‘I wake up every night in a cold sweat. Just wondering if they’re still alive.’
Key Ideas Friendship across class Acceptance (Albert) versus the search for understanding (Michael) Instinct and intuition

t: Michael and Albert - An Evolving Relationship
b: An Evolving Relationship Michael and Albert begin the film on opposite sides of a strict class line: the nephew of a colonel and his uncle’s groom. The search for the girls pulls them into the same experience, and by the end they talk as equals. Weir uses their friendship to suggest that the Rock does not recognise rank. It also leaves both men unsettled: Michael is haunted, and Albert’s confident common sense gives way to a dream he cannot explain. Of all the relationships in the film, theirs is the one that changes most. Beginning Middle End At the picnic Albert treats Michael as a mate rather than a master, passing him the bottle, and Michael responds in kind. As the girls cross the creek, Albert comments freely on their looks; when Michael calls him ‘crude’, he answers, ‘I say the crude things. You just think ’em.’ Albert is sure the girls are dead, but he helps Michael search anyway. When Michael decides to stay on the Rock overnight, Albert covers for him with his uncle. The next day Albert finds Michael, realises the scrap of lace in his hand matters, goes back up and finds Irma. In their last scene together, Michael admits he cannot stop thinking about the Rock: ‘It comes back at night in dreams.’ Albert answers with a ‘funny dream’ of his own, in which his sister Sara appears, with a strong scent of pansies. Sentence starters: Although they come from opposite ends of the social ladder, Michael and Albert...; As the search draws them together...; Weir uses the friendship between the nephew and the groom to...; Set against the class-bound world of the Fitzhuberts... + grows into..., crosses..., outlasts..., unsettles..., moves from... to..., challenges... Comparative statements to agree, disagree or partly agree with: Albert adapts to the disappearance more easily than Michael does. Albert’s practical knowledge of the bush matters more in the search than Michael’s determination. The friendship changes Michael far more than it changes Albert. For Michael the search becomes personal in a way it never does for Albert. Albert is content to leave the mystery unsolved; Michael cannot let it go.

Dreams Late in the film each man describes a dream. Michael’s returns him to the Rock. Albert’s brings him his sister Sara, which catches the audience off guard, because the film has only just revealed that they are brother and sister, and because Sara has just died. Weir offers no explanation. You could read the dreams as signs of a connection between people and places that logic cannot reach; as evidence that the Rock’s influence has spread beyond the picnic ground; or as Weir’s way of showing that the most important truths in the film arrive through feeling rather than reason.

Albert and Sara Albert and Sara are brother and sister, separated in the orphanage. The film never brings them together: Albert does not know his sister is at the college a few miles away, and Sara does not keep in touch with him. On the night of Sara’s death, Albert dreams that she visits him to say goodbye.
Key Ideas Class and lost opportunity Mystery and the supernatural Dramatic irony

Mrs Appleyard and Miss McCraw Mrs Appleyard relies on Miss McCraw as the embodiment of reason and order. That the most rational person in the film is ‘spirited away’ shakes Mrs Appleyard’s belief that the world can be controlled.

t: Mrs Appleyard and Miss McCraw - Key Quotes
b: Key Quotes Mrs Appleyard: She had come to ‘depend so much on Greta McCraw’ and her ‘masculine intellect’. Mrs Appleyard: ‘How could she allow herself to be spirited away?’

t: Mrs Appleyard and Miss McCraw - Key Ideas
b: Key Ideas The limits of reason Dependence and control

Mademoiselle and Miss Lumley Weir dresses the two junior mistresses as opposites: Mademoiselle in lace and pearls with soft, loose hair, Miss Lumley in tartan and spectacles in dull colours. Mademoiselle goes on the picnic; Miss Lumley stays behind, like Sara. Mademoiselle stands up to Mrs Appleyard and remains at the college to the end, whereas Miss Lumley stays silent until she finally resigns.

t: Mademoiselle and Miss Lumley - Key Quotes
b: Key Quotes Miss Lumley: Irma’s discovery is ‘wonderful news’. Mademoiselle: Irma is ‘prettier than ever’.

t: Mademoiselle and Miss Lumley - Key Ideas
b: Key Ideas Appearance versus reality Fear of authority Curiosity and the need for answers

t: Mademoiselle and Miss Lumley - Appearances Are Deceiving
b: Appearances Are Deceiving In many ways the two women are presented as opposites, and it is easy to typecast them: Mademoiselle is glamorous, French and sympathetic to the girls; Miss Lumley defers to Mrs Appleyard, is unfashionable, wears spectacles and is a little afraid of the girls. But Weir makes both more complicated than they appear. Costume: Mademoiselle is dressed in lace, pearls, soft ribbons and flowered hats, with her hair loosely waved; Miss Lumley wears tartan, plain blouses and spectacles, in drab colours. Vocabulary: refined, delicate, romantic, feminine, ornamented, warm (Mademoiselle); plain, severe, practical, subdued, dutiful, colourless (Miss Lumley). Phrases for analysis: emotionally attuned to the girls, softened by beauty and art, sympathetic to youth and feeling ; bound by duty, anxious to please authority, restrained and correct, fearful of disorder . Miss Lumley Mademoiselle Beginning Is aligned with Sara, because neither is allowed to go to the picnic. Goes to the picnic. Compares Miranda to a work of art. Middle Calls Irma’s return ‘wonderful news’ and is sharply rebuked; flinches under Mrs Appleyard’s anger; keeps hoping the others will be found. Questions Edith about what she saw, both in bed and back at the Rock; hands the police a piece of Miranda’s clothing for the dogs; is crushed when only Irma comes back; embraces Irma as ‘prettier than ever’, then quizzes her about her statement to the police. End Hides behind the piano when the girls turn on Irma; insists that strapping Sara up was ‘for her own good’; resigns. Brings Irma back to class and leaves her there; loses her temper with Edith and slaps her; is still at the college at the end, keeping Mrs Appleyard company at dinner. What motivates them? Statements to weigh up: Miss Lumley mostly wants to keep her position and avoid her headmistress’s anger; Mademoiselle cares deeply about the girls; Mademoiselle’s warmth is partly about being admired; Miss Lumley knows that some of what she is told to do is wrong but is too frightened to refuse; both women claim to act from duty when they are acting from feeling. Topic sentence to develop: Weir shows that behind the professional manner of the college’s teachers lie fear, loyalty and longing, and these, not reason, decide how they act.

Irma and the Other Girls When Irma returns, the girls who once envied and admired her surround her in the gymnasium demanding ‘Tell us, Irma!’. Her vivid red dress sets her apart from their white uniforms. The scene turns into a frightening display of mob behaviour, showing how quickly civilised behaviour collapses when people are desperate for answers.

t: Irma and the Other Girls - Key Ideas
b: Key Ideas Mass hysteria and mob mentality The desire for certainty The collapse of civility
Scene Summaries and Analyses The sequences below follow the order of the film. Use them to locate evidence quickly; the Analysis notes suggest how each sequence connects to the big ideas.

Sequence 1 : The Opening Summary : Hanging Rock emerges from mist while Miranda’s voice-over says ‘What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.’ A title card gives precise factual details about the disappearance. Appleyard College is then shown framed against a foreground of wild summer grass. Analysis : The order is significant. We see the Rock first, then the facts, then the college. From the outset Weir establishes the three forces of the film: nature as a fundamental force, the human need for factual order, and civilisation. The facts tell us what happened but not why, so the film begins with the mystery already unsolved.

Sequence 2 : St Valentine’s Morning Summary : The girls dress, lace each other’s corsets, and exchange Valentine cards and poems. Miranda and Sara share a tender moment. Flowers are everywhere. Mrs Appleyard addresses the girls about gloves, snakes, ‘tomboy foolishness’ and returning ‘at about 8’. Sara is told she is not to go on the picnic. Analysis : Weir portrays the students as elegant, refined and innocent, but also sheltered, uniform and restrained. The cultivated flowers represent a version of nature that has been domesticated and controlled. Mrs Appleyard’s warnings reveal an institutional fear of disorder, danger and lost time.

Sequence 3 : The Picnic Summary : The drag, driven by Mr Hussey, carries the girls, Miss McCraw and Mademoiselle to the Rock. Miranda opens a gate to let the party through. The picnic is laid out with cake, china and white dresses. Nearby, Colonel and Mrs Fitzhubert picnic with their nephew Michael and their groom Albert. Mr Hussey’s and Miss McCraw’s watches are found stopped at twelve. Much of the party grows drowsy and falls asleep. Analysis : The picnic and the characters’ clothing appear incongruous against the ancient landscape; civilised behaviour seems intrusive or strangely detached from the wilderness. The gate is the first threshold between the familiar world and the unknown. The stopped watches signal that the Rock operates outside measured, human time.

Sequence 4 : The Climb Summary : Miranda, Marion, Irma and Edith get permission to take measurements at the base of the Rock. Michael watches them cross the stream; Albert makes crude remarks. The girls climb higher, the rocks becoming increasingly maze-like. Near the top they fall asleep, then wake. Miranda, Marion and Irma, now without shoes and stockings, walk between two great rocks. Edith screams and runs back down. Miss McCraw is seen climbing alone. Analysis : Successive thresholds (the gate, the stream, the narrowing passages) create the sense that the Rock is drawing the girls towards it. Miranda’s line that ‘everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place’ suggests acceptance of a different kind of time, while Edith’s ‘when are we going home?’ clings to ordinary chronology. Shedding clothes signals liberation from social convention.

t: Sequence 5 : The Return of the Drag
b: Sequence 5 : The Return of the Drag Summary : The drag arrives back at the college late at night. Mrs Appleyard, who has been waiting, hears from Mr Hussey that ‘no one knows... We were asleep.’ Analysis : The schedule Mrs Appleyard imposed has collapsed. Mr Hussey’s admission that everyone was asleep suggests that the rational, conscious mind was absent at the very moment of the event, an early sign that reason will not provide an answer.

Sequence 6 : The Investigation Summary : Sergeant Bumpher leads the inquiry. Edith is examined by the doctor and asked ‘Was there a man?’ Mrs Bumpher reports that the town believes ‘it couldn’t be local.’ Michael first says he saw three girls, then four. Asked what he was thinking of as the girls crossed the creek, he points to a swan vase. Edith returns to the Rock and remembers a red cloud and Miss McCraw climbing in her drawers; Bumpher fixates on the missing skirt. Search parties, a tracker and dogs comb the Rock. Analysis : Each line of inquiry looks for an explanation that fits society’s assumptions: a male attacker, an outsider, a sexual crime. Memory proves unreliable. Bumpher’s dismissal of the red cloud shows that the authorities seek only the kind of explanation that fits their worldview. The film suggests rational thinking can be more concerned with preserving a sense of control than with discovering the truth.

Sequence 7 : Michael’s Search Summary : Against Albert’s advice, Michael rides to the Rock and searches alone, staying overnight. He becomes disoriented, struggles to climb and falls asleep. Albert finds him dazed and injured, clutching a scrap of lace. Following Michael’s trail, Albert discovers Irma alive. Analysis : Michael succeeds where the official searches failed, perhaps because he is guided by emotion and intuition rather than logic. Yet the Rock also overwhelms him, rewarding curiosity while frustrating the desire for certainty.

Sequence 8 : Irma Recovers Summary : Irma recuperates at the Fitzhuberts’ home, shrouded beneath white gauzy fabric. The doctor tells Bumpher her condition is ‘very strange.’ She cannot remember what happened. The townspeople gather, demanding ‘we’ve got a bloody right to know.’ At the college, Miss Lumley calls the news ‘wonderful’; Mrs Appleyard says it ‘makes it worse.’ Analysis : Irma’s return should solve the mystery but instead deepens it. Her lost memory denies rational explanation even to someone who was there. Mrs Appleyard’s reaction reveals her real priority: one survivor with no story is worse for the college than a clear answer of any kind.

Sequence 9 : ‘Tell Us, Irma!’ Summary : Before leaving for Europe, Irma visits the college in a vivid red dress. In the gymnasium, where Sara has been strapped to the wall to cure her stooping, the girls surround Irma demanding answers. The scene becomes hysterical; Miss Lumley cowers behind the piano and Mademoiselle intervenes, slapping Edith. Analysis : Irma’s red links her to the red cloud and suggests she has been transformed. The scene exposes the breakdown of social conventions: fear of the unknown and desperation for answers turn the ‘refined’ young ladies into a mob. Sara’s literal restraint is a stark image of the college’s oppressive control.

Sequence 10 : The College Unravels Summary : Parents withdraw their daughters. Miss Lumley resigns. Mrs Appleyard drinks alone and tells Sara she must return to the orphanage. Sara is later found dead in the greenhouse by the head gardener. That night Albert dreams of his ‘kid sister’. Mrs Appleyard tells Mademoiselle that Sara’s guardian collected her. Analysis : The greatest damage comes not from the Rock but from within the institution. Mrs Appleyard’s need for control turns into cruelty, and the most vulnerable person pays for it. Her lie about Sara shows her preserving appearances to the end.

Sequence 11 : The Ending Summary : At dinner, Mrs Appleyard, dressed more softly than ever before, reminisces about Bournemouth, where ‘nothing changed – ever,’ and wonders how Miss McCraw could ‘allow herself to be spirited away.’ A final voice-over reports that the searches continued without result and that Mrs Appleyard died ‘while attempting to climb the rock.’ The film closes on slow-motion images of the picnic, with Miranda turning to wave. Analysis : Mrs Appleyard, the film’s champion of order, is finally drawn to the Rock herself. Her dishevelled hair and black mourning clothes contrast with her immaculate appearance at the start. The closing return to the picnic, filmed to resemble old footage, leaves the audience suspended in the moment before the disappearance, and suggests that nature is timeless while society can be disrupted and destroyed.
