Close Analysis of Key Elements Weir tells this story with very little dialogue and almost no explanation of what his characters are thinking, so most of the meaning sits in what we see and hear: setting, costume, props, sound and the order of scenes. The notes below follow the film from start to finish, pairing each key moment with evidence, readings and sentence starters.

The Opening and Closing Scenes The film opens with a prologue card: On Saturday 14th February 1900 a party of schoolgirls from Appleyard College picnicked at Hanging Rock near Mt. Macedon in the state of Victoria. During the afternoon several members of the party disappeared without trace... The card states the mystery outright, and its precise date and place give the impression of a true story, although the events are fiction. Over the credits the Rock slowly takes shape through mist, ancient and unmoved. At the close a narrator’s voice reports what became of Mrs Appleyard and the college and repeats that the girls were never found, while the screen shows grainy, jerky images of the picnic, as if they were old documentary film. Weir wraps an unexplained event in the trappings of a historical record. The two framing sequences set up the contrast the whole film explores. People want dates, places and outcomes they can record; the Rock offers none of these, and it outlasts every record. The dated prologue reflects a habit of pinning experience down to the day and hour, as though that makes it knowable. Naming a real place grounds the story in a map the audience could visit, making the loss feel concrete. The Rock taking shape through the mist presents nature as something that was there long before the characters and will remain long after them. Cloud shadows sliding across the Rock turn hours into seconds, making human time look brief beside it. The closing narration gives the illusion of a case that has been tidied up and filed. The grainy, jerky final footage borrows the look of an old newsreel, offering the audience a false sense of documentary certainty. The last, lingering shots of the girls leave the audience with faces rather than answers.

t: The Opening and Closing Scenes - Contrasting the Opening and Closing
b: Contrasting the Opening and Closing The two sequences are similar, but not identical. Some statements describe both; others suit one more than the other. Ideas to sort and compare: people see themselves as standing apart from the landscape, yet the film keeps placing them inside it; the girls’ youth and grace seem to echo the beauty of the bush; facts seem as solid as the Rock itself; the story is a small event set within a much older place; the landscape holds a power that no one in the film can direct; people seem breakable beside the permanence of stone; the natural world sits beyond the reach of explanation; the Rock shows how little people actually know; what we know is as fixed as the landscape. Sentence building: Weir opens and closes his film with... / The prologue and the final narration both... / By beginning and ending with... + suggest / frame / establish / return to + the belief that / a concern with / the hope that / the illusion that... + yet / but / even so / at the same time...

Picnicking Picnics are the reason anyone visits Hanging Rock in this film. The Fitzhuberts eat at a little folding table with Michael, sipping tea from fine china in near silence, while Albert, as their servant, eats apart. The college party holds its own meal, complete with a toast to ‘St. Valentine’ and Miranda cutting a heart-shaped cake. Both picnics are ceremonies with fixed rules, and they tell us a lot about how this society behaves even when it is supposed to be relaxing. Weir sets these rituals against the old, rough bush around them. Watch for things that look out of place: the white tablecloth, the china, the iced cake, the girls’ white dresses and gloves, parasols and hats, the drag with its harnessed horses, Mr Hussey’s pocket watch. Word bank for incongruity: look out of place in / clash with / jar against / sit awkwardly within / intrude upon / seem cut off from + the ancient bush / the rugged slopes of the Rock / the indifferent landscape / a world older than the colony / the wild country around them . Sentence starters: During the picnic, Weir...; The ritual of the meal...; Even at leisure, the colonists...; While the Fitzhuberts sit at their table, Albert...

After the Meal When the meal is over, Edith looks across at the Fitzhuberts and says they ‘might be the only living creatures in the whole world’. Weir immediately cuts to ants swarming over the remains of the St Valentine’s cake. The joke is pointed: the picnic is one small gathering in a landscape crowded with other life, and the moment people stop eating, the bush begins taking back what they have left. After eating, the picnickers fall back on habits that mark them as ‘civilised’: Mr Hussey checks his watch. Irma says she would wear Miranda’s jewelled watch even in the bath. Marion wants to measure the Rock. Miss McCraw reads. Mademoiselle likens Miranda to a Botticelli angel. Ways to read these moments: the colonists turn every experience into something they can count, own or label; even their leisure is a way of making the strange familiar; their habits are a kind of armour against a place they do not understand; knowing the time, the measurement or the artistic comparison gives them a feeling of mastery. Topic sentence to develop: Through the rituals of the picnic, Weir shows a society that carries its rules into the bush and finds that the bush takes no notice of them. Linking phrases: During the picnic...; Weir presents...; This shows...; Here Weir suggests...; The effect is...; The same idea returns when...; Weir develops this through...; Similarly...; In addition...; By contrast...

Thresholds A threshold is the line where one space becomes another, like a doorway between a house and the street. The film is built around two such spaces: the enclosed, rule-bound world of the college and the open, unknowable world of the Rock. On the way from one to the other the girls pass several physical boundaries, and each marks a further step away from the habits and expectations they started the day with. Threshold: boundary, border, crossing point, doorway, the point of no return, stepping out of..., passing into..., the edge of..., moving beyond. Civilised world: the enclosed and familiar, rules and timetables, protection, propriety, supervision, routine, the known. Natural world: the open and unmapped, the wild, instinct, release, danger, wonder, the unknown.

The Gate At the foot of the Rock the drag stops at a gate, and someone has to open it. A gate is an obvious symbol, but Weir surrounds this one with details that deepen it: Immediately before the gate scene, Michael and Albert, men from different classes, share a drink. The three girls who will vanish, Miranda, Irma and Marion, ride at the front of the drag, and it is Miranda who jumps down to open the gate. Miranda removes her hat, leaving it in the drag, to open the gate. Just before the gate opens, the camera rests on an old notice board, its notices faded past reading. As soon as the gate swings open, Miranda watches birds wheel overhead, and the horses rear and whinny in their harness. Sentence starters: By having Miranda open the gate herself, Weir...; The weathered notice board suggests...; The horses’ panic as the gate swings open...

The Stream To begin their climb, against Mrs Appleyard’s orders, Miranda, Marion, Irma and Edith must first cross a creek. Albert, watching from the bank, makes a crude comment about the girls. Miranda drops a flower into the water as she crosses, and Weir then gives us a close shot of the creek itself, dark and full of weed. Possible readings: The flower reads like a gift or offering, turning a simple crossing into something closer to a rite. Albert’s leering remark reminds us how exposed the girls are once they leave the party behind. The cloudy water hints that what follows will be impossible to see clearly. Gate, then creek, then rocks: each boundary pulls the girls one step further in, building a sense that the outcome is already decided.

The Rocks The last boundary is the Rock itself. Near the top the girls find a maze of boulders, monoliths and narrow gaps rather than a single summit, and at the end of the sequence Miranda, Marion and Irma pass through one of these gaps and out of sight. Words to describe how Weir presents the rocks: towering, labyrinthine, enclosing, ancient, hypnotic, looming, cave-like, swallowing, silent, monumental, beckoning, impenetrable ; the gaps work as doorways or passages . Sentence frame: At the summit, Weir frames the rocks as... and..., so that the final passage the girls enter becomes a doorway into...

Time Stops As the girls rest after lunch, one of them reads Shakespeare’s sonnet ‘Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day’, a poem preoccupied with seasons, months and the passing of beauty. Soon afterwards Mr Hussey discovers that his watch has stopped. Despite his warning about the time, four girls set off up the Rock, ostensibly to measure it. Partway up they gossip about Sara, and Irma calls her a ‘doomed’ little deer. Then, in slow motion, they take off their shoes and stockings. Each character’s words reveal an attitude towards time: Miranda: ‘Don’t wear it anymore. Can’t stand the ticking above my heart.’ – she feels constrained by human constructs of time and seeks to escape them. Miss McCraw: ‘Stopped at twelve. Never stopped before. Must be something magnetic.’ – she is dependent on time as a scientific construct and searches for a rational cause. Mr Hussey: ‘Well after two, I’d say. We’d better be careful. I promised Mrs Appleyard I’d have you lot back at the college by eight.’ – his first loyalty is to the timetable he has promised to keep. Marion: ‘I should like to make a few measurements of the rock if we have time.’ – she treats time as one more quantity to manage. Irma: ‘We’ll be back long before tea.’ – she is confident, perhaps naively, in the relentless, predictable passage of time. Miranda: ‘Everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place.’ – she is fatalistic about, even acquiescent to, a larger order that blurs temporal boundaries. Edith: ‘When are we going home?’ – she is reliant upon institutional order and patterns. Attitude vocabulary: bound by, resistant to, trusting in, anxious about, governed by, indifferent to, at ease with, unsettled by + the clock, the college’s timetable, the schedule promised to Mrs Appleyard, time as fixed and measurable, a time older than the colony, the stopping of the watches, a sense of fate . Miranda’s attitude differs from the others: where most characters measure, obey or depend on time, she rejects her watch and accepts that events happen at their ‘right time’, as though she belongs to nature’s timescale rather than the college’s.

t: Time Stops - Film Techniques and Time
b: Film Techniques and Time Weir also plays with time through cinematic devices. Action frequently happens in slow motion, suggesting time is not always linear. Compare two short scenes: Miranda crosses the stream (00:23:20–00:23:43): a young girl, in the open air, in slow motion, to the sound of pan pipes. Mrs Appleyard waits (00:34:49–00:35:08): an older woman, alone indoors, with nothing to hear but a ticking clock. Statements to weigh up: The colonists’ fixation on punctuality looks absurd beside the Rock’s age. Counting the hours is one more way the characters try to keep control of a world they do not understand. When the watches stop, so does the characters’ confidence in their own reasoning. The film imagines time as something that can stretch, pause or loop rather than simply move forward. Some characters are ruled by the clock, while others, like Miranda, seem to step outside it.

The Search for an Explanation The drag comes back to the college without Miranda, Irma, Marion or Miss McCraw. Mrs Appleyard’s first question is not what has happened but ‘Why are they so late?’, which she asks aloud as Mademoiselle climbs down. From here on, the adults’ main project is to fit an inexplicable event into a rational account. What someone says or does What it shows about ‘rational’ thinking Mr Hussey, the first to give an account, tells Mrs Appleyard and then Sergeant Bumpher: ‘No one knows. No one saw her leave. We were asleep.’ Being unconscious or asleep prevents the rational mind from witnessing, so reason is absent at the very moment of the event. Sergeant Bumpher asks Edith ‘Was there a man?’ and the doctor checks her for evidence of assault. For the authorities, the most rational explanation of girls disappearing is a male attacker: they look for an answer that fits their assumptions. Mrs Bumpher reports the town’s view: ‘It couldn’t be local... No one around here would do a thing like that.’ The townspeople decide the danger must have come from outside, because the alternative would threaten their picture of themselves as decent. Michael tells Sergeant Bumpher he saw three girls climbing the Rock, then recalls that it was four. Human memory is not rational or reliable, yet it is all the investigation has to work with. Edith, back at the Rock, remembers ‘It was a cloud... it was red’ and that Miss McCraw was climbing without her skirt, in her drawers. Bumpher ignores the cloud and fixates on the missing skirt. Bumpher seeks a rational explanation that fits with his existing worldview, dismissing anything inexplicable. Sentence starters: In the days after the picnic, the townspeople try to explain the disappearance by... The police inquiry reveals how badly the community needs... When Bumpher brushes past Edith’s ‘red cloud’, Weir shows that official reasoning cannot... The search for an explanation seems driven less by the truth than by a wish to protect... By leaving the disappearance unexplained, Weir exposes the limits of...

Costume, Hair and Undress In a period film, clothes and hair carry a great deal of meaning. Mrs Appleyard’s hair is piled high in a severe pompadour, while Miranda’s falls long, fair and loose. The police wear brass-buttoned uniforms; the working men go about in shirt sleeves and waistcoats, which in 1900 was startlingly informal. Michael wears a top hat even to a picnic.

Hair Compare Mademoiselle’s hair when she leaves for the picnic with its state when she returns. Mrs Appleyard, meanwhile, comes down the stairs with every strand in place, which will not last. Miranda: naturalistic, natural, untamed, romantic, innocent – connecting her to nature and freedom. Mademoiselle: carefully arranged before the picnic; dishevelled, tangled and in a state of disarray after it – the day at the Rock has loosened the order she brought with her. Mrs Appleyard: formal, rigid, upright, severe, restrained, carefully arranged – embodying institutional control, until it unravels in her final scenes.

t: Costume, Hair and Undress - What Each Group Wears
b: What Each Group Wears In the scenes from 00:38:14 to 00:45:56, notice what each costume says about rank and the rules a character lives by: gloves and hats for formality; jewellery and watches for wealth; flowers for romance or nature; uniforms for a role or trade; high collars and buttoned shirts for propriety. Look at Mrs Appleyard, Mr Hussey, the police, the search party (the Aboriginal tracker is dressed in a red coat), the doctor, Michael and Mademoiselle.

t: Costume, Hair and Undress - A State of Undress
b: A State of Undress Before they vanish, the girls take off their shoes and stockings, and Edith later reports that Miss McCraw looked ‘funny’ because she was climbing without her skirt. Phrases for interpreting this: shedding the rules of the college, stepping out of their roles, answering the pull of the landscape, unburdened, instinctive, exposed, vulnerable, freed from propriety, closer to the earth, ritualistic, trance-like .

Michael’s Quest Three stories run side by side in the film: the disappearance, Mrs Appleyard’s mistreatment of Sara, and Michael Fitzhubert’s private search. Michael’s thread suggests that reasoning and procedure get nowhere with the Rock, and that only someone willing to be drawn in by it can bring anything back. The question to keep in mind: why is it Michael who finds a missing girl?

How Michael Thinks On the day of the picnic, Michael followed the girls part of the way up the Rock. Asked by Sergeant Bumpher ‘As the girls were jumping the creek, what were you thinking of?’, Michael gives no answer in words; he points to a swan-shaped vase holding a native flower, a rare native bloom among the film’s imported ones. Weir follows the gesture with a shot of Miranda and then of a living swan. Michael says, ‘I wake up every night in a cold sweat. Just wondering if they’re still alive.’ Albert believes that if ‘the bloody cop and the bloody... tracker and the bloody dog can’t find ’em, well, no one bloody can.’ But Michael believes ‘they may be out there dying of thirst.’ Readings this evidence supports: Michael follows feeling rather than reasoning; he is bound to Miranda in a way he cannot put into words; he cares less for social convention than his family does; the Rock has taken hold of him personally; his imagination lets him sense what others miss; the search is also a search for who he is.

An Individual Search While most characters have given up on finding the girls, Michael cannot let the mystery go. He first searches with Albert and finds nothing, marking his route with scraps of paper as he goes, a methodical approach. He chooses to stay on the Rock overnight and sends Albert back to tell his uncle he is spending the night in Woodend. The sunset glows a deep orange-red. The next day he searches alone. Near the summit he falls asleep, and the soundtrack replays the girls’ voices from the day of the picnic. Words for analysis: drawn in by..., gives himself up to..., guided by feeling, obsessed with..., unlike the searchers who..., passes beyond..., the Rock claims..., changed by..., receptive, haunted . Sentence frame: Weir suggests that Michael succeeds in finding one of the girls where others fail because...

Irma Returns Once Albert has brought Michael down, he goes back up the Rock to trace the scrap of white lace Michael was clutching, and finds Irma. He hesitates, assuming she is dead, then realises she is breathing. It should be a moment of pure relief, yet it makes everything harder: if Irma is here, where are the others, how did the searchers miss her, and how has she survived a week on the Rock? The doctor can only call it ‘Remarkable.’

Writing About Mystery Evidence from quotes and cinematography: As Albert reaches Irma, the soundtrack fills with a hollow rush of wind through the rocks. Word gets out and townspeople crowd in, some demanding answers, some ready to search again. Outside Bumpher’s house, a man shouts, ‘We’ve got a bloody right to know.’ Mrs Appleyard tells her students they can ‘thank the Lord for this merciful deliverance of our dear classmate Irma’. Mrs Appleyard chides Miss Lumley, saying that ‘this makes it worse’. Irma lies recovering under pale, gauzy drapes. As the doctor lists Irma’s injuries, he tells Bumpher that her unmarked feet are ‘very strange’. The head gardener says that ‘there’s some questions got answers and some haven’t’. Analytic phrases: creates a sense of, hints at, draws attention to, unsettles, lends the scene, leaves the audience with, underlines, complicates, foregrounds, withholds . Mystery phrases: refuses a clear answer, leaves the question open, beyond the reach of reason, the comfort of explanation is denied, an ambiguity the film never resolves, clues that lead nowhere, the limits of what people can know, a puzzle without a key, the inexplicable, a silence at the heart of the story . Practice topic: Peter Weir’s film explores a world filled with mysteries beyond human understanding. Discuss. Possible topic sentences: Weir shows that the colonists’ confidence in their own order cannot survive an event they cannot explain. The police inquiry demonstrates how quickly reasoning runs out in the face of the Rock. Picnic at Hanging Rock sets the townspeople’s hunger for answers against a mystery that offers none. By withholding explanation at every turn, Weir makes uncertainty the experience of watching the film. Picnic at Hanging Rock shows how uneasy people become when the world will not explain itself. Linking language: Weir returns to this idea when...; A further example is...; This is echoed in...; The same pattern appears when...; This becomes clearer still in...; similarly, likewise, in the same way, beyond this; however, yet, by contrast, whereas, although.

Mrs Appleyard’s Story Mrs Appleyard built the college’s rules and its reputation, and she stands for an institution whose job is to shape and supervise young women. Her standing depends on how those young women appear to the world. When the girls vanish, and the inquiry turns up the detail that Irma’s corset is missing, the scandal strikes at everything she has staked her name on. She is a tragic figure in the classic sense: she cannot bend, and so she breaks. Holding ever tighter to status, routine and control, she unravels as each of them fails. We are told she died ‘while attempting to climb the rock’, the very place that defeated her idea of order.

t: Mrs Appleyard’s Story - Mrs Appleyard’s Nature
b: Mrs Appleyard’s Nature Her formal, ornate and old-fashioned hairstyle. The watch she wears pinned to her chest. Nearly every conversation she has turns into a reminder of the rules. Her unsympathetic interactions with Sara Waybourne. Her dark clothing and black dresses. Later in the film she wears a brooch holding a photograph of her late husband. Her belief that finding ‘only one’ girl ‘makes it worse’. Her insistence that Appleyard College is not a ‘charitable institution’. She is typically shown at her desk, standing higher than other characters, or in an over-the-shoulder shot. At dinner she recalls holidays in Bournemouth, where ‘nothing changed – ever’. Vocabulary: imperious, severe, proud, status-conscious, brittle, anxious, unbending, joyless, isolated, snobbish, exacting, repressed, formidable . Sentence frames: Through..., Weir presents Mrs Appleyard as...; Mrs Appleyard’s... is revealed when...

t: Mrs Appleyard’s Story - Mrs Appleyard’s Setting
b: Mrs Appleyard’s Setting Weir characterises Mrs Appleyard through the rooms she inhabits as much as through her clothes and behaviour, above all her study, and occasionally her bedroom. The loud, steady ticking of the clock in her study keeps her need for order audible in every scene she is in. The portrait of Queen Victoria, framed by the flag, above her desk shows where her loyalties lie: with empire, rank and authority. Photographs of her husband and forebears on the walls tie her to the past and to inherited respectability. A painting of a tiger on the study wall hints at both the force of her authority and something wilder kept out of sight.

t: Mrs Appleyard’s Story - Mrs Appleyard’s End
b: Mrs Appleyard’s End Everything Mrs Appleyard stands for depends on order and certainty, so the events at the Rock hit her harder than anyone. The night before she dies, she dines with Mademoiselle in a softer gown than we have seen her wear before. Over dinner she remembers holidays in Bournemouth with her late husband, ‘a delightful place’. She admits she had come to ‘depend so much on Greta McCraw’ and her ‘masculine intellect’, wondering, ‘How could she allow herself to be spirited away?’ Her last image is of a woman in black mourning dress and veil, looking straight into the camera, as the narrator reports she died ‘while attempting to climb the rock’. Question to answer: What does Mrs Appleyard’s need for control cost her, and others?

Unresolved Mysteries A weak essay on this idea says little more than the Rock is strange and nobody knows why . A strong one works through each unanswered question, sets out the evidence and tests more than one reading against it.

t: Unresolved Mysteries - 1. Why Is Irma the Only One to Come Back?
b: 1. Why Is Irma the Only One to Come Back? Evidence: When Miranda says she has stopped wearing her jewelled watch, Irma says she would wear it ‘always... even in the bath.’ Before the girls disappear, Irma says to the prone Edith, ‘Poor Edith. We’ll go back soon.’ Irma has no memory of what happened on the Rock. The three who are never found share an initial: M iranda, M arion and Miss M cCraw. Irma does not. When Irma visits the college again she is dressed in vivid red, the same colour as the cloud Edith saw. Possible interpretations: Irma’s love of jewels and comfort ties her to the human world, so the Rock lets her go; she belongs partly to both worlds; her return deepens the mystery instead of solving it; even someone who was there cannot explain what the Rock did; she comes back changed, a hint of what the others may have become.

t: Unresolved Mysteries - 2. Why Does the Rock Act on Each Person in Its Own Way?
b: 2. Why Does the Rock Act on Each Person in Its Own Way? Evidence: At the picnic, a drowsiness settles over many of the adults, the Fitzhuberts included. Miranda, Marion and Irma are drawn upwards; Edith calls the place ‘nasty’. Michael and Albert stay alert while others doze. Brought back to the Rock with Bumpher and Mademoiselle, Edith seems untouched by it. The first police search party turns back halfway, beaten by heat and fatigue. Searching alone, Michael loses his way, struggles on the rocks and finally sleeps. In the last search after Irma is found, the party lounges at the foot of the Rock as if at another picnic. Possible interpretations: the harder people push to investigate, the less the Rock gives them; its effect depends on how open each person is to what cannot be explained; those who come with curiosity are drawn in, while those who come with fear or procedure are kept out; it tempts people out of their social roles and into a different kind of time; it exposes character rather than acting on everyone equally; it frustrates anyone who demands certainty; no rule predicts who it will take.

t: Unresolved Mysteries - 3. What Happened to Sara?
b: 3. What Happened to Sara? Weir gives us clues about Sara that point in different directions at once. Before her last interview with Mrs Appleyard, Sara sits on her bed beneath a painting of a mother with two babies, repeating ‘This is not a charitable institution.’ Mrs Appleyard tells Mademoiselle that Sara’s guardian has fetched her, which does not seem to be true; what she actually tells Sara is ‘You will be returned to the orphanage.’ The next shot shows luggage loaded into a carriage, though we later realise it is at the Fitzhuberts’ house. Leaving Mrs Appleyard, Sara gives a small, private smile, as if she has made up her mind. That night Albert dreams of his sister, who says, ‘I’ve come a long way to see ya, and now I must go.’ Possible interpretations: Sara takes her own life, pushed to it by Mrs Appleyard; Mrs Appleyard kills her; Sara’s death is the Rock’s influence reaching back into the college; wanting certainty about Sara is as hopeless as wanting it about the girls; Weir suggests the ‘civilised’ world holds mysteries as dark as the bush; death is Sara’s only way out of the institution.

t: Unresolved Mysteries - 4. What Happened to Mrs Appleyard?
b: 4. What Happened to Mrs Appleyard? Evidence: Her last appearance is in mourning dress, as if she is grieving for her college, her reputation, or her own sense of who she is. Her face in that scene is calm and set, much like Sara’s before her death. She confesses how much she relied on Miss McCraw, and cannot fathom how such a mind could be ‘spirited away... like a silly schoolgirl.’ Possible interpretations: she goes to face the Rock and it destroys her; she goes in search of answers; she wants to be free of the life she has built; by climbing, she gives up the order she defended all her life; she follows the path Sara took, out of an unbearable situation. Activity: Arrange the four mysteries on a spectrum from mysterious, unsettling and disturbing to makes sense, can be accepted . Which do you find least and most explicable, and why?

Time: Finite and Infinite The characters cut time into years, months, days and hours, and the cutting gives them a sense of control. Most live by the clock; Miranda is the striking exception, trusting that everything happens at ‘exactly the right time’. Weir keeps placing the short, counted span of a human life against the Rock’s vast and uncounted age. Time as finite and measurable: ‘What time is it?’; the grandfather clock in Mrs Appleyard’s study; the regular beat of classical music; ‘can’t stand the ticking above my heart’ (Miranda, of her watch); the date and year at the opening of the film; Minnie and Tom rushing to get dressed because time has got away from them; ‘Blowed if me watch hasn’t stopped’; ‘When are we going home?’; ‘I’d wear it always’ (Irma, of Miranda’s watch); ‘We’d better be careful. I promised Mrs Appleyard...’. Time as infinite and endless: ‘Everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place’; slow-motion filming of Miranda; the thrumming of the Rock; ‘What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream’; the haunting pan flutes; the footage of the picnic at the end of the film, simulating the limited frames of historic film; the Rock is ‘quite young, geologically speaking’; ‘Waiting a million years, just for us’; the girls losing track of time and dancing on top of the Rock; the opening shot of Hanging Rock emerging from mist.

Organising Evidence for Essays For each key idea, gather evidence from three areas before you plan. Tick off what you can use, then note quotes, actions or scenes for each. Characters: Miranda, Marion, Irma, Edith, Sara, Mrs Appleyard, Mademoiselle, Miss McCraw, Michael, Albert, Bumpher. Symbols: the Rock, thresholds, animals, the swan, flowers, costume, hairstyles, mirrors, watches, clock sounds, contrasting settings. Film techniques: slow motion, the prologue card, the closing voice-over, pan-pipe music, classical music, thrumming sounds, shrieking sounds, science-fiction-like sounds. Guiding questions for each idea: Nature as a fundamental force: how do these elements show that nature is powerful, mysterious, frightening, fascinating or beyond human control? Rationality and control: how do they show that humans yearn for order and certainty, as opposed to the irrationality and disorder of nature? Class and civilisation: how do they show aspects of institutions, authorities, social divisions, rules and conventions? Time: how do they show aspects of time, systems, routines, measurement and cycles?

t: Organising Evidence for Essays - A Paragraph Frame
b: A Paragraph Frame Topic: Picnic at Hanging Rock presents a natural world that people can observe but never grasp. Discuss. Topic sentence: From its opening shot of the Rock emerging from mist, Picnic at Hanging Rock presents the bush as something the characters can see but never penetrate. Initial examples: When..., Weir shows that the landscape...; Through..., he makes the Rock seem...; As a result, the bush appears... Link: The same impenetrability returns when... Further examples: As..., the audience sees...; By..., Weir leaves... Synthesising sentence: Across these moments, the natural world remains... and..., always just beyond understanding. A second topic sentence to try: Almost every time the colonists venture into the bush around Hanging Rock, Weir shows them ill at ease.

t: Organising Evidence for Essays - Unpacking Topics into Sub-Ideas
b: Unpacking Topics into Sub-Ideas Is the attempt to explain the disappearance in Picnic at Hanging Rock doomed from the start? Discuss. List other ways to say ‘explain’ and ‘doomed’, then pick a sub-idea: Every explanation the community offers falls apart, leaving the Rock as silent as before. The police inquiry, with its questions about men and missing skirts, shows official reasoning looking in the wrong place. Weir builds the film so that the audience, too, is denied an answer. The search fails to explain the Rock but succeeds in exposing the searchers: their fears, prejudices and need for respectability. Even without answers, the characters keep asking, and Weir suggests the asking itself is part of being human. Weir shows that the structures people build to keep order give way when they meet the bush. To what extent do you agree? From the stopped watches to the failed searches, Weir shows each of the colony’s systems faltering at the Rock. Within days of the picnic, the college’s calm routines give way to rumour, anger and loss. Police, school and town alike prove unable to act effectively against something they cannot name. Rank and office protect no one: the headmistress, the sergeant and the colonel are all left helpless. Yet order does not collapse at once; it frays slowly, as each pretence of control is tested and found wanting. In Picnic at Hanging Rock , the respectable surface of colonial society hides what lies beneath it. Discuss. Split the topic into two halves: the respectable surface, and what lies beneath. Gather words and examples for each, then write a paragraph that first shows the polished face Weir gives his characters and settings, and then shows what that face conceals. In Picnic at Hanging Rock , the real danger to order comes from the people who enforce it rather than from the Rock. Do you agree? List dangers that come from the Rock against dangers that come from society’s own enforcers, then write a paragraph on each side. A process for time and order topics: underline the key words; list other ways of saying them; go back to your notes for examples; group the examples into three or four sets, one per body paragraph; write a topic sentence for each set; then draft. Practise on: Set against the age of the Rock, human attempts at order look small ; In Picnic at Hanging Rock , the land itself seems ageless and unreadable ; In Picnic at Hanging Rock , the bush makes the college’s rules and routines seem absurd .
Film Techniques

List of Techniques Film Techniques in Picnic at Hanging Rock Technique Definition / Effect Example in the film Extreme long shot Shows a subject from a great distance, often dwarfed by its surroundings. The girls appear tiny against the towering pinnacles of the Rock, emphasising human insignificance. Low-angle shot Camera looks up at a subject, making it seem powerful or threatening. The Rock is frequently shot from below, so it towers over and dominates the characters. High-angle shot Camera looks down on a subject, making it seem small or vulnerable. Marion looks down on the picnickers ‘like a lot of ants’; Mrs Appleyard is often positioned above others. Framing How elements are arranged within the frame to direct attention or suggest relationships. Characters are enveloped by foliage or enclosed by rock walls, appearing subsumed by nature. Slow motion Footage played slower than real time, creating a dreamlike or significant effect. Miranda at the stream and the final picnic images, suggesting a moment outside ordinary time. Soft focus and diffused light Blurred edges and hazy light that soften the image. The morning at Appleyard and the picnic glow like paintings, idealising the girls and the bush. Dissolve One image fades gradually into another, linking them. Michael’s swan vase gives way to Miranda and then to a real swan, linking the three. Voice-over Narration heard over the images. Miranda’s opening ‘dream within a dream’; the closing report of Mrs Appleyard’s death. Diegetic sound Sound that exists within the world of the film. The ticking of clocks, the thrum of the Rock, cicadas and birdsong. Non-diegetic sound Sound added for the audience, such as the score. Zamfir’s pan flute and Bruce Smeaton’s music over the landscape. Soundscape The combination of music, effects and ambient sound that builds atmosphere. A low rumble and shrieking, insistent noise during the climb create unease. Costume Clothing used to communicate character, class and ideas. White muslin, gloves and hats at the college; Irma’s red dress on her return; Mrs Appleyard’s black mourning clothes. Mise-en-scène Everything placed in the frame: setting, props, costume, lighting, actors’ positions. Mrs Appleyard’s study with its grandfather clock and portrait, signalling order and authority. Symbolic colour Colour used to carry meaning. White suggests innocence and conformity; red links Miss McCraw’s dress, the red cloud and Irma’s return. Cross-cutting Cutting between two scenes happening at the same time. Moving between the college and the Rock, or between Sara and Albert on the night of her death. Close-up Tightly frames a face or object to reveal emotion or detail. Stopped watches, Miranda’s face, Sara’s photograph of Miranda. Point-of-view shot Shows what a character sees. Michael watching the girls cross the stream; the girls looking up at the Rock. Archival effect Footage styled to look like old film. The final picnic images simulate the limited frames of historic film, as if the past is a lost record.

Framing the Rock How Weir frames the Rock is one of the most reusable pieces of evidence in the film. The camera presents the Rock as something that acts on the characters. Useful vocabulary: What the Rock does (verbs): towers over, dwarfs, encloses, conceals, swallows, lures, beckons, traps, dominates, overwhelms. What the Rock is (nouns): labyrinth, barrier, gateway, prison, predator, refuge, mystery, force, portal, wilderness. What the Rock is like (adjectives): towering, ancient, mysterious, claustrophobic, menacing, alluring, hypnotic, overwhelming, otherworldly, unknowable. How characters are framed within nature: vulnerable, subsumed, enveloped, immersed, diminished, overshadowed. ‘Through low-angle shots that make the Rock tower over the climbing girls, Weir portrays nature as an ancient, dominating force that dwarfs human ambition.’

Sound and Music The soundtrack is one of Weir’s main tools for creating mystery. Notice how each element connects to an idea: Sounds in Picnic at Hanging Rock and the ideas they connect to Sound What it connects to Classical music (such as Beethoven) European culture and its sense of measured, orderly time Pan pipes The allure of the bush; an ancient, drifting time; release from the college’s rules String quartet and parlour music Polite society, manners and rank Thrumming of the Rock A presence in the landscape that cannot be explained Shrieking, insistent noise Panic and dread when the characters meet the unknown Ticking clocks Schedules, discipline and the urge to control Electronic, otherworldly tones Forces outside ordinary experience; time that no longer behaves normally ‘Weir’s soundtrack sets the steady tick of the college’s clocks against the shapeless drone of the Rock, so that the characters’ faith in measured time sounds smaller with every scene.’ Listen for the beat. Parlour and classical music keep strict time, the pan pipes drift with only a loose pulse, and the thrumming of the Rock has no beat at all. Each level of rhythm matches a different relationship with order. The music also sets the mood of each scene. Other ideas to connect it to: the rules of polite society; the wish to be free of them; the college’s order imposed on the bush; unanswered questions and the frustration they cause. Other topic sentences for a paragraph that refers only to sound: Weir’s soundtrack pits the measured music of the college against the formless sound of the Rock. The film’s sound design reminds the audience that the bush holds forces the characters will never understand. The pan pipes suggest that the bush offers an escape from the narrow expectations placed on the girls. In Picnic at Hanging Rock , music marks the line between human convention and the much older rhythms of the landscape.

Costume Costume tells us about class, conformity and transformation. The schoolgirls: white dresses, gloves and hats suggest elegance, innocence and respectability, but also fragility and restraint. Those who climb remove hats, gloves, shoes and stockings; Edith keeps hers on. Mrs Appleyard: dark, severe dresses, an ornate, old-fashioned hairstyle and a watch pinned to her chest. Later she wears a brooch with her late husband’s photograph, and at the end her carefully arranged hair becomes dishevelled. Miss McCraw: a dark red dress and a veil to keep flies off her face. Mademoiselle: lace blouses, frills, pearls, lace gloves and softly waving hair – elegant and romantic. Miss Lumley: plaid, simple printed blouses, spectacles and muddy colours – sensible, muted, utilitarian. Irma’s return: a vivid red dress among the white uniforms, linking her to the red cloud and marking her transformation. Uniforms: the police, the doctor and the searchers (including the Indigenous tracker in a red coat) are identified by their roles, showing how society organises people by function and class.

Symbols Hanging Rock Symbolises the power of nature and humanity’s attraction to and fear of it Ancient and unknowable, it exists beyond human understanding, control and time Represents not only the external natural world but people’s inner nature: their instincts, feelings and desires Watches and Clocks Represent the human need to measure, organise and control time Miranda rejects her watch; Irma would wear it ‘always’; Hussey’s and McCraw’s watches stop at twelve Mrs Appleyard’s pinned watch and the grandfather clock in her study embody institutional order Flowers Cultivated flowers represent nature domesticated, arranged and controlled by civilisation Reinforce a European ideal of feminine beauty imposed on the Australian landscape Contrast with the wild grasses and growth at the Rock; Miranda’s flower offering at the stream suggests a pact with nature The girls carry red roses to the St Valentine’s picnic; when Mademoiselle visits Irma, Irma’s robe is covered in flowers; the red hat Irma wears on her return looks almost like a rose Albert’s dream of his sister comes with the ‘strong’ smell of pansies; in Mrs Appleyard’s final scene, a white rose sits on her desk Thresholds: the Gate, the Stream, the Rocks Each one takes the girls a step further from the college’s world and into the unknown The cloudy creek hints that what follows will not be seen clearly One boundary after another makes the girls’ path feel already decided The Swan Associated with Miranda through Michael’s swan vase and the dissolve to a real swan Like the ‘Botticelli angel’, suggests grace, purity and something otherworldly Represents Michael’s romantic, intuitive connection to Miranda and the natural world A white swan glides on the water twice and appears beside Michael’s bed once; only Michael sees it, and in its final appearance it flies away off-screen Animals The world of the Rock features ants, cicadas, lizards and snakes: strange, ancient and beyond control The world of civilisation features horses, dogs and turkeys: tame, obedient and dependent Marion’s comparison of people to ‘a lot of ants’ reverses the hierarchy, making humans seem insignificant The Colour Red Miss McCraw’s dark red dress, the red cloud Edith remembers, and Irma’s red dress on her return Suggests danger, passion and transformation in contrast to the white of innocence and conformity Clothing: Corsets, Gloves and Stockings Symbolise the restraint society places on young women Removing them on the Rock signals liberation; Irma’s missing clothing becomes an obsession for the investigators The Botticelli Angel Mademoiselle’s comparison idealises Miranda as a work of art: beautiful, pure, and not quite of this world Shows how the characters see Miranda through European cultural ideals rather than as she is Mirrors Miranda is first seen combing her hair at a table, her reflection shown in multiple mirrors Our first glimpse of Irma when Mademoiselle visits her after her return is a blurred reflection in a mirror Near the end, Mrs Appleyard combs her hair while looking mournfully into a mirror Suggest the quest for identity: reflecting, examining and confronting the self; more than one identity; hidden feelings Dreams Michael dreams of the Rock; Albert dreams of his sister on the night of her death Disconnected from the rational mind, dreams suggest connections between people and nature that transcend logic Mrs Appleyard’s Study Its clock, desk and portrait of her husband represent authority, order and the past As events spiral, it becomes a place of drinking and isolation, symbolising the collapse of her control

t: Linking a Symbol to a Key Idea
b: Linking a Symbol to a Key Idea A model, using vocabulary from the notes on mirrors: In Picnic at Hanging Rock , Weir uses mirrors to show characters searching for a sense of who they are. Again and again a character is caught studying her reflection, as if identity has to be questioned before it can be trusted. In the opening sequence Miranda combs her hair before a set of mirrors, and her face appears several times at once, a self too complex to be held in a single image. Try the same with animals ( strange, safe, familiar, obedient, ancient, threatening, beyond control, untameable, tame, dependent ), flowers ( transformation, romance, loss, beauty, youth, innocence, fragility, the domestic world, ephemerality, the passing of time, refinement, transience, grief, death, connection to emotions, civilisation, respectability, the ordered natural world, traditional femininity ) and the swan ( idealisation, transformation, purity, of the natural world, dreamlike quality, transcendence, serenity, conventional beauty, unattainable, beyond the human world, out of reach, freedom ).
Written Exemplars

t: Sample 1: Model Picnic at Hanging Rock Essay
b: Sample 1: Model Picnic at Hanging Rock Essay Topic: How does Weir depict the natural world as a source of both fascination and fear? Introduction In Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975), Peter Weir constructs the Australian bush as a place that draws people in at the very moment it threatens to consume them. Through his framing of the ancient Rock, his treatment of time and the haunting soundscape of the film, Weir presents a landscape that is at once enchanting and menacing to the members of colonial society who visit it. Ultimately, the film suggests that nature’s allure and its danger come from the same source: it lies beyond the reach of human understanding and control. Body Paragraph 1 From the opening sequence, Weir establishes the Rock as an alluring yet ominous presence that overshadows the civilised world. The film begins not with Appleyard College but with the Rock emerging slowly from mist, accompanied by Miranda’s voice-over: ‘what we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.’ By placing the Rock first, before the factual title card and the image of the college, Weir signals that nature is the primary force in the film, older and more powerful than the society that tries to explain it. As the girls climb, low-angle shots make the pinnacles tower over them, while narrow passages enclose them in a labyrinth of stone. The girls are enthralled, gazing upwards as if hypnotised, yet the same framing diminishes them, rendering them vulnerable within a landscape that seems to be swallowing them. Through this framing, Weir positions viewers to share the girls’ fascination while sensing the threat they cannot see. This is how the film makes nature’s allure and its danger inseparable. Body Paragraph 2 Weir further portrays nature as captivating and frightening by showing that it operates outside the measured, human time on which civilisation depends. Mrs Appleyard’s instruction to return ‘at about 8’ and Irma’s confidence that they will be back ‘long before tea’ reflect a society organised by schedules. At the Rock, however, these certainties dissolve: Mr Hussey’s and Miss McCraw’s watches stop at twelve, and Miss McCraw can only speculate that there ‘must be something magnetic.’ For Miranda, this escape from clock time is liberating. She cannot ‘stand the ticking above [her] heart’ and, at the summit, declares that ‘everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place.’ For Edith, by contrast, the loss of ordinary time is terrifying, as her repeated plea, ‘when are we going home?’, reveals. Weir thus shows that the timelessness of nature is fascinating to those willing to surrender to it and frightening to those who cling to human order. Body Paragraph 3 The soundscape of the film reinforces this duality, making the bush seem both enchanting and unsettling. Gheorghe Zamfir’s pan flute drifts over images of the girls crossing the stream, imbuing the landscape with an ethereal, romantic beauty and associating it with freedom from the restrictions of the college. Yet beneath this music Weir layers a low, insistent rumble that seems to emanate from the Rock itself, and as Edith flees, her screams merge with a shrieking, discordant noise. These sounds destabilise the idyllic images and evoke a sense of forces beyond human comprehension. Even after Irma is found, an eerie rush of wind through the rocks suggests that nature’s mystery remains intact. Through this contrast between seductive melody and menacing sound, Weir ensures that the audience never fully trusts the beauty of the bush. Conclusion Weir’s Picnic at Hanging Rock depicts the natural world as a source of fascination precisely because it is a source of fear. Through framing that dwarfs the characters, a treatment of time that defies human measurement and a soundscape that blends beauty with menace, Weir presents a landscape that invites surrender while threatening destruction. In refusing to explain the disappearance, the film leaves its audience in the same position as its characters: drawn to a mystery that cannot be solved.

Sample 2: Paragraph Rewrite Topic: In Picnic at Hanging Rock , the passing of time deepens rather than resolves the mystery of the girls’ disappearance. Discuss. Original paragraph (does not fully respond to the topic) Irma’s return provides hope that the mystery of the other girls’ disappearance might eventually be solved. When Irma is found, the townspeople gather together to find answers and renew the search. One man even shouts, ‘we’ve got a bloody right to know,’ showing that people are still determined to discover what happened. However, Irma cannot remember what happened to her on the Rock. The doctor also describes Irma’s condition as ‘very strange,’ while Mrs Appleyard says that her return ‘makes it worse.’ These examples show that Irma’s return does not solve the mystery and that the characters still have lots of unanswered questions. What is wrong with it? The topic sentence argues the opposite of the topic (hope of resolution) and never mentions time. It shows that questions remain unanswered, but not how Irma’s return creates new questions. It does not explain why Mrs Appleyard says Irma’s return ‘makes it worse’. It ends by summarising events rather than making a larger point about Weir’s message. Rewritten paragraph Rather than bringing the investigation closer to the truth, Irma’s return a week after the picnic only multiplies the questions surrounding the disappearance. As news spreads, the townspeople gather outside Bumpher’s house, and one man’s insistence that ‘we’ve got a bloody right to know’ reveals a community that assumes time and effort will inevitably produce answers. Yet Irma cannot remember what happened on the Rock, and the doctor’s verdict that her condition is ‘very strange’ turns the one surviving witness into a fresh mystery. Mrs Appleyard’s response, that the discovery ‘makes it worse’, is telling: a single survivor with no story removes the possibility of a simple ending, leaving the fate of the others more uncertain than before. Weir underscores this as Irma recuperates shrouded beneath white gauze, an image that veils her as completely as the mist veils the Rock. Through Irma’s return, Weir suggests that the passage of time does not erode a mystery but entrenches it, exposing the limits of a society that believes everything can be explained.

Sample 3: Essay Plan Topic: How does Weir explore the relationship between knowledge and control in Picnic at Hanging Rock ? This topic has two ideas, and both must be addressed. You might show how characters are motivated more by one than the other, how the desire for one leads to the other, or how the two come into conflict. Contention Weir suggests that characters seek knowledge in order to gain control, but that the Rock exposes the limits of both, forcing them to confront a world that cannot be understood or mastered. BP1: People initially seek knowledge as a way of gaining control over the world. Miss McCraw studies the Rock through geometry and geology – she tries to understand nature through measurement and logic. Marion wants to ‘make a few measurements of the rock’ – knowledge as a way of claiming the landscape. Mrs Appleyard’s warnings about snakes, ants and ‘tomboy foolishness’ – knowing the dangers in advance is meant to keep the girls safe and controlled. Sergeant Bumpher questions witnesses (‘Was there a man?’) – seeks a rational explanation that will restore order. BP2: Weir shows that attempts to gain knowledge often reveal the limits of human control. Michael changes his memory from three girls to four – memory and perception are unreliable. Bumpher dismisses Edith’s red cloud and fixates on Miss McCraw’s missing skirt – the authorities accept only knowledge that fits their worldview. The watches stop at twelve: ‘Must be something magnetic’ – the instruments of control fail. The doctor finds Irma’s condition ‘very strange’ – investigation deepens rather than solves the mystery. BP3: Ultimately, people must accept that complete knowledge and control are impossible – and those who cannot accept this are destroyed. Mrs Appleyard says finding only one girl ‘makes it worse’ – uncertainty threatens her need for order. Her control turns to cruelty towards Sara, and her college collapses. The head gardener: ‘There’s some questions got answers and some haven’t’ – acceptance of uncertainty. Mrs Appleyard dies ‘while attempting to climb the rock’ – the champion of control is consumed by what she could not understand.

Practice Analytical Text Response Topics Topics on The Lottery and Other Stories take the same three shapes as any Section A topic: construction (how does Jackson portray...?), relationship (how two ideas connect) and idea / message (what the stories suggest). Because this is a collection, the strongest essays draw on several stories, and often place examples from two different stories in the same paragraph. Treat ‘The Lottery’ as your anchor story: it shows almost every key idea and technique in the collection. The four key ideas underneath most topics are social judgement and exclusion , insecurity and dissatisfaction , unexpected events that expose our struggles , and the violence and cruelty beneath a civilised society . 1. How does Jackson portray social judgement and exclusion? 2. In Jackson’s stories, anyone who questions the community’s expectations is treated as a danger. Discuss. 3. In Jackson’s stories, cruelty hides in the most familiar places. Discuss. 4. How does Jackson show the lengths her characters go to in order to fit in? 5. Jackson’s characters are driven above all by the fear of being left out. Do you agree? 6. Jackson’s characters are often shut out, and just as often shut themselves away. Discuss. 7. How does Jackson reveal the unhappiness beneath respectable lives? 8. In Jackson’s stories, discontent leads characters to imagine a different life. Discuss. 9. In Jackson’s stories, characters who chase something better are seldom rewarded. Discuss. 10. How does Jackson use moments of disruption to reveal her characters’ weaknesses? 11. In Jackson’s stories, social expectations encourage intolerance and hostility. Discuss. 22. How does Jackson expose the darker aspects of human behaviour beneath ordinary life? 23. In Jackson’s stories, what appears safe and familiar is often unpredictable. Discuss. 27. Beneath the surface of ordinary life lies a world of fear and insecurity in Jackson’s stories. Discuss. 28. To what extent do unexpected events create vulnerability and insecurity in Jackson’s stories? 29. How does Jackson depict the pressure to conform to social expectations? 30. In Jackson’s stories, appearances are frequently mistaken for reality. Discuss. 31. How does Jackson portray the gap between the lives people lead and the lives they imagine? 32. How does Jackson challenge the distinction between insiders and outsiders? 33. Jackson suggests that maintaining social order is more important to communities than protecting individuals. Discuss. 34. Jackson’s stories suggest that the world is more frightening when everything appears normal. Discuss. 35. How does Jackson turn ordinary encounters into moments of crisis? 36. ‘The morning of June 27th was clear and sunny.’ In Jackson’s stories, the most ordinary days hold the greatest danger. Discuss. 37. ‘There’s always been a lottery.’ Jackson’s stories show how tradition is used to excuse cruelty. Do you agree? 38. ‘She was not satisfied with her clothes, her face, her apartment.’ Jackson’s characters are trapped by their own expectations. Discuss. 39. Introduction and Context

Overview The Lottery and Other Stories (1949) is Shirley Jackson’s only collection of short stories published in her lifetime. Its twenty-five stories are mostly set in ordinary places: New York apartments, offices, buses and trains, small towns and suburban streets. Jackson finds something unsettling in each of them. Her characters are lonely, dissatisfied or anxious to fit in, and her communities are polite on the surface but capable of exclusion, prejudice and violence. The collection ends with its most famous story, ‘The Lottery’, in which a friendly village gathers on a sunny morning to stone one of its own.

t: America After the Second World War
b: America After the Second World War The stories were written in the 1940s, in the years during and immediately after the Second World War. Post-war America prized stability, prosperity and conformity: suburbs expanded, the ideal family was a breadwinning husband and a homemaking wife, and pressure to fit in was intense. At the same time, the war had revealed how ordinary people could take part in organised cruelty, and the late 1940s saw growing suspicion of anyone considered different or disloyal.

t: America After the Second World War - Analysis
b: Analysis Jackson’s stories expose the anxieties beneath this ideal of order. Her communities enforce sameness, punish difference and turn on outsiders. When you write about conformity, social judgement or ‘the violence beneath a civilised society’, you are writing about fears that were very much alive when Jackson wrote.

Gender Roles Middle-class women in the 1940s were expected to marry, keep house and raise children; single women in the city, like the protagonists of ‘The Daemon Lover’ and ‘The Villager’, lived with the anxiety of ageing outside these expectations. Men were expected to be confident, practical and dominant.

Analysis Many of Jackson’s characters struggle with these roles. Some, like David in ‘Like Mother Used to Make’ or the restless women of ‘The Tooth’ and ‘Elizabeth’, do not fit them; others, like Tessie Hutchinson with her dishes in the sink, play them dutifully until it is too late. Jackson shows both the pressure to conform and the price of conforming.

Race and Prejudice America in the 1940s was deeply segregated, and racism was often expressed through polite, respectable behaviour rather than open hostility. Two stories, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ and ‘Flower Garden’, examine this directly.

Analysis Jackson is interested in the gap between how people see themselves and how they behave. Mrs Wilson thinks she is generous; the people of the town think they are protecting their community. Both stories show prejudice maintained by people who believe themselves to be good.

The Reception of ‘The Lottery’ ‘The Lottery’ was first published in The New Yorker in June 1948. It provoked one of the largest reader responses in the magazine’s history: hundreds of letters, many angry, confused or disturbed, and some asking where such lotteries were held. Readers were shocked that a story could show ordinary, likeable people carrying out a murder as calmly as a town meeting.
Analysis The reaction proves Jackson’s point. Readers recognised the village as their own, which is exactly what made the story so disturbing. Its power comes from its ordinariness.

t: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story
b: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story

g: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story
b: Shirley Jackson (1916–1965) Shirley Jackson was born in San Francisco and spent most of her adult life in North Bennington, Vermont, where her husband, the critic Stanley Edgar Hyman, taught at Bennington College. She raised four children while writing novels, short stories and humorous accounts of family life. As an outsider in a small New England town, she experienced the kind of suspicion and gossip her stories depict. She is best known today for ‘The Lottery’ and for her novels The Haunting of Hill House (1959) and We Have Always Lived in the Castle (1962), and is regarded as a major writer of psychological suspense and the uncanny.

g: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story
b: Why the Short Story? A short story has little room for explanation. Jackson uses this to her advantage. She often: opens with a description of the protagonist’s ordinary routine or a pleasant setting; introduces an unexpected event, stranger or disruption; lets tension build through small, everyday details and dialogue; ends abruptly, often with the protagonist excluded, defeated or trapped, and without explaining what it all means. The reader is left to fill the silence, and that is where much of the unease comes from.

t: Reading the Collection as a Whole
g: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story
b: Reading the Collection as a Whole Although each story stands alone, the collection is designed to be read together. A figure named James Harris (or Jim, or Jamie) appears in many stories in different guises: a missing fiancé, a writer, a dinner guest, a neighbour, a stranger in a blue suit. The book is divided into parts introduced by epigraphs from Joseph Glanvill’s seventeenth-century treatise on witchcraft, and ends with an epilogue: verses from the old ballad ‘James Harris, The Daemon Lover’, in which a mysterious lover carries a woman away to her doom.

t: Reading the Collection as a Whole - Analysis
g: Shirley Jackson and the Short Story
b: Analysis These links suggest that the strangeness in each story is part of a larger pattern. James Harris works almost like a demon or tempter who drifts through ordinary lives, exposing the dissatisfaction and fear already present beneath the surface. In essays, connecting stories through these recurring figures and motifs shows the examiners that you understand the collection, not just individual stories.

t: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories
b: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories

t: How the Stories Can Be Grouped
g: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories
b: How the Stories Can Be Grouped This guide concentrates on twelve stories that together cover the collection’s key ideas. A useful way to study them is in groups: Discontent and identity: ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘Like Mother Used to Make’, ‘The Villager’ Cruelty taught and normalised: ‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘Charles’ Insiders and outsiders: ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, ‘Flower Garden’ Challenging or yielding to expectations: ‘Elizabeth’, ‘The Tooth’, ‘Of Course’ The anchor story: ‘The Lottery’

g: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories
b: Unexpected Events Expose Our Struggles Jackson uses unexpected events and strangers to expose characters’ hidden fears, insecurities and dissatisfaction with their lives. A fiancé fails to arrive; a stranger knocks on the door; a man on a train tells a child a violent story. The disruption does not create the problem so much as reveal what was already there.

g: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories
b: Insecurity and Dissatisfaction Jackson shows how people feel uncertain about their identities and dissatisfied with their lives, often imagining that another life might make them happier. The protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ is ‘not satisfied with her clothes, her face, her apartment’; Miss Clarence in ‘The Villager’ once wanted to be a dancer; Clara Spencer in ‘The Tooth’ drifts away from her own identity altogether.

g: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories
b: Social Judgement and Exclusion Jackson explores how social expectations pressure people to conform and leave those who do not fit in feeling judged, anxious and excluded. Mrs MacLane is frozen out of the town in ‘Flower Garden’; Mrs Walpole fears her neighbours in ‘The Renegade’; Tessie Hutchinson is cast out in the most final way possible.

t: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society
g: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories
b: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society Jackson reveals how violence, cruelty and hostility can exist beneath the polite and orderly surface of everyday life. Physical violence features in only a few stories, so think of this idea more broadly: cruelty, insensitivity, aggressive intolerance and a lack of compassion. Strangers mock, neighbours gossip, children learn to relish violence, and a whole village picks up stones.

g: Structure and Themes in The Lottery and Other Stories
b: Endings Jackson’s stories often end grimly, and these endings are some of the most useful evidence you have. Compare: ‘The Daemon Lover’: ‘No matter how often or how firmly she knocked, no one ever came to the door.’ ‘Like Mother Used to Make’: David thinks miserably of his own warm home and hears faintly down the hall the sound of laughter. ‘The Villager’: ‘Her shoulders ached.’ ‘The Witch’: ‘Prob’ly he was a witch.’ ‘The Renegade’: Mrs Walpole closes her eyes, ‘suddenly feeling the harsh hands pulling her down, the sharp points closing in on her throat.’ ‘Flower Garden’: Mrs Winning ‘swung around without speaking and started, with great dignity, back up the hill toward the old Winning house.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘It isn’t fair, it isn’t right,’ Mrs. Hutchinson screamed, and then they were upon her. Some endings shut characters out (exclusion); some leave them trapped in disappointment (defeat and resignation); some show cruelty becoming normal. Very few offer justice or resolution.
Language and Style

An Understated, Ordinary Voice Jackson writes in a plain, calm, almost conversational style. She describes terrible things in the same tone as a morning’s errands. In ‘The Lottery’, the stoning is introduced through the same matter-of-fact narration as the gathering of the villagers and their chat about tractors and taxes. This flatness is deliberate: by refusing to signal horror, Jackson makes the reader feel the horror of how normal cruelty has become.

Everyday Detail Jackson builds her worlds from small, concrete details: coffee, dishes in the sink, the neat chairs in David’s apartment, a lollipop, a bus ticket. These details make the settings feel real and familiar, which is what makes the disruptions so unsettling. They also carry meaning: the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ repeatedly finds ‘nothing to eat’, and her lack of appetite suggests the emptiness of her life.

Dialogue and Polite Speech Characters in Jackson’s stories are often unfailingly polite while saying cruel or prejudiced things. Mrs Wilson’s generosity in ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ is full of assumptions; the neighbours in ‘The Renegade’ cheerfully suggest ways to kill a dog; Mrs Harris in ‘Of Course’ imposes her views through seemingly friendly conversation. Listen for the gap between the tone of what is said and what it means.

Irony Irony runs through the collection: a lottery whose ‘prize’ is death; a sunny summer day for a murder; a title, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, that mocks performative politeness; a mother in ‘Charles’ who never suspects the badly behaved boy is her own son.

Unnamed and Symbolic Names Some characters have no name at all: the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘the little boy’ in ‘The Witch’. This makes them seem anonymous and interchangeable, as if their stories could belong to anyone. Other names are pointed: Laurie suggests a crown of laurels, a symbol of glory; Walpole has been read as meaning ‘foreigner’; Clara means ‘clear’ or ‘bright’; Mrs Winning belongs to the family that always wins.

Setting and Weather Jackson often sets disturbing events against pleasant weather. The village of ‘The Lottery’ gathers on a ‘clear and sunny’ morning ‘with the fresh warmth of a full-summer day’. Ask whether the weather in a story reinforces ordinary life, contrasts with it, mirrors the characters’ feelings, or creates an ironic contrast with them.

Open Endings Jackson rarely explains. We never learn what happened to Jamie Harris, who the man on the train really was, or where Clara Spencer is going. The reader is left uneasy, and must decide for themselves what the story reveals.

Story Summaries and Analyses The collection contains twenty-five stories. The VCAA 2027 text list sets twelve of them for study, and they are the twelve below: learn them well enough to use them flexibly across many topics. Jackson originally subtitled the collection The Adventures of James Harris , and a man of that name (or a man in a blue suit) drifts through many of these stories. Watch for him: he usually arrives just as a character’s grip on her ordinary life starts to loosen.

‘The Daemon Lover’ Summary : On the morning she is to marry Jamie Harris, an unnamed woman of thirty-four prepares anxiously. She writes to her sister Anne, agonises over whether to wear a blue silk dress Jamie has already seen or a print dress she fears looks too young, tidies her apartment and stocks food for their new life. Jamie does not arrive. By late morning she leaves him a note and goes looking for him. At the building where he said he lived, the superintendent and his wife have never heard of him, and the couple who lent their apartment to a man in a blue suit know almost nothing about him. The delicatessen man brushes her off, the newsdealer and a customer turn her questions into a joke, and the florist, while trying to sell her flowers, ‘remembers’ a man buying chrysanthemums. An old shoeshine man and a twelve-year-old boy finally say they saw a man with flowers go into a run-down house. On the top floor she knocks at a door and seems to hear voices and laughter, but no one answers. The other door opens on an empty attic where a rat watches her with an ‘evil face’, and she flees, tearing her dress. For weeks afterwards she returns to knock, morning and evening, but ‘no one ever came to the door.’ Analysis : The protagonist is defined by deep-seated dissatisfaction: she is ‘not satisfied with her clothes, her face, her apartment’ and hopes marriage will transform her life. In the 1940s, a woman unmarried at thirty-four faced real social pressure, which explains her urgency. The recurring lack of food (‘There was nothing to eat in the apartment’) suggests a life that is empty and hollow. Jackson slowly undermines the reader’s trust in her: she cannot clearly picture Jamie’s face, nobody official will confirm he exists, and the only people who claim to have seen him (a vague old man and a cheeky boy) are as unreliable as she is. The reader is pushed to re-read everything she has said. The title comes from an old Scottish ballad, ‘The Daemon Lover’, also known as ‘James Harris’, in which a lover lures a woman away with promises of a new life and then destroys her. ‘Daemon’ can mean demon, but also a guiding or inspiring spirit; Jamie is both, offering hope and then vanishing cruelly. The casual cruelty of strangers (‘the boy grinned insolently at her’) shows how easily individual suffering is dismissed. The real conflict is internal, between hope and reality, and the door that never opens is one of Jackson’s starkest images of exclusion. Links to other stories : Jamie’s blue suit returns in ‘The Tooth’ and ‘The Witch’; the lonely single woman pinning her hopes on a Harris reappears in ‘Elizabeth’ and ‘The Villager’.

‘Like Mother Used to Make’ Summary : David Turner shops carefully for dinner and returns to his small, neat apartment, which he has painted and furnished himself with great pride. He lets himself into the untidy apartment of his neighbour Marcia (she has no key to his, and he likes it that way) to leave her a reminder about dinner. Marcia arrives late, loud and hungry, and admires his home. David serves a cherry pie, only his third attempt, and worries it is too sour. When Mr Harris, a large man from Marcia’s office, calls by, Marcia lets him assume the apartment is hers, calls David ‘Davie’, and claims the pie as her own. David, unable to assert himself, washes every dish, is gently edged out by Marcia’s hostess manner, thanks her for dinner, and accepts her key. He ends in Marcia’s cluttered apartment, hearing laughter from his own home across the hall, and miserably begins to clean. Analysis : Jackson contrasts David’s control (‘small quick movements’, ‘the neat small table and four careful chairs’) with Marcia’s disorder (‘Marcia arrived with a shout and fresh air and disorder’). David’s home is an extension of his identity, so losing it is a psychological as well as a physical displacement. His pleasure in domestic activities challenges traditional ideas of masculinity, and his passivity makes him complicit: he never tells Mr Harris the truth. Dramatic irony drives the second half, since the reader knows what Mr Harris does not. Cleaning Marcia’s apartment is David’s weary attempt to rebuild a sense of order and self. The title is ironic: the comforts of home ‘like mother used to make’ are made by a man and claimed by a woman who did not make them. Links to other stories : The swapped identity in a borrowed apartment mirrors ‘The Villager’; the home as a symbol of the self also drives ‘The Renegade’ and ‘Flower Garden’.

‘The Villager’ Summary : Miss Hilda Clarence, about thirty-five, came to Greenwich Village from a small town twelve years ago hoping to become a dancer, but now works as a stenographer. She carries a novel she read only ‘up to page fifty and only carried now for effect’. Answering an advertisement, she visits an apartment to look at furniture for sale. The owner, Nancy Roberts, has left her a note to come in and look around. Miss Clarence finds the apartment dirty and the furniture not to her taste, but she lingers over a book of modern-dance photographs and tries one of the poses. Artie Roberts phones and tells her they are selling because he has the chance to go to Paris. When another prospective buyer, Harris, arrives, he assumes she is the owner, and she slips into the role, telling him she is a dancer and that ‘Artie’s going to Paris’. After he leaves, she writes a note for Mrs Roberts and returns to her own life. Analysis : Harris’s unexpected arrival is the catalyst that exposes Miss Clarence’s disappointment with her life. She tells herself she has ‘a good job’ and lives ‘better than she would have in her home town’, but her props (the half-read novel, the occasional dance recital) show how much she cares about appearing sophisticated. The Robertses seem to live the artistic life Miss Clarence came to the city for (Arthur is an artist with a chance to go to Paris), so she simply borrows it. The dance pose symbolises her abandoned ambition, and the strain it causes shows how hollow the attempt is. The story has no climax and no change: the pretence brings only brief relief. The final line, ‘Her shoulders ached’, suggests the weight of carrying unfulfilled dreams. Links to other stories : Compare David’s lost apartment in ‘Like Mother Used to Make’ and Elizabeth’s thwarted ambitions in ‘Elizabeth’.

‘The Witch’ Summary : A four-year-old boy, Johnny, travels on a nearly empty train with his mother and baby sister, looking out the window and announcing what he sees. Bored, he tells his mother he saw ‘a big old ugly old bad old witch’ and told her to go away. An elderly, friendly stranger sits beside him. Johnny gives silly answers to the usual questions (he is ‘Twenty-six’, his name is ‘Mr. Jesus’, his baby sister is ‘twelve-and-a-half’), and his mother corrects him. The man asks whether he loves his sister, then calmly tells a gruesome story about killing his own little sister, cutting her into pieces and putting her head in a cage with a bear. The mother is horrified and orders the man away, but the boy is delighted. As he leaves, the man and the boy share a laugh. The mother insists he was only teasing, gives Johnny a lollipop, and the boy decides ‘Prob’ly he was a witch.’ Analysis : The story shows how children learn what behaviour is normal. The baby ‘strapped securely to the seat’ and the boy rewarded with a lollipop suggest a world of control and reward, yet the boy greets violence with breathless excitement (‘Did you cut her all in pieces?’). Children in Jackson’s fiction are often less bound by social convention than adults: the mother reacts with horror because that is what respectable adults must do, while the boy simply enjoys the story. The old man appears just after the boy imagines a witch, as if the fantasy has summoned him, and he is the only adult who takes the boy’s imagination seriously. Evil arrives in a pleasant, everyday setting behind a harmless exterior, which makes it more disturbing. The boy’s final explanation turns real violence into a fairy tale. Links to other stories : The stranger who unsettles an ordinary journey recalls Jim in ‘The Tooth’; children who absorb cruelty appear in ‘The Renegade’ and ‘The Lottery’.

‘The Renegade’ Summary : Mrs Walpole, new to a small country town, is rushing her twins, Jack and Judy, off to school when a neighbour phones to say that the family dog, Lady, has been killing Mr Harris’s chickens and must be dealt with. Shaken, she goes to see Mrs Nash, who has already heard. On her way through town, neighbours offer increasingly cruel advice: Mr White suggests tying a dead chicken around the dog’s neck, and the grocer and his customer suggest worse, in a tone of amusement. Lady comes home ‘quietly, harmlessly’, with flecks of blood on her legs. When the twins return, they gleefully describe a spiked collar that would cut the dog’s head off if she chased a chicken, while patting Lady affectionately. Mrs Walpole goes outside for air but feels as though she is the one being punished. Analysis : The title is deliberately ambiguous. A renegade is someone who rejects conventional behaviour; the dog is one, but so in a sense is Mrs Walpole, an outsider who cannot bring herself to have Lady killed. The neighbours’ casual enthusiasm normalises violence: Lady kills by instinct, but the townspeople plan cruelty calmly and with pleasure. Even Mrs Walpole’s own first impulse is to beat the dog, so no one is entirely innocent.
