Theme Analysis

Insecurity and Dissatisfaction Jackson’s protagonists are frequently discontented. The woman in ‘The Daemon Lover’ suffers from deep-seated dissatisfaction, anxiety about her appearance and ageing, and insecurity about her desirability; she hopes marriage will let her reinvent herself. Miss Clarence in ‘The Villager’ disguises her disappointment that she never became a dancer. Elizabeth Style pins her hopes on Jim Harris. Clara Spencer escapes her grey life entirely, at the cost of her identity. Jackson suggests that these characters’ unhappiness is shaped both by society and by themselves. Social expectations about marriage, success and femininity set the standards they fail to meet, but their own fantasies of another life deepen their dissatisfaction. As one useful interpretation puts it, the protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ intensifies her own unhappiness through her thoughts, choices and actions, while the happiness of others accentuates her dissatisfaction.

Social Judgement and Exclusion Jackson’s communities decide who belongs. People who challenge social expectations are judged, excluded or punished: Mrs MacLane for employing Mr Jones, Mrs Walpole for her uncontrolled dog, David for failing to be the right kind of man. Insiders police the boundaries out of fear of becoming outsiders themselves: Mrs Winning abandons her friend because she is anxious about losing belonging and respectability. Useful vocabulary: conformity, gatekeepers, ostracise, marginalise, alienated, exclusionary, respectability, social status .

Unexpected Events Expose Our Struggles A stranger arrives, a fiancé disappears, a dog kills chickens, a man on a train tells a story. In each case, the disruption exposes problems that already existed beneath the surface: Miss Clarence’s disappointment, David’s passivity, Mrs Walpole’s fear of her neighbours, the mother’s inability to control what her son learns. James Harris, who appears in story after story, embodies this idea: he enters characters’ lives unexpectedly and reveals the gap between how they see themselves and how others see them. Useful vocabulary: catalyst, disruption, destabilise, unravel, expose, vulnerability .

t: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society
b: The Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society Physical violence features in only a few stories (‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘The Lottery’), so think of this idea as including cruelty, insensitivity, intolerance and lack of compassion. Jackson’s violence is often: Arbitrary – based on chance rather than any fair reason, like the lottery’s random selection; Ritualised – performed according to tradition, like the annual drawing; Normalised – treated as ordinary even when it is harmful, like the neighbours’ advice in ‘The Renegade’; Entrenched – so established that it is difficult to change, like the racism of ‘Flower Garden’. Jackson repeatedly shows that the most disturbing cruelty comes from ordinary, respectable people: friendly neighbours, polite mothers, children. Children both reveal the hidden prejudices of adults and occasionally resist them, highlighting the flaws in adult values.

Conformity and Tradition Many stories show a chain of social pressure: society establishes rules about how people should behave; adults teach children what is normal; fear of punishment pressures people to conform; people come to accept the rules without questioning them; and harmful attitudes are passed from one generation to the next. In ‘The Lottery’, even little Davy Hutchinson is given pebbles.

t: Key Vocabulary for the Four Ideas
b: Key Vocabulary for the Four Ideas Jackson’s characters are an odd assortment, but the same handful of ideas keeps surfacing across the collection. The longer stories tend to weave several together; the shorter ones often isolate one or two. Knowing the ideas in advance gives you something to look for as you read.

t: Key Vocabulary for the Four Ideas - Social Judgement and Exclusion
b: Social Judgement and Exclusion Jackson’s characters are always aware of being watched and assessed, and they do plenty of watching and assessing themselves. Many of the standards they apply belong to their time and place: women are supposed to keep spotless homes, men to provide. Most of the protagonists fall short of these standards somehow, and they are nervous about it, worried that their difference will show. Few of them openly question the rules; most simply try harder to obey them. Social judgement: cultural, community, public, accepted, unwritten, expected, dominant, mainstream, collective; expectations, standards, conventions, behaviours, rules, pressures, values, attitudes, roles. Exclusion: alienation, isolation, marginalisation, ostracism, loneliness, separation, detachment, disconnection, lack of belonging. Anxiety: tension, uncertainty, dread, unease, insecurity, emotional turbulence, nervousness, agitation, concern.

t: Key Vocabulary for the Four Ideas - Insecurity and Dissatisfaction
b: Insecurity and Dissatisfaction Almost every protagonist doubts something about the life they have chosen or the person they are. Even the ones who seem settled slip into daydreams of another life, often while gazing out of a window or through an open door. Another giveaway is fussing over appearances: trying on dress after dress, finding fault with the furniture, feeling that nothing they own is quite right. Dissatisfaction: discontent, restlessness, boredom, envy, resentment, disappointment, unfulfilled ambition, a sense of being stuck, longing. Insecurity: self-doubt, nervousness, embarrassment, fear of looking foolish, a sense of not measuring up, hesitancy, awkwardness, anxiety about others’ opinions. Struggling with identity: not knowing who one is, playing a role, being torn between selves, feeling like an outsider, losing one’s name or face, needing approval, a self that slips away.

t: Key Vocabulary for the Four Ideas - Unexpected Events Expose Our Struggles
b: Unexpected Events Expose Our Struggles Each story turns on a surprise: an event no one planned, or a stranger who walks in. Sometimes the surprise seems hopeful, a promise that life is about to change. Sometimes it leaves the protagonist more exposed and uncertain than before. Now and then it makes a character value what they already have. Either way, the disruption forces characters, and readers, to see an ordinary life differently. Unexpected events: a sudden twist, a broken routine, a shock, an interruption, a change of plan, a revelation, a day that goes wrong. Unexpected encounters: a chance meeting, a stranger’s arrival, a brief conversation that lingers, an uninvited guest, a newcomer who unsettles everyone, an outsider who sees too much.

t: Key Vocabulary for the Four Ideas - The Violence Beneath a Civilised Society
b: The Violence Beneath a Civilised Society Underneath the good manners of Jackson’s characters, violent thoughts, and sometimes violent acts, are never far away. Some violence is treated as everyday common sense, like the town’s advice on how to deal with a chicken-killing dog. Some is genuinely frightening, like the stranger on the train describing to a small boy how he killed his own little sister. Even in the gentler stories, characters bully, sneer or imagine harm. Jackson does not approve of violence; she shows how close to the surface of ordinary life it sits. Violent thoughts and actions: cruelty, aggression, spite, bullying, sudden rage, revenge fantasies, delight in others’ pain, the urge to punish, brutality. Beneath a civilised veneer: behind polite smiles, under good manners, inside respectable homes, at the heart of a friendly town, in the middle of an ordinary day, hidden by routine, dressed up as tradition, masked by neighbourliness.

Story and Theme Grid Use this grid when you plan a Section A essay. Find the idea in the topic, read down the column, and choose three or four stories: usually one or two where the idea is central, supported by others where it is present. Every rating below is based on what happens in the story itself, and the evidence under the grid shows where to find it. Key: •• = central to the story; • = present and usable; blank = not a strong choice for that idea. Story Insecurity Judgement Unexpected Violence Conformity Gender Children ‘The Daemon Lover’ •• • •• • • •• ‘Like Mother Used to Make’ • •• •• • •• ‘The Villager’ •• • •• • ‘The Witch’ •• •• • •• ‘The Renegade’ • •• •• •• •• • •• ‘Charles’ • • • •• ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ •• • • •• •• ‘Flower Garden’ •• •• •• • •• • • ‘Elizabeth’ •• • •• • • ‘The Tooth’ •• •• • ‘Of Course’ •• •• •• • • ‘The Lottery’ •• • •• •• • •• Column headings: Insecurity = insecurity and dissatisfaction; Judgement = social judgement and exclusion; Unexpected = unexpected events and strangers expose our struggles; Violence = violence and cruelty beneath a civilised society; Conformity = conformity and tradition; Gender = gender roles, marriage and the domestic sphere; Children = children and how they learn adult values.

Insecurity and Dissatisfaction Central: ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘The Villager’, ‘Flower Garden’, ‘Elizabeth’, ‘The Tooth’. ‘The Daemon Lover’: she ‘was not satisfied with her clothes, her face, her apartment’, and pins her hopes on a marriage that never happens. ‘The Villager’: her novel was read ‘up to page fifty and only carried now for effect’; the story ends, ‘Her shoulders ached.’ ‘Flower Garden’: Mrs Winning calls her home ‘This dreary old place’ and thinks of the cottage, ‘This could have been mine’. ‘Elizabeth’: she believes ‘something wonderful would happen to change her whole life’. ‘The Tooth’: Clara thinks, ‘you’d think my own face would know me’. Present: David’s need for order in ‘Like Mother Used to Make’; Mrs Walpole’s resentment of her routine in ‘The Renegade’.

Social Judgement and Exclusion Central: ‘Like Mother Used to Make’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, ‘Flower Garden’, ‘Of Course’, ‘The Lottery’. ‘Like Mother Used to Make’: David is edged out of his own home, saying only ‘Guess I better be getting along, Marcia.’ ‘The Renegade’: Mrs Walpole, a newcomer, thinks of Mr White, ‘anyone would tell on a chicken-killing dog; but he doesn’t have to be so pleased about it’. ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’: Mrs Wilson judges Boyd by race: ‘Boyd will eat anything.’ ‘Flower Garden’: the elder Mrs Winning says ‘you ought to talk to her about that colored man working there’; young Mrs Winning thinks, ‘pretty soon they’ll stop coming to me first, they’ll tell someone else to speak to me.’ ‘Of Course’: Mrs Tylor judges by appearances (‘Nice people, obviously’), then is judged in turn. ‘The Lottery’: when Tessie protests, the crowd replies, ‘Be a good sport, Tessie’ and ‘All of us took the same chance.’ Present: the mocking strangers in ‘The Daemon Lover’; the mother scanning other mothers in ‘Charles’; the woman on the bus in ‘Elizabeth’ (‘Dried-up old maid’).

Unexpected Events and Strangers Central: ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘Like Mother Used to Make’, ‘The Villager’, ‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘Flower Garden’, ‘Elizabeth’, ‘The Tooth’, ‘Of Course’. Almost every story has one, so choose the stories where the disruption reveals the most. A man disappears: Jamie Harris in ‘The Daemon Lover’. A man arrives: Mr Harris in ‘Like Mother Used to Make’ (‘I just thought I’d stop by’) and Harris in ‘The Villager’ (‘You’re Mrs. Roberts?’). A stranger tells a story: the old man in ‘The Witch’ (‘shall I tell you about my little sister?’). A phone call: ‘He’s been killing my chickens’ in ‘The Renegade’. A newcomer: Mrs MacLane in ‘Flower Garden’; Daphne Hill in ‘Elizabeth’; the Harrises in ‘Of Course’. A guide: ‘My name is Jim,’ in ‘The Tooth’. Present: Boyd’s visit in ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, where each fact about his family overturns Mrs Wilson’s assumptions; the revelation in ‘Charles’ (‘We don’t have any Charles in the kindergarten’); the second drawing in ‘The Lottery’.

t: Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society
b: Violence and Cruelty Beneath a Civilised Society Central: ‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘The Lottery’. ‘The Witch’: a pleasant elderly man in a blue suit says he ‘pinched her and I pinched her until she was dead’. ‘The Renegade’: the twins explain the spiked collar: ‘The spikes cut her head off.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘Although the villagers had forgotten the ritual and lost the original black box, they still remembered to use stones.’ Present (cruelty rather than physical violence): the jeering strangers in ‘The Daemon Lover’; Laurie’s invented violence in ‘Charles’; the boys’ war game in ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ (‘We stand them in the ground and run over them with tanks’); Howard’s racist name-calling and the town’s freezing-out of Mrs MacLane in ‘Flower Garden’; Elizabeth’s treatment of Daphne.

Conformity and Tradition Central: ‘The Renegade’, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, ‘Flower Garden’, ‘Of Course’, ‘The Lottery’. ‘The Lottery’: ‘There’s always been a lottery’; ‘no one liked to upset even as much tradition as was represented by the black box.’ ‘Flower Garden’: after eleven years the two Mrs Winnings ‘had grown to look a good deal alike’; she is ‘officially a Winning’. ‘The Renegade’: the grocer insists, ‘Won’t do to have a dog going around killing chickens, Mrs. Walpole.’ ‘Of Course’: Mrs Tylor keeps saying ‘Of course’, ‘feeling as though she had been saying nothing else all morning’. ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’: Mrs Wilson’s charity follows the assumptions of her society, not the facts in front of her. Present: the pressure to marry in ‘The Daemon Lover’; David’s surrender to politeness in ‘Like Mother Used to Make’; the mother’s lollipop rewards in ‘The Witch’.

t: Gender Roles, Marriage and the Domestic Sphere
b: Gender Roles, Marriage and the Domestic Sphere Central: ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘Like Mother Used to Make’. ‘The Daemon Lover’: she begins a letter, ‘Anne, by the time you get this I will be married.’ ‘Like Mother Used to Make’: David’s pride in his home (‘it pleased him to have only one key to his home’) is taken over by Marcia, who claims the pie: ‘I haven’t made but two, three pies before’. Present: ‘The Villager’ (Harris: ‘What I need is a wife.’); ‘The Renegade’ (Mrs Walpole’s morning revolves around her husband and children); ‘Flower Garden’ (Mrs Harris: ‘Let that husband of yours do the housework for a change.’); ‘Elizabeth’ (‘Because they were not married, Robbie was reluctant to take her anywhere’); ‘The Tooth’ (Clara’s last instruction to her husband is about the milkman and eggs); ‘Of Course’ (the absent Mr Harris sets every rule); ‘The Lottery’ (‘Wife draws for her husband’).

t: Children and How They Learn Adult Values
b: Children and How They Learn Adult Values Central: ‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘Charles’, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, ‘The Lottery’. ‘The Witch’: Johnny is delighted, not frightened: ‘Did you cut her all in pieces?’ ‘The Renegade’: the twins describe the collar while Jack kisses the dog’s head. ‘Charles’: Laurie invents Charles to report his own behaviour; the teacher: ‘We don’t have any Charles in the kindergarten.’ ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’: the boys have not absorbed Mrs Wilson’s prejudice. Johnny: ‘She’s screwy sometimes.’ Boyd: ‘So’s mine.’ ‘The Lottery’: ‘someone gave little Davy Hutchinson a few pebbles.’ Present: Howard’s name-calling in ‘Flower Garden’; Carol’s ‘I want to go to the movies’ in ‘Of Course’.

Strong Combinations Community against an outsider: ‘The Renegade’, ‘Flower Garden’, ‘The Lottery’ (with ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’ for prejudice in a single home). Women and the life they hoped for: ‘The Daemon Lover’, ‘The Villager’, ‘Elizabeth’, ‘The Tooth’. The intruder who exposes the self: ‘Like Mother Used to Make’, ‘The Villager’, ‘The Witch’, ‘Of Course’. Children as mirrors of adults: ‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘Charles’, ‘The Lottery’.
Character Analysis

The Protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ Unnamed and thirty-four, she is anxious, self-critical and desperate to be transformed by marriage. Her search for Jamie exposes her to the indifference and mockery of strangers. She represents the collection’s lonely women, shut out from the happiness they long for.

t: David Turner and Marcia (‘Like Mother Used to Make’)
b: David Turner and Marcia (‘Like Mother Used to Make’) David is careful, controlled and highly organised, finding pleasure in domestic order traditionally coded as feminine. Marcia is careless, loud and hungry, comfortable taking what is not hers. Their contrast challenges gender expectations, and David’s inability to assert himself leaves him excluded from his own home.

Miss Clarence (‘The Villager’) A woman who came to the city with dreams and settled for a job. Her readiness to assume another person’s identity, and to call herself a dancer, reveals her longing to be seen as someone more interesting than she believes she is.

t: The Little Boy and the Stranger (‘The Witch’)
b: The Little Boy and the Stranger (‘The Witch’) The boy, named only once (his mother calls him ‘Johnny’), is fascinated rather than frightened by violence. The stranger, friendly and well-dressed, is a figure of casual menace. The mother tries and fails to protect her son from what he has heard.

Mrs Walpole (‘The Renegade’) An outsider in a country town, anxious to be accepted. As the community’s advice grows more violent, she comes to identify with the dog, and the story ends with her imagining the punishment closing in on her.

Laurie and His Mother (‘Charles’) Laurie projects his own misbehaviour onto an invented boy; his mother believes every word. Together they show how people misinterpret what is in front of them and see what they want to see.

t: Mrs Wilson (‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’)
b: Mrs Wilson (‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’) A well-meaning mother whose generosity rests on racial stereotypes. When Boyd challenges her assumptions, her defensiveness exposes how deeply entrenched her prejudice is.

t: Mrs Winning and Mrs MacLane (‘Flower Garden’)
b: Mrs Winning and Mrs MacLane (‘Flower Garden’) Mrs Winning longs for independence from her husband’s family but ultimately chooses conformity, abandoning her friend. Mrs MacLane, the outsider, behaves decently and is punished for it.

Elizabeth Style (‘Elizabeth’) A woman clinging to a failing career and a cooling relationship, anxious about being replaced. Her hopes in Jim Harris suggest that, like other Jackson protagonists, she imagines escape through someone else.

Clara Spencer (‘The Tooth’) A wife and mother whose identity dissolves on her journey to the dentist. Her escape with the man in the blue suit is one of the few endings in the collection that breaks free of social expectations, though it may also be a breakdown.
Mrs Tylor (‘Of Course’) Mrs Tylor judges her new neighbours by appearances, then feels pressured to agree with Mrs Harris’s rigid views. She shows how politeness can become a form of conformity.

Tessie Hutchinson (‘The Lottery’) Is Tessie a transgressor, victim or follower? She arrives late and jokes about the lottery, encourages her husband to ‘get up there’, and does not question the ritual until her family is chosen. She then protests that it ‘wasn’t fair’ and even tries to include her married daughter to improve her odds. She is chosen by chance, not for any crime, and is killed by friends and family. Most readers see her as a follower who becomes a victim: her protest is against her own selection, not against the lottery itself.

The Enforcers of ‘The Lottery’ Authority figures: Mr Summers and Mr Graves organise the lottery and keep it running efficiently. Defender of tradition: Old Man Warner criticises villages that want to give it up and insists ‘There’s always been a lottery.’ Social conformists: Mr Adams mentions villages that have stopped the lottery but still takes part in the stoning. Complicit participants: Mrs Delacroix, Tessie’s friend, chooses a stone so large she needs both hands; Bill Hutchinson silences his wife; the children gather stones.

James Harris Harris appears throughout the collection: as Jamie, the fiancé who vanishes in ‘The Daemon Lover’; as the visitor who prompts Miss Clarence’s lie in ‘The Villager’; as Marcia’s colleague in ‘Like Mother Used to Make’; as the man in the blue suit in ‘The Tooth’ (and a blue-suited stranger in ‘The Witch’); as the Harris family whose chickens die in ‘The Renegade’; as the neighbours in ‘Of Course’; and as Elizabeth’s dinner date. He enters characters’ lives unexpectedly, disrupts their routines and exposes problems that already exist. Some readers see him as a demon or tempter, the ‘daemon lover’ of the ballad that closes the book.

Literary Device Tracker Literary Devices in The Lottery and Other Stories Device Definition / Effect Example Situational irony When what happens is the opposite of what is expected. A ‘lottery’ whose winner is stoned to death (‘The Lottery’). Dramatic irony When the reader knows something a character does not. Readers suspect Laurie is Charles long before his mother does (‘Charles’). Foreshadowing Hints of what is to come. Bobby Martin stuffing his pockets with stones (‘The Lottery’). Pathetic fallacy and ironic setting Weather or setting that mirrors, or ironically contrasts with, events and feelings. ‘The morning of June 27th was clear and sunny’ before a murder (‘The Lottery’). Symbolism An object, colour or action that represents an idea. The black box; doors and windows; the man in the blue suit. Motif An image or idea that recurs across the collection. James Harris; food and hunger; closed doors. Characterisation through objects Revealing character through possessions and spaces. David’s ‘neat small table and four careful chairs’ (‘Like Mother Used to Make’). Character contrast Placing characters side by side to highlight their differences. David’s order against Marcia’s disorder; Mrs Winning against Mrs MacLane. Understatement Presenting something as less significant than it is. The calm narration of the stoning (‘The Lottery’). Dialogue Speech that reveals character, attitudes and tension. ‘Shut up, Tessie’ (‘The Lottery’); Mrs Wilson’s offers of charity (‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’). Anonymity Leaving characters unnamed so they seem universal or diminished. The protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’; ‘the little boy’ in ‘The Witch’. Symbolic names Names that carry meaning. Laurie (laurels), Clara (clear, bright), Mrs Winning. Twist ending A final revelation that changes the meaning of the story. ‘We don’t have any Charles in the kindergarten’ (‘Charles’). Open ending An ending that leaves key questions unanswered. Clara running into the sand with Jim (‘The Tooth’). Allusion A reference to another text or tradition. The comic strip behind ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’; the ballad of the Daemon Lover. Imagery Vivid sensory description. ‘The waves ringing on the shore like bells’ (‘The Tooth’).

Symbols and Motifs Windows and Doors Represent the divide between the life characters have and the life they long for Windows offer glimpses of escape and imagination: Miss Clarence dreaming of the building ‘crowned with flower gardens’, the boy looking out of the train window Closed doors signal exclusion: the door that never opens at the end of ‘The Daemon Lover’ An open window can let chaos in, as when Marcia’s papers blow wildly around her floor James Harris A recurring figure who enters ordinary lives unexpectedly and exposes hidden dissatisfaction Represents the possibility of a different life, and the danger of pinning hope on it Linked to the demon lover of the ballad that closes the collection The Blue Suit Worn by Jim in ‘The Tooth’ and the stranger in ‘The Witch’ Its colour and confidence contrast with the greyness of the protagonists’ lives Food and Hunger The protagonist of ‘The Daemon Lover’ finds ‘nothing to eat’, suggesting an empty life David’s cooking represents care and order; Marcia, ‘always hungry’, consumes what he makes Homes and Keys Homes represent identity and security; David’s single key gives him ‘a pleasant feeling’ Losing control of a home (David) or being trapped in someone else’s (Mrs Winning) shows loss of self The Black Box and the Stones The shabby black box stands for a tradition that has lost its meaning but not its power The stones, remembered when everything else is forgotten, show violence outliving reason Weather Fine weather often creates an ironic contrast with cruelty or disappointment Makes disturbing events seem more ordinary, and therefore more frightening Can reinforce the protagonist’s bleak emotional world, or contrast with disturbing events and dissatisfaction ‘The Daemon Lover’: she worried ‘at the window, over whether it would be a fine day’; ‘The Lottery’: ‘clear and sunny, with the fresh warmth of a full-summer day’; ‘Flower Garden’: ‘It seems as though spring would never come... I get so tired of the cold’; ‘Elizabeth’: a dream of ‘a hot sunny garden’, then ‘it was raining’; ‘The Tooth’: ‘she ran barefoot through hot sand’; ‘Like Mother Used to Make’: papers ‘blown wildly around the floor’ Children Reveal the hidden prejudices and cruelty of the adults around them Sometimes resist adult attitudes, exposing their absurdity ‘Flower Garden’: Howard’s taunting of Billy Jones repeats what he has heard from the adults, yet his simple wish to keep playing with Davey shows up how needless his mother’s coldness to Mrs MacLane is ‘The Witch’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, ‘Charles’ and ‘The Lottery’ all show children absorbing, testing or exposing adult values Gardens and Flowers In ‘Flower Garden’, the garden represents Mrs MacLane’s independence and her friendship with Mrs Winning Its growth through the work of Mr Jones becomes the cause of her exclusion Names Unnamed characters seem anonymous and universal Symbolic names (Laurie, Clara, Winning, Walpole) carry ironic meaning
Written Exemplars

t: Sample 1: Model The Lottery and Other Stories Paragraph
b: Sample 1: Model The Lottery and Other Stories Paragraph Topic: Jackson’s characters are driven above all by the fear of being left out. Do you agree? This paragraph uses a structure that works well for a collection: topic sentence, story one, link, story two, synthesising sentence. In many of her stories, Jackson depicts characters whose need for social acceptance is so strong that they repress or lie about aspects of themselves to appear more desirable or successful to others. In ‘The Daemon Lover’, the unnamed protagonist seeks social acceptance and happiness through marriage. Though the protagonist knows she is ‘haggard and lined’, she is unable to accept that on the day of her supposed wedding, her ‘young’ fiancé is missing because he has used and jilted her. When she finally locates him, her unwillingness to admit the truth results in her coming back to his door ‘many times’, where she is always locked out, representing that this dream is not possible for her. ‘The Villager’ also features a character who lies to herself and others in an attempt to appear more successful. In this story, Miss Clarence tells herself she has ‘a good job’ and is living ‘better than she would have in her home town’. But this attitude disguises a discontent that she has not pursued the dreams of being a dancer she had when she was younger. She compulsively lies to a stranger that she is a ‘dancer’, revealing her desire to be seen as someone more accomplished and interesting than she believes herself to be. At the story’s end, Jackson describes how the protagonist’s ‘shoulders ached’, symbolically representing the burden of carrying dissatisfaction. Through these examples, Jackson demonstrates that the desire to be accepted and admired by others can cause individuals to construct false identities and deny the bitter reality of their lives.

t: Sample 2: Model The Lottery and Other Stories Essay
b: Sample 2: Model The Lottery and Other Stories Essay Topic: In Jackson’s stories, cruelty hides in the most familiar places. Discuss. Introduction Shirley Jackson’s The Lottery and Other Stories (1949) is set in the most familiar places imaginable: city apartments, trains, small-town streets and village squares. Yet beneath these ordinary surfaces Jackson uncovers cruelty that is all the more disturbing for being so casual. Through stories such as ‘The Lottery’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘The Witch’ and ‘Flower Garden’, Jackson suggests that cruelty is learned, normalised and enforced by respectable people, and that the polite rituals of community life can disguise, and even sustain, a deep lack of compassion. Body Paragraph 1 Jackson’s most chilling insight is that the familiar rituals of community life can sanction violence, as ‘The Lottery’ makes devastatingly clear. The story opens on a morning that is ‘clear and sunny, with the fresh warmth of a full-summer day’, and the villagers gather to chat about ‘planting and rain, tractors and taxes’. This deliberately ordinary setting, narrated in a calm, understated voice, lulls the reader into expecting a harmless civic event. The tradition is upheld by authority figures, Mr Summers and Mr Graves, and defended by Old Man Warner, who dismisses villages that have abandoned it as a ‘pack of crazy fools’ and insists ‘there’s always been a lottery’. Even Mr Adams, who mentions that other villages are ‘talking of giving up the lottery’, joins the crowd at the end. That ‘although the villagers had forgotten the ritual and lost the original black box, they still remembered to use stones’ suggests a violence that has outlived any meaning the tradition once had. By embedding a murder in the routine of a village fair, Jackson exposes how communities can perform cruelty while believing themselves civilised. Body Paragraph 2 Jackson further suggests that cruelty is passed on through everyday family life, as children learn from the adults around them what is normal. In ‘The Renegade’, Mrs Walpole’s neighbours respond to her dog’s killing of chickens with cheerful, increasingly violent advice, and her own children delight in imagining how a spiked collar would make ‘the spikes cut her head off’. Their laughter turns a domestic problem into a scene of shocking cruelty, and the story ends with Mrs Walpole ‘suddenly feeling the harsh hands pulling her down, the sharp points closing in on her throat’, as if the community’s violence had turned on her. Similarly, in ‘The Witch’, a friendly stranger on a train tells a little boy that he ‘cut off her head and her hands’, and the boy responds not with fear but with breathless excitement: ‘Did you cut her all in pieces?’ The pleasant setting of a train journey, complete with a baby ‘busy with her rattle and her toast’, makes the boy’s fascination deeply unsettling. Through these children, Jackson reveals that cruelty is not an aberration but something absorbed and repeated within ordinary homes. The same acceptance of violence appears in ‘The Lottery’, where ‘someone gave little Davy Hutchinson a few pebbles’. Body Paragraph 3 However, Jackson’s cruelty is not always physical: in many stories it takes the quieter form of exclusion, enforced through polite social behaviour. In ‘Flower Garden’, the town never openly attacks Mrs MacLane; instead, neighbours advise Mrs Winning to speak to her ‘about that colored man’, and Mrs MacLane recognises that soon ‘they’ll tell someone else to speak to me’. The cruelty lies in silence and withdrawal, culminating as Mrs Winning turns away ‘without speaking’ and walks ‘with great dignity’ back to the old Winning house. The phrase ‘great dignity’ is bitterly ironic: respectability itself is the instrument of exclusion. In ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’, Mrs Wilson’s apparently generous offers to Boyd are built on racist assumptions, and her offence when he declines shows how prejudice can hide behind kindness. In these stories, Jackson suggests that the most damaging cruelty is often performed by people who believe they are behaving well. Conclusion Across The Lottery and Other Stories , Jackson reveals that ordinary social settings are not refuges from cruelty but often its source. Whether in the ritual of the village lottery, the casual advice of neighbours, a story told on a train, or the polite withdrawal of a friend, Jackson exposes a society in which violence and prejudice are normalised beneath a civilised surface. Her quiet, matter-of-fact style ensures that readers recognise these communities as their own, and that recognition is what makes her stories so disturbing.

Sample 3: Essay Plan Topic: How does Jackson use unexpected events to make her characters face what they would rather not see? Contention Jackson uses unexpected encounters to expose the dissatisfaction, prejudice and cruelty that already lie beneath ordinary lives, though her characters do not always confront these truths; often they retreat from them. BP1: Jackson uses unexpected encounters to expose individuals’ dissatisfaction with their identities and their desire for a different life. ‘The Villager’: Harris’s unexpected arrival prompts Miss Clarence to invent a more successful identity as a ‘dancer’, exposing her disappointment with her own life; ‘Her shoulders ached.’ ‘The Tooth’: the man in the blue suit offers Clara visions of ‘the waves ringing on the shore like bells’, exposing her longing to escape her grey life. BP2: Jackson portrays unexpected encounters as exposing the prejudices and cruelty that exist beneath the polite surface of society. ‘After You, My Dear Alphonse’: Boyd’s visit exposes Mrs Wilson’s racist assumptions beneath her ‘kindness’. ‘The Witch’: the stranger’s violent story exposes the boy’s fascination with cruelty and the mother’s powerlessness to control what he learns. ‘Of Course’: the new neighbours expose the pressure to conform behind neighbourly politeness. BP3: However, Jackson also suggests that unexpected encounters do not always lead to genuine confrontation; characters often avoid the truth. ‘Like Mother Used to Make’: Mr Harris’s arrival exposes David’s passivity, but David fails to challenge Marcia’s assumption of ownership over his home. ‘The Daemon Lover’: the protagonist refuses to admit she has been jilted and keeps knocking at a door that never opens. ‘Charles’: Laurie’s mother learns the truth only at the very end, after weeks of choosing not to see it.

Introduction From the very beginning of your schooling career, you have been introduced to several different methods of writing essays. Although all structures have their advantages and disadvantages, it is essential that you have a fool-proof method of writing essays for your end of year examination. Having a solid method of writing analytical essays and practicing these throughout the year will result in a strong foundation, enabling you to tackle any essay question with confidence. The key to success lies not only in understanding the content but also in being able to present your ideas in a clear, structured, and coherent manner. With a well-practised approach, you will be able to break down complex texts, analyse them effectively, and construct a well-supported argument that demonstrates both depth and clarity of thought. In the following, we will explore a structured approach to writing an analytical text response. By familiarising yourself with this framework, you will be better equipped to organise your ideas, manage your time efficiently, and ultimately maximise your performance in the exam.

Reading the Question First Before you write anything, underline the topic’s key terms and its instruction word. The instruction word tells you what kind of answer is wanted. “To what extent” asks for a degree of agreement, so your contention has to say how far you agree. “Discuss” asks you to examine more than one side. “How does Weir…” asks for technique and effect. An introduction that answers a different instruction from the one in the question will lose marks even if the writing is good.

What a Strong Introduction Does A strong introduction does three things in order, and it does them briefly. It names the text, the author and the form. It states your contention, which answers the question directly and takes a position. It then outlines three arguments, in the order your body paragraphs will follow. The reader should be able to predict the essay from the introduction alone. Here is a short example built on a question about the short story “The Lottery”, to show the three moves working together: In Shirley Jackson’s short story “The Lottery”, the villagers take part in a ritual none of them questions. I agree that they conform out of fear of being excluded, although the story suggests this fear is learned rather than felt. Jackson builds this pressure through tradition, through the language of fairness and through the isolation of Tessie Hutchinson. The first sentence is the text, author and form. The second is the contention, and it qualifies the answer with “although” so that the position can be defended. The third sentence is the outline: three arguments, in the order they will appear.

Common Mistakes Opening with a general statement about life, society or human nature instead of the text. Assessors want to see the text in the first sentence. A contention that avoids the question. “Jackson writes about a village” is a fact, not an argument. An outline that lists events , such as “first the lottery starts, then Tessie protests”. Name the arguments, not the plot. An introduction that repeats the body. The introduction should promise the argument; the body paragraphs deliver it. Three arguments that do not connect. If you cannot write a single sentence that links them, the contention is probably too broad.

Checking Your Introduction Before you move on, check four things. Does the first sentence name the text, author and form? Does the contention answer the instruction word? Does the outline name three arguments in the same order your body paragraphs will use? Could you defend every sentence of it in the next three paragraphs? If the answer to any of these is no, fix it now, because the body paragraphs cannot repair an introduction that promises the wrong essay.

t: What is Needed in an Essay
b: What is Needed in an Essay An essay is a structured piece of writing that presents an argument in response to a topic. In Section A, every essay has the same shape: an introduction, three body paragraphs, and a conclusion. Each part has a set job, and the introduction and conclusion follow the same structure.

g: What is Needed in an Essay
b: Introduction The introduction tells the marker which text you are writing about, what you think about the topic, and how your essay will prove it. Write it in three moves, in this order. 1 Text, author and form Name the text, its author (or director) and its form: novel, film, play, short story collection. 2 Contention Your answer to the topic, in one clear sentence. 3 Three arguments Outline the argument of each body paragraph, in the order they will appear. Topic: ‘The desire for social acceptance shapes the behaviour of many of Jackson’s characters.’ Do you agree? Model introduction 1 In her 1949 short story collection The Lottery and Other Stories , Shirley Jackson exposes the quiet pressures that sit beneath ordinary American life. 2 Jackson suggests that the desire for social acceptance shapes much of her characters’ behaviour, although it is often the fear of exclusion, rather than a wish to belong, that drives them. 3 Her characters conform to avoid the judgement of their communities, construct false versions of themselves in order to appear successful, and, at their worst, take part in cruelty so that they are not the ones left outside.

g: What is Needed in an Essay
b: Body Paragraphs An essay normally has three body paragraphs, one for each argument named in your introduction and in the same order. Build each one with Th.E.S.A.M.L. Th Thematic-based topic sentence Your topic sentence needs to be based upon a theme in the text, not a character. ✗ ‘Tessie Hutchinson is stoned to death by the villagers.’ ✓ ‘Jackson suggests that blind loyalty to tradition allows ordinary people to commit extraordinary cruelty.’ E Evidence Quotes and scenes from the text that support the theme. S Symbols Symbols that relate to this theme — including historical and social context, and setting. A Authorial intention What was the author intending? M Metalanguage Discuss the metalanguage the author uses around this theme. L Linking sentence Link back to your contention. Only the Th and L elements need to appear in this order — the middle elements can be woven through the paragraph.

g: What is Needed in an Essay
b: Conclusion The conclusion has the same structure as the introduction. Return to the text, author and form, restate your contention, and sum up your three arguments, this time as conclusions you have proven rather than ideas you are about to explore. Use fresh wording and do not add new evidence. 1 Text, author and form Name the text, its author (or director) and its form: novel, film, play, short story collection. 2 Contention Restate your contention, in fresh words. 3 Three arguments Sum up what each body paragraph proved, in the same order. Model conclusion 1 Across The Lottery and Other Stories , Shirley Jackson presents a world in which belonging is never guaranteed. 2 The need to be accepted is one of the most powerful forces in her characters’ lives, and fear of exclusion, more than a wish to belong, is what drives them. 3 They conform to escape judgement, invent more impressive versions of themselves, and join in cruelty rather than become its target, revealing how fragile, and how dangerous, the desire for acceptance can be.
Planning

Deconstructing the Prompt When first planning your essay, you must directly respond to the prompt that is presented to you, and consider the key authorial messages that could help you respond with insight. This involves three important steps: Find the key concepts. This will most likely correlate with the key concepts you have studied throughout the unit, you should also make sure to identify synonyms of these concepts too! Find any instructional verbs. These are words that instruct you to answer the prompt in a certain manner, in English the main verbs to look out for is discuss, do you agree, to what extent or how. Identify any expectations/limitations. These ore words that limit what you con include in your essays and set on expectation on what you should be discussing. Example prompt: ‘In Jackson’s stories, characters conform because they are afraid of being excluded.’ Do you agree? This prompt has three key concepts: conform , afraid and excluded . The instructional phrase is “Do you agree?”, which allows you to agree, disagree or argue a conditional position. The word because is the expectation to test: the topic claims fear is the reason characters conform, so a strong response asks whether fear is the only reason, or whether habit, tradition, ambition or cruelty also play a part. As The Lottery and Other Stories is a collection, you are expected to range across several stories, such as ‘Flower Garden’, ‘The Renegade’, ‘Of Course’ and ‘The Lottery’. Consider the historical context of small-town and suburban America in the late 1940s, where respectability and belonging mattered and difference was viewed with suspicion.

Contention Now that you understand what the prompt is asking, we can begin to think about our interpretation of Jackson’s message. Let’s consider the prompt again: ‘In Jackson’s stories, characters conform because they are afraid of being excluded.’ Do you agree? We can approach this in multiple ways. Here are three simplistic interpretations (agree, disagree, somewhere in between): Jackson suggests that her characters conform because they are afraid of being left out. Jackson implies that conformity in her stories comes from habit and tradition rather than fear. Jackson shows that some characters conform out of fear, while others resist. However, these interpretations are quite general and lack specificity. They don’t tell the reader exactly what you are arguing. Let’s improve them with more precise language and deeper knowledge of the text: Jackson suggests that fear of exclusion drives much of her characters’ conformity, as Mrs Winning’s abandonment of Mrs MacLane in ‘Flower Garden’ shows, but reveals that this fear is most dangerous when it hardens into a community’s cruelty towards outsiders. Jackson implies that conformity is often unthinking rather than fearful, as in ‘The Lottery’, where villagers preserve a ritual whose meaning they have long forgotten, suggesting that habit can be as powerful as fear. Jackson presents conformity as a choice made under pressure, contrasting characters who give in, such as Mrs Winning, with those who quietly resist, such as Mrs MacLane, and showing that resistance in her communities always carries a cost. These improved interpretations use specific language, engage with the complexity of the characters’ motivations, and demonstrate a sophisticated understanding of the collection’s ideas.

Extending Sentences - Connectives To create a ’sophisticated’ idea you need to avoid single ideas, all of the contentions above are singular and lack connections to other ideas. We can connect them together using three simple connectives (and their advanced synonyms!) Useful Conjunctions and Their Purposes Conjunction Purpose Synonyms Because This conjunction explains why the information you have stated is true, demonstrating greater understanding of the author’s purpose. As, as a result of, considering, being, for, through, seeing as. But This conjunction adds contradictory information, allowing for greater debate. However, nevertheless, yet, despite, even so, nonetheless, except. So This conjunction allows for inferencing the cause and effect of the statement, which demonstrates greater thinking and ideas about the text. Therefore, consequently, accordingly, leading to. From here, we can take these singular idea contentions and extend them with these connectives in order to make multi-idea contentions that can create sophisticated links between ideas:
Topic Sentences Now we can create topic sentences that allow to explore complex ideas linked using BECAUSE, BUT & so.

t: Authorial Message/Intent - NOT PLOT OR CHAPTER!
b: Authorial Message/Intent - NOT PLOT OR CHAPTER! The sentence should be focused on an authorial message, not just a concept or character­ make the author active -the most common start is the author + verb: E.g Jackson explores/communicates/illustrates etc.

b: Authorial Verbs Analytical Verbs for Text Analysis Conveys Explores Demonstrates Emphasises Communicates Depicts Illustrates Challenges Identifies Frames Reveals Highlights States Implies Suggests Underlines

t: Authorial Message/Intent - NOT PLOT OR CHAPTER! - Prepositional Phrases
b: Prepositional Phrases Another way to structure this sentence is to use a prepositional phrase at the beginning of the sentence that introduces ideas to vary your sentence structure: Throughout the collection, Jackson explores.. Textual Analysis Phrases and Sentence Starters Throughout By (authorial verb) In keeping with With an eye to Through From the outset In the absence of Under the By Beyond the Within the To the extent During Concerning the Without

t: Authorial Message/Intent - NOT PLOT OR CHAPTER! - Specificity and Relevancy
b: Specificity and Relevancy Examiners punish vague or general statements, especially those that lack clear links to the topic or the author’s message. For example: By showing that characters want to fit in, Jackson shows that conformity matters in her stories. This is not technically incorrect, but it is far too general and superficial. It doesn’t demonstrate insightful analysis, nor does it show a clear understanding of Jackson’s authorial intent. This kind of vague sentence would not receive full marks. Here’s an improved version: By charting Mrs Winning’s retreat from her friendship with Mrs MacLane in ‘Flower Garden’, Jackson portrays conformity not as a free choice, but as the price of belonging in a community that polices its boundaries. This is better. It is clear, specific, well structured, and shows awareness of the idea (conformity and exclusion), character motivation and authorial message. It also links directly to the contention: that fear of exclusion drives the characters’ conformity. The issue you will face is that there is only so much you can discuss in your paragraph from here, as you have only examined one idea: conformity is the price of belonging. To fix this, let’s go back to an old friend:

t: Authorial Message/Intent - NOT PLOT OR CHAPTER! - Because, But, So - Make a Complex Sentence!
b: Because, But, So - Make a Complex Sentence! Too often, students fail to complete long paragraphs because they are stuck repeating themselves or have run out of things to say about the topic they introduced. Therefore, if we have two ideas in our topic sentence, we can ‘hinge’ these sentences together, which demonstrates complex understanding, writing and structure. All of these are key parts of the rubric you are judged on! Here’s an example: By charting Mrs Winning’s retreat from her friendship with Mrs MacLane, Jackson conveys how the fear of exclusion pushes characters to abandon their own judgement, ultimately suggesting that a community which rewards conformity turns its members into the enforcers of its prejudice. Now, you have two linked ideas: The fear of exclusion pushes characters to abandon their own judgement. In doing so, they become the people who enforce the community’s prejudice. This provides a clear structure for an entire paragraph and sets you up to use a hinge sentence later to develop further layers, such as how this pattern reaches its most extreme form in ‘The Lottery’. By planning your paragraph in this way, you’ll ensure: Specific and sophisticated analysis Strong authorial intent Complex understanding of the characters’ motivations and Jackson’s critique of conformity in post-war American communities

Interrogating the Topic Every Section A topic is new, and every topic is more than a single concept. The exam will never ask “tell me everything the author says about punishment”. It will modify the concept, by asking about its causes, its consequences, its impact, or its relationship with another idea. Reading time is where you take the topic apart before you commit to a contention.

t: Questions to Ask of Every Topic
b: Questions to Ask of Every Topic Absolutes. Look for words such as all , no one , only , always . Is the claim true for everyone in the text? If not, who is the exception, and why (class, gender, race, belief, family)? Modifiers. Adverbs and adjectives change the question. “Punished” and “justly punished” are different essays. “Moments” and “lasting, ordinary moments” are different essays. Define each modifier before you plan. Connotation. “Fear that is justified” is not “irrational fear”. “Infatuation with youth” implies shallowness and impermanence that “love of youth” does not. Comparison. Most , more than , as guilty as , strongest : these words require you to weigh one thing against another, not discuss one thing alone. Connections. “Change is inevitable” implies nothing can stay the same. “Interplay” means two ideas act on each other, not a one-way cause. The verb. Celebrates , condemns , warns , mocks each tell you the author’s attitude. Do not flatten them into “presents”.

Two Kinds of Quotation Topic Quotation topics do not all work the same way, so read them closely. The quote as a key moment. The quote is attached to a question (“How is the idea of truth explored?”). The panel has chosen a passage that matters to the question. Decide where it fits in your sequence of ideas and discuss it there. The quote as the proposition. The quote is the claim you are asked to assess (“To what extent does the author demonstrate this to be true?”). Here the quote is the topic. Treating it as one piece of evidence would mean missing the question entirely.

Ordering Is Not Connecting “Firstly”, “secondly”, “initially”, “subsequently” put paragraphs in order. They do not explain how one idea relates to the next. A connection says why paragraph two follows paragraph one: it builds on it, qualifies it, complicates it, or shows its consequence. Before you write, check two things in your plan: that every topic sentence answers the topic, and that you can state the link between each pair of paragraphs in one phrase.

Concepts Worth Rehearsing Recent Section A topics have centred on concepts such as hardship, home, control, social convention, threat, knowledge, punishment, truth, choice and privilege. The panel can and does introduce new ones. A useful revision routine: take each concept, ask what your text says about it, then ask what it says about the concept’s causes, its consequences, and its relationship to a second concept. You build knowledge and practise the skill at the same time.

The Dynamics of a Text The study design asks you to analyse the dynamics of a text. These are lenses for knowing your text so well that any topic can be answered. They do not sit in separate boxes: a character’s motivation usually connects to a tension, a setting or a point of view. Make one page of notes for each lens, with evidence.

1. Character Motivations Ask why each character does what they do. Is the drive emotional (fear, anger, joy), moral (duty, loyalty, compassion), self-image (wanting to seem good or honourable), or cultural, religious and social (beliefs strong enough to compel action)? Note where motivation changes : a character driven by money early may be driven by conscience later. One quotation can support several readings. When Old Man Warner insists, “There’s always been a lottery”, his loyalty could be read as reverence for tradition, as fear of change (he warns that without it “they’ll be wanting to go back to living in caves”), as pride in his own status (“Seventy-seventh year I been in the lottery”), or as superstition about the harvest (“Lottery in June, corn be heavy soon”). Choose the reading the topic needs, and use the words of the quote as your evidence for it. For Picnic at Hanging Rock , try the same exercise with Mrs Appleyard’s decision to send Sara back to the orphanage, Michael’s search on the Rock, or Irma’s return.

2. Tensions in Relationships Tension is the friction between two characters: betrayal, misunderstanding, conflicting desires, secrecy, trauma, gender expectations, social order. Look at the language a character uses about the other. Line up the key relationships and note what rubs them against each other and whether it is resolved.

3. The Function of Settings Naming the setting in your introduction earns little. Explaining what a setting does earns a great deal. Ask: of all places, why this one? Does it mirror a character’s mood, or contrast with it to raise tension? Does it confine characters or free them? Does it give someone authority or take it away? Useful phrasing: “the setting functions as a physical manifestation of”, “the confined setting reinforces”, “the setting intensifies the conflict between”. For Picnic at Hanging Rock , the Rock functions as an ancient, indifferent force that dwarfs the girls, while Appleyard College functions as a fortress of imported order. For The Lottery and Other Stories , the sunny village square makes the ritual feel routine, and in ‘Flower Garden’ the cottage and its garden stand for the life Mrs Winning gave up.

4. The Complexities of the Plot Map the plot on one large page. Is it linear or non-linear? Are there flashbacks, flash-forwards, frame narratives, dream sequences, circular endings? Then ask why the author chose this sequence. A structural choice (the title card and slow-motion picnic that frame Picnic at Hanging Rock ; the calm, ordinary build-up of ‘The Lottery’ before the stoning) is evidence you can use.

t: 5. The Role of Point of View
b: 5. The Role of Point of View Whose voice do we hear? Whose perspective are we denied? Is the narrator reliable, and how do we know? Do characters see the same person differently? Does the audience know things characters do not (dramatic irony)? Useful phrasing: “by aligning the audience with”, “the limited perspective heightens”, “from Mrs Walpole’s point of view, however”.

Beyond the Dynamics The study design also names: ideas, concerns and conflicts (not “themes”: turn a theme into the concerns and conflicts it raises); structures and language features (symbolism, dramatic irony, parallel plots, repetition, stage directions, film techniques), always explained for how and why ; and the historical, social and cultural values of the world of the text, used as evidence in body paragraphs rather than only as a line in the introduction.

Connect the Lenses Once each lens has its own page, link them. A mind map or colour coding works well: mark the quotes that serve more than one lens (a line that reveals a motivation and uses a key language feature), because those are the most flexible pieces of evidence on exam day. Some lenses will matter more for your text than others; that is expected.

Five Ways to Substantiate No assessor counts types of evidence. But a response that draws on only quotations shows a narrower range than one that also uses characters, structure, plot, setting, language features and context. Quality beats quantity: each piece of evidence must be explained, not just included.
Writing the Introduction

Topics There are three types of questions you may receive on a SAC or exam. These are the ’Discuss’, ’To what extent’ and ’Do you agree?’ statements. These are all tackled in a slightly varying manner. Discuss : This is probably the most common type of prompt that you will encounter. When dealing with such prompts, it is important that you discuss as many aspects of it as possible. One way to improve your discussion here is to include a paragraph that rebuts the prompt, like what you do in your persuasive essays. However, since it is a discuss prompt, you do not need to make the two sides of your argument extremely distinct. To what extent: These topics require you to make a decision. Never say ’it is to some extent’ in your contention. You really need to assign a portion of something. The best way to do this is to start with subordinating conjunctions like ’whilst” or ’although”. To What Extent questions rarely want you to agree or disagree - they want you to explore a shade of grey. How: The ’How’ topics usually focus on the construction of a text - your evidence should contain metalanguage like ’characterisation’ for instance.

Introduction The introduction is the first piece of your writing that will be examined. For this reason, it should be clear, direct and show your understanding of the topic. The introduction is there to show your examiner how you wish to respond to the set topic. If your topic contains a quote, ensure that you mention it somewhere in your introduction to show you are addressing the topic.

Writing Body Paragraphs

Body Paragraphs The body paragraphs form majority of your essay. The body paragraphs are the main reasons that the contention your provided is true. Your body paragraphs need to be able to demonstrate your understanding of the text and the fluency of your language. You should ensure that every sentence (and thus every word) brings something towards your argument.

Structure Below is the structure for a body paragraph using ’Th.E. S.A.M.L.’ Method. This method of writing body paragraphs was developed in order to maximise possible marks. Only the ’TH’ and ’L’ elements of this structure need to be in the order given. Th Thematic-based topic sentence Your topic sentence needs to be based upon a theme in the text, not a character. ✗ ‘Tessie Hutchinson is stoned to death by the villagers.’ ✓ ‘Jackson suggests that blind loyalty to tradition allows ordinary people to commit extraordinary cruelty.’ E Evidence Quotes and scenes from the text that support the theme. S Symbols Symbols that relate to this theme — including historical and social context, and setting. A Authorial intention What was the author intending? M Metalanguage Discuss the metalanguage the author uses around this theme. L Linking sentence Link back to your contention. Only the Th and L elements need to appear in this order — the middle elements can be woven through the paragraph.

Basic Example ’Th.E S.A.M’ Jackson suggests that blind loyalty to tradition allows ordinary people to commit extraordinary cruelty. In ‘The Lottery’, Old Man Warner insists that “There’s always been a lottery”, dismissing the villages that have given it up as a “Pack of crazy fools”. The battered black box, which the villagers refuse to replace even as it grows “shabbier each year”, symbolises a ritual whose meaning has decayed while its authority remains. Writing in the years after the Second World War, Jackson warns that cruelty is most dangerous when it is habitual and shared. Her flat, matter-of-fact narration of the stoning, in which “someone gave little Davy Hutchinson a few pebbles”, makes the violence more disturbing by presenting it as ordinary. In this way, Jackson shows that loyalty to tradition can blind a community to its own cruelty.

t: Writing About Ideas: Adding Adjectives to Nouns
b: Writing About Ideas: Adding Adjectives to Nouns One of the easiest ways of improving your writing is to add adjectives to nouns, this helps us to create an ’idea phrase’. Hinge Sentences In your topic sentence, you can introduce two related ideas. This creates room for a more complex, insightful paragraph. But remember: when you shift focus from the first idea to the second, you must signal this change to the reader clearly. This is where the hinge sentence comes in. A hinge sentence acts like a bridge: it acknowledges what you’ve already explored, then transitions to the second idea you introduced in your topic sentence. Here’s how that works: By charting Mrs Winning’s retreat from her friendship with Mrs MacLane, Jackson conveys how the fear of exclusion pushes characters to abandon their own judgement, ultimately suggesting that a community which rewards conformity turns its members into the enforcers of its prejudice.

t: Hinge Sentences - Evidence + Analysis of First Idea
b: Evidence + Analysis of First Idea In ‘Flower Garden’, Mrs Winning’s friendship with Mrs MacLane survives only until the town begins to disapprove of Mrs MacLane hiring Mr Jones. When her mother-in-law urges her to “talk to her about that colored man working there”, Mrs Winning’s private thoughts reveal what really moves her: “pretty soon they’ll stop coming to me first, they’ll tell someone else to speak to me.” Jackson shows that her concern is not for her friend, or even for what is right, but for her own place in the community.

t: Hinge Sentences - Hinge Sentence (transitioning to Second idea)
b: Hinge Sentence (transitioning to Second idea) However, Jackson does not leave Mrs Winning as a mere victim of social pressure; she shows her becoming its agent.

t: Hinge Sentences - Analysis of Second Idea
b: Analysis of Second Idea When Mrs MacLane asks whether the town’s coldness is “because of Mr. Jones working here”, Mrs Winning denies it, then privately thinks, “The nerve of her, trying to blame the colored folks.” Having absorbed the town’s prejudice, she now voices it as her own. Her final gesture, as she “swung around without speaking and started, with great dignity, back up the hill toward the old Winning house”, is deeply ironic: the “dignity” she preserves is the dignity of belonging, bought at the cost of her friend. By using a hinge sentence, you show your reader that you’re not just stacking ideas but developing an argument, deepening your interpretation, and showing the author’s nuanced message. Concluding Dependant Phrases Paired with Analytic Verbs Concluding Dependant Phrase Analytic Verb Even if Jackson recognises... questions... Whilst Weir endorses... illustrates... Whether or not Jackson implies... reveals... In order to explore ... Weir ... demonstrates...
Writing the Conclusion

Conclusion If you think of a conclusion as less of summarising everything, and more of combining all of these conflicting ideas and messages into one overall conclusive point. We can do this by using the following structure.

Structure The structure for a conclusion can follow the same structure as an introduction. However, instead of introducing the text, you are concluding your discussion. Here is an alternative method: Topic: ‘In Jackson’s stories, characters conform because they are afraid of being excluded.’ Do you agree? Conclusion Structure for Analytical Essay Writing Purpose in Conclusion Example Sentence Overview of how the whole text demonstrates the key concepts in the essay topic Fundamentally, The Lottery and Other Stories explores the pressure to belong, and how readily ordinary people give up their own judgement to avoid standing apart. Summary of the complications of this topic Throughout the collection, Jackson complicates the idea that fear alone drives conformity, showing that habit, tradition and the pleasure of belonging can be just as powerful, as the villagers of ‘The Lottery’ reveal. Focus on the key authorial message in conclusive language Therefore, Jackson warns that a community which punishes difference turns its members into the enforcers of its prejudice, as Mrs Winning becomes in ‘Flower Garden’.
