t: Strapleton Community Voice: Public Post by Daphne Lower
b: Strapleton Community Voice: Public Post by Daphne Lower Background information The website Strapleton Community Voice has a social media page for the exclusive use of residents of the town of Strapleton. Members use Strapleton Community Voice to share information and concerns about the local area. Daphne Lower is a member of the group and created the post on the following page. Strapleton Community Voice Public group 11,727 followers Daphne Lower 2 October at 11:35 I want to share with you a dilemma I encountered this morning as I was taking my usual stroll around our picturesque park and lovely lake area. I noticed a new sign near the water saying: DO NOT FEED THE BIRDS. Metres away from the new sign stood a man and two children busily feeding a flock of wild ducks, totally ignoring the very clear message not to do so. What should I do, if anything? This is what went through my mind … When I was growing up, we often fed wild birds. My mum had a little wooden bird feeder hanging from a tree in our front yard. Every morning, she’d lower the rope attached to the bird feeder, place a sprinkling of seed inside and carefully hoist it back up. That bird feeder attracted all sorts of beloved parrots and we would watch them, in awe of their majesty. On family trips to the beach, we’d eat hot chips and throw some to the swarm of seagulls begging at our feet. Even on the few times we ventured overseas, we saw lots of people donating scraps of their lunch to pigeons or scattering bread for the ducks at the local park. Everybody, everywhere, fed wild birds back then. Today, millions of Australians continue to feed wild birds. Why do we do it? It’s easy to see why we do it. Feeding birds feels like an act of kindness and seems to be mutually beneficial. We help the birds survive and, in return, we get enjoyment, feeling as though we are giving back to our community and connecting with the world around us. Taking time to appreciate nature is a great way to improve psychological wellbeing. In our increasingly technology-saturated world, it’s healthy and happy, even uplifting, to unplug and recharge. The duck-feeding dad probably worked pretty hard to coax his kids away from their screens in order to do something outdoors for a change. Unfortunately, despite the immense health benefits that humans gain from feeding birds, the same can’t be said for the birds! Yes, in some parts of the world, certain species of birds would not survive the long winter without humans lending a helping hand. But I wish more people understood that supplementary feeding, even though it might feel like an act of love and nurturing, is often the opposite. Giving wildlife the wrong food in the wrong amount isn’t only unhelpful, it can be downright dangerous. This is the reason I am posting today. I have read that wildlife experts agree that supplementary feeding creates an imbalance in nature that can have drastic consequences. It increases the numbers of some species and this, in turn, decreases those of other species. The rainbow lorikeet, for example, has taken great advantage of its good looks, so its numbers have soared due to supplementary feeding. Sadly, the rainbow lorikeet’s population boom has caused numbers of the much plainer scaly-breasted lorikeet to plummet. Even the most well-intentioned bird lover can upset Mother Nature without meaning to do so. Left uneaten in damp conditions, seeds and bread rot, grow mould and introduce disease to the birds. The uneaten food also attracts pests such as rats, mice and cockroaches. The more food these pests get, the more they breed. Feeding birds is unnecessary. Native birds will be healthy and happy if left to eat only their normal diet of insects, nectar, seed or fruit. Most people don’t realise that bread — the most popular choice of food to give to wild birds — is actually one of the worst things to feed to wild birds because it contains huge quantities of sugar and salt. But should we put Strapleton’s ducks on a diet or ban bird feeding altogether? Perhaps the real problem is not so much that we are feeding wild birds, but rather that people don’t understand how often, how much and what to feed them. Seeds, duck pellets, a sprinkle of oats or a small handful of peas or corn are acceptable options. If you must feed the birds in our neighbourhood, PLEASE try to do so as an occasional treat, not as an everyday occurrence. Think of it as giving them a healthy snack, not a five-course meal! As I watched those kids and their dad endlessly lob carbs into our beautiful, clean lake, the wild ducks scrambled over one another to fight for every doughy morsel that they could stuff their beaks with. I wrestled with my conscience. I didn’t want to start a confrontation or accuse the dad and his kids of committing a crime against nature, but I desperately wanted to take them under my wing and politely explain a few choices that we can make to better care for our feathered friends. Hence my dilemma … What action would you have taken?

t: Our Local Gym: Emergency Meeting Speech by Sandy Gestalt
b: Our Local Gym: Emergency Meeting Speech by Sandy Gestalt Background information Our Local Gym is a fitness centre that caters to a local community. Until recently, the facility was supported by a council subsidy. This funding has been withdrawn and reallocated to other council projects. The Our Local Gym committee has called an emergency meeting for members of the gym to vote on a proposal to keep the facilities operating. The chair of the Our Local Gym committee, Sandy Gestalt, presented the following speech with accompanying slides. Thank you for attending this emergency meeting to vote on the future of Our Local Gym. We find ourselves in an uncomfortable position, but as a group of people who have worked together – worked out together – for years, we know that together we can save Our Local Gym, and ensure its future. Before we move on to possible solutions to our situation, I want to acknowledge the history and the value of Our Local Gym to both you, our members, and to the wider community. Our Local Gym has been in operation for 47 years. We built it from scratch with council support, local fundraisers and fees from you, our members. We have, for years, been a safe space for all people, and for the young and young-at-heart. This space is where you have built your fitness, your strength and your confidence. While larger commercial gyms have flourished, they cater for a different clientele – for people who perhaps are looking for a more competitive place to achieve their fitness goals. People who flock like moths to the flame to shiny new equipment, giant flatscreen TVs, obnoxiously loud music, matching athleisure wear – and who love posting gym selfies on their socials. But Our Local Gym has never been that; we just provide an opportunity for anyone to experience success at any level of fitness. At Our Local, we value acceptance for all bodies and all fitness journeys. We train for life. However, we have recently lost the annual council grant we have relied on for decades to keep Our Local open. As you know, we tried to appeal to the council to reverse its decision but, unfortunately, we missed the deadline and the funding has already been reallocated. The council grant was important to Our Local for two reasons: it supported the maintenance of our building and it enabled us to keep our fees low, in line with the needs and lived experience of our community. In seeking alternative funding, we have considered a series of bleak options: raising admission costs beyond what our community (including young families, refugees and seniors) can afford; privatising the fitness centre; or closing the facility entirely and watching Our Local be demolished and turned into a carpark. But we have found another option. A lifeline. We have been approached by a company about the neglected shopfront on the south side of our building. This group sees real potential in the vintage, grassroots community vibe of our building. The proposal includes an agreement that they will upgrade the shopfront at their expense, and they will pay us rent, which will cover what we have lost in the council grant. This will guarantee Our Local Gym’s low membership and admission fees, and may even leave extra funds for upgrades. The group is Long Live Lollies. Long Live Lollies is a popular confectionery company. You might be familiar with this brand – they sell lollies at reasonable prices in a retro-themed shop. Recently, their own lease has been terminated. This offers us a chance for a win–win situation. Clearly, while this proposal solves our immediate financial problems, it does present challenges. Our Local Gym and Long Live Lollies do not, at first glance, share much in terms of values. Our Local offers education about nutrition and the best fuel for our bodies and supports members of the community for whom fitness can feel out of reach, while Long Live Lollies sells foods with limited nutritional benefit. There is no doubt that bringing these two businesses together in one building presents a serious clash. Taking into account this clash of purposes – we are for community and they are for profit – I want to make it clear why we support this proposed partnership. The first is – unsurprisingly – money. Long Live Lollies have been nothing but a sweet delight to work with. They understand our dire financial position, offering us up-front rent payments that will keep the lights on and the doors open. They are keen to see our gym thrive and be part of the Our Local Gym community. So they will also pay for gym memberships for their employees – a concrete gesture that shows their support. The second: while eating lollies excessively isn’t great, the occasional treat, or sugar hit, can be a joy. At Our Local, we know that fun and laughter are as important to our health as regular exercise. This partnership can bring colour and deliciousness to our doorstep. And so, we hope that a new community will be enticed to Our Local. Perhaps parents who don’t know we exist will take their children to buy treats from Long Live Lollies, discover us – and join up! We don’t have the advertising budget of large commercial gyms. This is an opportunity to broaden our reach by tapping in to the customer base and marketing expertise of Long Live Lollies. Before we vote, remember that we are not just voting for ourselves. We are voting for the many who cannot attend tonight and for those we hope to reach in the future. This is the only viable solution, and we as a community understand the need for compromise. To save Our Local Gym – this wonderful place where we all get so much for our bodies and souls – we will need to bend and stretch some uncomfortable and perhaps stiff muscles. It will not be perfect but, if we can make it work, it will allow our imperfect community to flourish.

t: Lighting the way: a new year, a new celebration
b: Lighting the way: a new year, a new celebration by Jack Adut, 2025 Background information Every year the regional town of Timberoona hosts a fireworks display to usher in the new year. This annual tradition has been an important event on the community calendar for more than 50 years. Over the past few years, however, some residents have been concerned about the impact of the event on the town and have been seeking alternative ways to celebrate New Year’s Eve. Local resident JackAdut submitted the following article with accompanying images to the community newsletter Timberoona: Talk of the town. Like most people in our community, I consider New Year’s Eve to be a highlight on my social calendar. I look forward to participating in the many festivities held in the beautiful setting of Timberoona Park. The family picnics, roaming entertainment, food vans and showcasing of local musical talent in the rotunda create the perfect backdrop for the main event: the annual fireworks display. The spectacular pyrotechnics can be viewed from vantage points across the park and beyond, with veterans of the event knowing exactly where to set up their picnic rugs and folding chairs to secure the best view. It is with great anticipation that I await the collective countdown to midnight and the first big bang that reverberates through the air! As you can see, I’m all for the opportunity to welcome the new year with a big celebration, but it’s time to re-think the use of fireworks. It wasn’t until I saw firsthand the impact that our annual celebration has on the environment, some members of the community and their pets (not to mention the huge expense!) that I came up with a solution -a dynamic projected lightshow! Every year the fireworks display has an environmental effect on our local area. Exploding nine tonnes of fireworks generates waste and debris that is blown into the air and lands in waterways and nature reserves, posing a threat to our native flora and fauna. The smoke created by fireworks also pollutes the air and the explosions contribute to noise pollution. Imagine how much the carbon footprint of Timberoona could be reduced if we just replace fireworks with beams of light that are non-toxic, silent and, most importantly, a cleaner option. Add to this the fact that fireworks pose a serious safety and fire risk, especially in December at the height of summer. A single mistake, a single wayward spark, can have devastating consequences. The change to a projected lightshow is a no-brainer. I know how upsetting the loud explosions and high-pitched noises of traditional fireworks can be for little Fido or Fluffy. I understand the yearly dilemma: do I stay home with my beloved pet? Or do I go out and enjoy myself with my family and friends and hope my pet will be okay? Lights silently illuminating the buildings and landscapes in the park are the perfect solution. No more panicked pets cowering under the couch or climbing the curtains. No more scared and lost pets roaming the streets in dangerous traffic. No more frantic owners desperately searching the Timberoona Animal Shelter in the early hours of New Year’s Day. How great would that be? A projected lightshow could also offer the chance for some residents to attend the New Year’s Eve celebrations for the first time ever. I know of many locals who experience sensitivity to loud sounds and are unable to attend the spectacle. Over the years I have seen some children covering their ears and crying in distress because of the intensity and volume of the noise. It would be wonderful to think that these children could come along to enjoy the event without the fear of being so panicked and upset. A projected lightshow is a cheaper and smarter investment. The cost of New Year’s celebrations will drop from $1.6 million annually to $750 000. The money saved could fund more of the programs that are vital to the community, such as our meals for the homeless and our breakfast club programs. Money that would be much better spent on programs we need, rather than a single environmentally and financially disastrous event that lasts for 10 minutes. I’ve heard criticisms of the proposal to change to a light extravaganza because of the traditional appeal of fireworks. There is much nostalgia about maintaining the old-fashioned tradition of singing Auld Lang Syne’1 under a sky illuminated by colour and light with the thunderous sounds of the fireworks as backing music. Not to mention the tradition of having a romantic kiss with a loved one while feeling as if no-one else in the world is watching! Are these New Year’s Eve traditions really dependent on fireworks? Or, would this all be more spectacular without the deafening din and suffocating smoke? A lightshow offers the same ambience with so many advantages. We could have actual music that is choreographed to the movement of the lights! Many of you attended the lightshow held in Timberoona Park earlier this year, pictured below, to celebrate Community Week, and I think you’ll agree it was incredible! Crowds came from far and wide to listen to local musicians and DJs, and interact with the mind-bending illusions that were created with lights and projections. This event was a stunning success, proving that we can create magic in the night sky without a single explosion. Ultimately, this decision is about balance. It’s about finding a way to celebrate that keeps the wonder of New Year’s Eve alive while also being mindful of the needs of our community members, our environment and our future. Together, we have an opportunity to lead the way with a celebration that is spectacular, safe and sustainable.

t: An Open Letter from the Student Music Leadership Group, Narrow Valley
b: An Open Letter from the Student Music Leadership Group, Narrow Valley Background information The Narrow Valley region comprises small rural towns that border a large regional city. A group of young musicians who live in Narrow Valley have decided they want more opportunities to perform in their area. The group has written an open letter to the Narrow Valley community, which has been published on social media and in the local newspaper. In addition, copies have been displayed in shops and businesses. The following text is this open letter with images added by the young musicians. An open letter to the Narrow Valley community, young and old, who wish to see our region rejuvenated … Please allow us to introduce ourselves! We are a growing group of high-school music students, teachers and mentors from the five Narrow Valley secondary colleges. We are eager to seize opportunities to bring dynamic and long-overdue changes to our region through an inclusive, youth-driven, energetic and shiny new music festival. Our festival will provide a space for all budding musicians, regardless of age and abilities, tastes and styles to come together and enjoy music. Our passion, talents and all-encompassing abilities enable us to experiment with, explore and master all types of music, including rock, pop, opera, hip-hop (to name just a few), which are all played by our various orchestras, ensembles and solo artists. We celebrate diversity in our local region and already have thousands of followers on social media, who are sharing our endeavours every day. ‘What?!’, we hear you say. ‘An unrelenting cacophony disrupting the peace and quiet of our streets? Corrupting the impressionable? Shattering windows? Driving the dogs, cats and budgerigars crazy? What type of music did you say? Another music festival? The cost? And …what about our Gorgeous Gardens Festival?’ Yes. What about our garden festival? Who doesn’t love a garden? Like music, gardens never fail to nourish the soul. However, our garden festival is tired. The number of visitors is dwindling – fast. Council data shows that the visitor numbers have dropped by 50 per cent over the past five years and it can only be expected that this trend will continue if we don’t plant some new ideas. With a decline of those proportions, the income from the festival is dwindling dangerously, too. It’s time for a change in tempo and style! For generations, the same Gorgeous Gardens organising committee has done a remarkable job of planning and hosting this event – planting and replanting – but we now need some companion planting. Consider our proposed music festival as ‘festival fertiliser’ that will re-germinate interest and energy in our regional towns, otherwise stagnation will fully set in and we will end up in the compost bin. Few music festivals enjoy the geographical advantages that our region offers. We have a natural amphitheatre overlooking the valley, which could provide not only perfect acoustics but also a stunning backdrop for performances, particularly at twilight. Imagine this cathedral-esque space with the surrounding trees lit up for an evening performance, casting light and shadow on our home-grown superstars. Imagine the sounds of melodic folk tunes wafting across the valley, of hard rock and metal exploding into the night, or the sounds of jazz sizzling under the summer sunset. Like all semi-rural areas, we have buildings that have been standing silent and empty for a long time, including old town halls that could provide brilliant spaces for lessons, workshops and jamming. Our towns can proudly boast that our spaces are accessible to people of all abilities, so musicians and audiences alike can fully enjoy the festival offerings wherever they are staged. The district’s gardens could be opened for a different purpose – not just for admiration but also for musical events. Rock with your roses or mix some Mozart among the marigolds. Dare to put some tubas with your tubers! Melodious offshoots will enrich your world! We know that our Narrow Valley region has seen some tough economic times lately and it might seem that a music festival is a frivolous waste of money. However, we see it as an opportunity to establish innovative partnerships with regional businesses – including fresh food producers, cafes and delicatessens, local artisans and artists – as one solution to overcome financial concerns. Our student bodies don’t just include musicians who can be involved but also media students, foodies, technology gurus and writers. We are confident that we can entice visitors, tourists and music lovers from far and wide to stay, eat and explore. We can see only increased prosperity for our region. Imagine, too, how a visitor to our festival will see new musicians not in the cutthroat world of television talent shows but against the wholesome natural backdrops and the quaint historic buildings that abound in our regional towns. Visitors will eat fresh produce made into delicious meals and buy local. Visitors, residents and local businesses will all be much richer, and not just financially! We are the youth of our region. Younger voices need to be heard so that our communities can find new energy, new purpose and new perspectives. It is time for generational change. We have talents that deserve to be seen and appreciated and nurtured – and not just on social media. Let’s share our triumphs. Let’s share our aspirations. Let’s provide opportunities for all . We invite you, the residents of the Narrow Valley region, to our initial meeting, next Tuesday, in the Narrow Valley Botanical Gardens. The meeting will be followed by a performance by the Narrow Valley North College band. Please bring your ideas, your energy and even any concerns, so that we can begin our shared journey towards a new, prosperous future through our state-of-the-art music festival. Yours, in harmony, The Student Music Leadership Group, Narrow Valley

t: Hapsey Happenings – Transcript of podcast, episode 32
b: Hapsey Happenings – Transcript of podcast, episode 32 Background information Hapsey Happenings is a podcast hosted by lifelong Hapsey resident Janelle Tanley. She discusses local events and issues, and promotes the conservation of the town’s local environment. In the most recent episode of her podcast, Tanley discusses a proposed development plan for the Hapsey Wetlands by Nature+Adventure Group, who run commercial excursions into unspoilt areas. The following text is a transcript of this episode, with images provided by Tanley. Hello and welcome to Hapsey Happenings. I’m your host, Janelle. I’m sure all of you listening have heard about the recent development plan that has been proposed for the Hapsey Wetlands, one of the very last protected sanctuaries in this local region. Nature+Adventure Group’s plan includes bike paths, boat ramps, kiosks and cafes. The local newspaper is being flooded with letters and emails from people for and against the plan, and my socials have also been overflowing. Let’s consider our wetlands. They are quite a distance from the town, so they’re mainly visited by nature lovers – people who don’t mind a walk from where they can leave their car. The paths are narrow and unpaved. Walkers have to be careful but this means the native flora is taken care of. My friends and I frequently meet in the wetlands to relax but we talk softly without disturbing the tranquil surroundings, so the native fauna can live in peace. But now, our wetlands seem to be just another area of Hapsey under threat of destruction. In my lifetime, I have often seen people bring proposals for developments to council meetings, which are disguised as plans to protect the environment, claiming that they will provide access for people who would otherwise be unable to enjoy the natural beauty of the area. The suggestion that this proposed ‘revitalisation’ will protect the environment and preserve the magnificence of this natural space for future generations sounds like something that is said to placate those of us who want this habitat to be kept as it is. In fact, the destruction of the natural home of over 40 different species of grasses to put up money-making ventures – cafes and so on – serves the interests of humans and businesses rather than the precious environment. As locals, we are the guardians of this area. Many of us have worked tirelessly to protect these native plants and animals from all kinds of danger. We know from experience what will happen if the development plan is approved. First, Nature+Adventure Group will send in digging machinery and desecrate the home of fragile species, which will be damaged beyond repair. Then, they’ll build footpaths and bike paths. Inevitably, one careless tourist will go stomping on a delicate fern to look at a frog and will take out an entire species that is unique to our wetlands. How are we going to protect these plants, flowers, insects and other animals from human intrusion? This current development plan will only be the start. Attracting walkers, cyclists and café patrons will only give impetus to further development. With increased traffic, Nature+Adventure Group will build car parks (and charge for parking) and facilities such as toilets and gift shops. If we let this proposal through, it will set in motion a chain of proposals that will erode the protection that we have provided for the wetlands all these years. Suddenly, this area will have been concreted over, and the Hapsey Wetlands will have become the Hapsey Wetlands Shopping Centre or the Hapsey Amusement Park! If we’re looking at increasing the opportunities for outdoor adventures in the Hapsey area, there are other equally scenic and tranquil places to the south of the town, where installing walking and cycling paths would not disturb the delicately balanced ecology of the natural wetlands. These would-be developers claim in their proposal that they have an ‘excellent record in terms of environmental responsibility’. They say that they see cycling and boating as leaving a ‘small footprint on the environment’ and as being environmentally responsible activities because these activities use no fossil fuels. They acknowledge that transporting equipment, such as bikes and boats, will leave a bit of a carbon footprint but that they are working towards reducing the impact of transporting their bikes and boats. Believe that if you like! I realise that these people feel that they are offering an excellent opportunity to the Hapsey community. They claim that they are very protective of our precious resource and that they share the goal of preserving this special place. But will an increase in the number of visitors promote the preservation of the wetlands? Will all these new visitors, grasping disposable coffee cups, share the values of those protecting the native inhabitants of the wetlands? Is the wetlands’ survival helped by people falling off bikes and out of boats? Aren’t these arguments just a selfish attempt to paint a commercial venture in a favourable light? Can we trust Nature+Adventure Group’s mission statement: ‘Above all, we acknowledge that environmental and ecological concerns are our number one priority in the expansion and development of our business’? We must consider what is best for our wonderful wetlands. I would love to hear from you, listeners of Hapsey Happenings – how do you feel about this? Leave your comments on my website. Don’t forget to follow the podcast to receive updates about the proposal for the wetlands.

Sample Analysing Argument Essays The three responses below were all written for the same task: Scenario 3 on the Practice Articles for Analysis page, a letter to the editor of the Westmere Courier by Priya Raman, a nurse who commutes to Melbourne by train. The first sits in the low range, the second in the middle range and the third in the high range. Each one has an introduction, three body paragraphs built around the letter’s main arguments, and a conclusion. Read the task and the letter first, then compare how each response handles argument, language, the visual and the audience.
The Task and Letter The task, background information and letter are reproduced below.

Sample Essay I (Low) In the letter ‘We deserve a train we can count on’ written by Priya Raman in the Westmere Courier, she talks about how the trains in Westmere are always late and the government needs to fix it. She is a nurse and she uses alot of persuasive techniques to get the reader to agree with her. Priya’s first argument is that the trains are late and it is affecting people. She uses an anecdote at the start about when her train was late last Tuesday. She says that it took ‘an hour and forty minutes’ when it is meant to take ‘an hour and five’. This is an anecdote and it makes the reader feel sorry for her. She also talks about a man who finished his crossword and ate his lunch and then fell asleep which is funny. Then she says she was ‘fifty minutes late’ for her shift. This makes the reader feel sympathy because nurses are important and the hospital was already short of staff. Priya also talks about a girl called Ella who is a nursing student and is nineteen. Ella has missed placement days because of the train. This is another anecdote and it is sad because she is young and has to get up at 4.30 in the morning. The reader will feel bad for Ella. Priya’s second argument is that the trains are getting worse. She uses statistics to show this. The graph shows that the trains arriving on time went from 88 to 69. This is a big drop and it shows the trains are getting worse. She also says ‘roughly one in three of us is late’. Statistics are used to make an argument more believable and the reader will believe her because it has numbers. The graph is grey and the last bar is darker then the others. She also uses a rhetorical question when she says ‘Some people will say, well, just drive.’ This makes the reader think about it. She then says driving would cost ‘close to $90 a day’ which is alot of money so the reader will agree that driving is not a good idea. Priya’s third argument is that the government does not care about people in Westmere. She compares the city lines to the country lines. The city has ‘new tunnels’ and ‘shiny new trains’ and Westmere doesn’t get anything. This is unfair and the reader will think the government doesnt care about people in the country. At the end she uses repetition, ‘I am asking’ three times. Repetition makes the argument stick in the readers head. She also invites the local member to catch the train with her which is a good way to finish. She says ‘I’ll even save you a seat. If the train turns up.’ This is humour and it makes the reader laugh. In conclusion, Priya Raman uses anecdotes, statistics, a graph and repetition to persuade the reader that the trains in Westmere need to be fixed. She is very persuasive because she is a nurse and she uses lots of different techniques.

Sample Essay II (Medium) In her letter to the editor of the Westmere Courier, titled ‘We deserve a train we can count on’, nurse and long-time commuter Priya Raman contends that the state government has neglected the Westmere train line and must commit to the track and signal upgrades it promised. Writing to an audience of mainly Westmere residents, many of whom would also rely on the train, as well as the local member of parliament, Raman uses a frustrated but at times humorous tone to argue that regional passengers are being treated as less important than those in the city. Raman first argues that the unreliable train service is having a real impact on the people who use it. She begins with a personal anecdote about her trip to work the previous Tuesday. By describing how she ‘sat on the 6.12 am train from Westmere for an hour and forty minutes’, she immediately places the reader on the train with her. The humorous image of the man across the aisle who was able to ‘finish his crossword, eat his lunch at half past seven in the morning and fall asleep’ exaggerates how long the delay lasted, and the audience are likely to find this amusing but also recognise it from their own experiences. As such, the audience, particularly other commuters, are more inclined to see Raman as one of them and trust her point of view. Raman then reveals that she was ‘fifty minutes late for a twelve-hour shift, on a ward that was already two nurses short’. This shifts the tone from humorous to serious, as the audience start to understand that the delays do not only affect commuters but also the patients who rely on nurses like her. The short sentence ‘This is a normal week’ emphasises how regular these problems have become. Raman also includes the anecdote of Ella, a nineteen-year-old nursing student who now catches an earlier train ‘just in case’. The audience are positioned to feel sympathy for Ella, as she is young and is already being disadvantaged by something she cannot control. Raman’s second argument is that the service is getting worse and that there is no real alternative to it. She uses the statistics from the Westmere Rail Users Group to show that ‘nearly nine out of every ten trains’ were once on time but now it is ‘fewer than seven’, and that ‘roughly one in three of us is late’. The use of the inclusive pronoun ‘us’ groups Raman together with the audience, encouraging them to see the problem as one that affects the whole community. The accompanying bar graph reinforces this, as each bar is lower than the one before it, showing a steady decline over two years. The final bar is shaded darker than the rest, drawing the reader’s eye to the lowest figure of 69 per cent. As a result, the audience are more likely to accept that the line is getting worse and is not just having a bad week. Raman then anticipates the argument that people should ‘just drive’ instead. She uses logic and statistics to rebut this, calculating that driving would cost her ‘close to $90 a day’, and she appeals to the audience’s sense of safety by describing driving home after a night shift ‘with your eyes closing’. As such, the audience are more likely to agree that the train is the ‘cheapest, safest and most sensible’ option, which makes its unreliability seem even more frustrating. Finally, Raman argues that regional people are being treated unfairly and that the government needs to act. She explains that the problems were identified ‘back in 2019’ but there has been ‘plenty of announcements and very little actual work’. This makes the government seem as though it only cares about looking like it is doing something, causing the audience to lose trust in their promises. Raman then compares the Westmere line to the city lines, which have had ‘new tunnels’, ‘new stations’ and ‘shiny new trains’. Although she says ‘Good on them’, the comparison makes the audience feel that regional people are an ‘afterthought’. She then lists the wider consequences for the community, such as young people moving away and nurses resigning from her hospital, which broadens her argument from a personal complaint to a community issue. Raman uses repetition of ‘I am asking’ to set out exactly what she wants, which makes her demands seem reasonable and clear. She ends by challenging the local member to catch the train with her, and the final line ‘If the train turns up’ uses humour to leave the audience with a reminder of how unreliable the service is. Overall, Priya Raman uses personal anecdotes, statistics, a bar graph and a comparison with the city to persuade the audience that the Westmere line has been neglected. She positions the audience to feel sympathy and frustration, and to support her call for the government to finally upgrade the line.

Sample Essay III (High) In a letter to the editor of the regional Westmere Courier, nurse Priya Raman contends that the Westmere train line has been left to decline while city commuters enjoy new investment, and that the government must deliver the long-promised track and signal upgrades with ‘a real start date and a real budget’. Her readership is a community that knows the train intimately, and Raman writes less to inform them than to give their shared frustration a shape and a target. Her tone moves from wry, almost weary humour into measured indignation, and finally into a pointed challenge to the local member, so that by the end of the letter a private inconvenience has become a public question of fairness. Raman’s first argument is that the failing service has real human costs, and she makes this case through story rather than statement. Raman opens not with an argument but with a scene. The 6.12 am train, the ‘signal faults’ outside Darrow and the man who manages to ‘finish his crossword, eat his lunch at half past seven in the morning and fall asleep’ are comic in their detail, and this is a deliberate choice. Humour allows Raman to establish herself as reasonable rather than shrill; she is laughing at the absurdity before she is angry about it. Yet the joke ends abruptly when she arrives ‘fifty minutes late for a twelve-hour shift, on a ward that was already two nurses short’. The stakes are suddenly raised from a ruined morning to patient care. Her credibility as a nurse is doing quiet work here. She never has to argue that her lateness matters, because the reader already understands what a short-staffed ward means. The two blunt sentences that follow, ‘This is not unusual. This is a normal week’, land with the flatness of someone stating a fact that should be shocking but no longer is, and it is this resignation that invites the reader’s outrage on her behalf. The anecdote of Ella widens the appeal. Where Raman’s own story speaks to fellow workers, Ella, who is ‘nineteen’, getting up at 4.30 and sitting ‘in a café she can’t really afford’, speaks to parents and to anyone worried about whether young people have a future in the town. The decline of the train is gradually connected to the decline of the town itself. Having made the problem personal, Raman then makes it measurable, arguing that the decline is real and that neither the alternatives nor the official excuses hold up. Her nine years on the line give her a before-and-after authority (‘something you could set your watch by’), but she is careful not to rest on memory alone. The Rail Users Group figures, translated into plain fractions, ‘nearly nine out of every ten’ and ‘fewer than seven’, are easier for a general reader to feel than a percentage, and the accompanying graph turns this decline into something almost physical: eight bars stepping steadily down, with the final, darkest bar marking 69 per cent as the low point so far. The grey, unadorned design gives the graph the look of neutral data rather than campaign material, which strengthens its authority, while the inclusive ‘us’ in ‘roughly one in three of us is late’ quietly recruits every reader who has stood on that platform into her argument. Raman then raises the obvious objection, ‘well, just drive’, in a dismissive voice before dismantling it with arithmetic, ‘close to $90 a day’, and with an image that is hard to forget: driving down the highway after a night shift ‘with your eyes closing’. By the time she concludes that the train is ‘the cheapest, safest and most sensible way’ to get to work, she has turned her opponents’ solution into further evidence for her own case. The same strategy appears in her response to the official explanation of ‘ageing infrastructure’. Rather than disputing it, she concedes it (‘I don’t doubt it’), and then uses the concession against the government: the problems were identified ‘back in 2019’, yet there have been ‘plenty of announcements and very little actual work’. The balanced structure of this phrase exposes the gap between words and action. Raman’s final argument is that regional people are being treated as an afterthought, and that the government must now act. Her indignation is at its most controlled in the comparison with the city. The list of ‘new tunnels’, ‘new stations’ and ‘shiny new trains’ is followed by ‘Good on them’, a concession that sounds generous but carries an edge of sarcasm. It allows Raman to avoid seeming resentful while still making the reader feel the unfairness, which she then names directly: people out here are ‘an afterthought’, as though ‘our time somehow matters less’. The short rebuttal ‘It does matter’ marks a turning point, after which the letter widens its consequences to the whole community, including nurses resigning from her hospital and people who ‘are simply left standing on the platform’. Her conclusion then shifts from description to demand. The repeated ‘I am asking’ gives her requests the rhythm of a formal petition, and the requests themselves are deliberately modest, which makes refusing them seem unreasonable. Her final move is her most pointed: an invitation to the local member, ‘who I notice drives to Melbourne’, to catch the 6.12 with her. The aside is barbed, quietly suggesting that those who make decisions about the train do not have to live with it. The closing line, ‘If the train turns up’, returns to the dry humour of the opening, but now the joke has a sting, leaving the reader with the very uncertainty the whole letter has been arguing against. Through a careful movement from comic anecdote to hard evidence, and from concession to challenge, Raman transforms a familiar local grievance into an argument about fairness and respect. Her readers are positioned not only to sympathise with her, but to see their own frustration reflected and justified, and to expect their local member to answer for it.

Exam Format The VCE English exam is a three-hour exam, plus 15 minutes of reading time. It has three sections, and you are required to complete all three sections. Each section is worth the same number of marks, so you should spend the same amount of time on each.
Exam Specifications

Overall Conditions The examination will be sat at a time and date to be set annually by the Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA). VCAA examination rules will apply. There will be 15 minutes of reading time and 3 hours of writing time. The examination will be assessed by a panel appointed by the VCAA. The examination will contribute 50 per cent to the study score.

Format The Task Book will be sixteen pages in length. The front page contains the general cover notes and instructions, including rules about what you can and can’t take into the exam. An English and/or bilingual printed dictionary is permitted. Mobile Phones and/pr any unauthrosied electronic devices are not permitted.
Exam Mindset, Timing and FAQs

How Your Paper Is Marked Each section is marked by at least two assessors, each giving a score out of 10, combined into a mark out of 20. If the two scores are too far apart, a third (or further) assessor reads the response. Assessors mark holistically against the expected qualities, and always in relation to the topic or title. They read every word and reward as far as they can. In 2025 the average for each section sat around 5.4 to 5.5 out of 10.

Attitude Is a Predictor An Australian study of students under test conditions, controlling for ability, found that attitude alone predicted results. “Confident striders” (prepared, and trusting that the test would be fair) did best; students who expected the test to be unfair and stressful tended to fulfil that prophecy. Practical takeaways: Trust the paper to be fair. Recent papers have been. A question may be phrased unexpectedly, but you are transferring skills you have practised to a new instance. A little nerves is useful. Adrenaline speeds thinking. Worrying about things you cannot control only takes up brain space. Confidence comes from preparation , not from hoping.

Habits of Successful Students Train for three hours. Do some study in three-hour blocks so the exam is not the first time you concentrate that long. Work out what breakfast keeps you going. Practise, get feedback, act on it, practise again. Eat well, sleep, and exercise to burn off anxiety when it tips from useful to unhelpful. Have a backup plan. No single exam decides your future. Missing a first-choice course often means a transfer a year later.

Time Discipline The three sections are worth equal marks, so give each one hour. The first marks in any response are the easiest to earn. An extra half hour polishing one essay gains far less than the same half hour spent on the next. Use the room clock, and when the hour is up, move on.

Plan, Then Write Planning is not extra work; it shifts the work. When you write without a plan, you are deciding what to say and how to say it at the same time, and your brain switches between the two and loses time. Plan first (only you need to read it), check it is relevant to the topic, then give your full attention to expression. Fluency is assessed in every section.

Frequently Asked Questions How many quotes should I use in Section A? There is no number. It depends on how many other kinds of evidence you use (structure, character, setting, language features, context), and every quote must be explained, not just included. Should I memorise a strong practice response? No, in any section. You cannot know the topic, title or text, and a memorised piece that does not answer the question cannot score highly. Which section should I do first? Personal choice. Some students do A, B, C in order; others start with whichever they plan fastest. Try different orders in practice exams. What should I do the night before? Put the books away and sleep. A year of preparation will not be changed by two more hours. What if I make a mistake? Cross it out neatly and keep going. If you realise mid-essay you have drifted, fix your topic sentences, but stay within your hour. Checking your plan early is the best prevention. What if I don’t get the score I want? You get the score you get. It is a snapshot of one day, and your skills keep growing after it.
Strategies for Addressing the Requirements

Section A In Section A you will write an essay that responds to one of the two given topics on a text you have studied. You can choose to write on either your Unit 1 text or your Unit 4 text. In your answer book you will need to identify the text on which you are writing and the topic (i or ii) you are responding to by shading the relevant box. Spend a few minutes unpacking the topic you feel most comfortable responding to. Look carefully at each term in the topic and make sure you understand its meaning and significance. Use the strategies for identifying topic words, direction words and limiting words outlined on pages 48–50 in English Year 12. Spend about 5 minutes writing a brief plan that includes your contention, three or four topic sentences and one or two pieces of textual evidence for each topic sentence. The following strategies will help you to address the Section A requirements and criteria. Address the topic in full. Strong responses take account of every word in the topic, including the limiting words, rather than writing about one key term in a general way. Use your dictionary. Make sure you understand the meanings of all the words in the topic. Your dictionary will also give you some synonyms for key terms in the topic, and using these will give your writing more variety and precision. Consider a range of textual features. Don’t limit your reasons and evidence to just what the characters say and do. While authors do use characters to explore ideas, they also use features such as narrative voice, structure, setting and imagery. Film techniques should be referred to when analysing a film, and an analysis of poetry will be enhanced by a consideration of poetic form and techniques. Discussing these features shows a deeper understanding of the text and a more sophisticated response to the topic. Integrate quotes and explain their significance. It is useful to include some direct quotes, as this is part of how you show your ‘knowledge and understanding of the text’ (criterion 2 for Section A). However, make sure you incorporate quotes into your discussion and thoroughly explain how they support the point you are making. If you use a quote and then mention it on its own, or place it at the end of a sentence without further explanation, it will be unclear to your assessor how the quote helps to advance your argument. Write precisely and expressively. Develop a wide vocabulary during the year by creating word banks (see the examples on pages 58–63 of English Year 12) and use a variety of words in your practice essays, so by the time you sit the exam you can make effective vocabulary choices in all your responses.

Section B In Section B you will write a text that responds to a given title and at least one piece of stimulus material. In the answer book, you will need to shade the box of your chosen Framework, and the box (or boxes) corresponding to the stimulus (or stimuli) you have responded to. The following strategies will help you to address the Section B criteria and weave the stimuli and title into your creative piece. Ensure your writing is clearly relevant to your chosen Framework. This involves integrating concepts and perspectives that you’ve explored during the year. When you are revising in preparation for the exam, refer to your notes and written pieces to stay aligned with the core ideas of the Framework. Integrate the title and at least one stimulus into your writing. You must use at least one of the stimuli. The stimulus should not just be referenced superficially; it should be woven into the fabric of your piece. This could mean, for example, using a text stimulus as the basis for a central idea; using a text stimulus as a direct quote at a key point in your text; or drawing inspiration from a visual stimulus to set a scene. Similarly, the title provided for your Framework should provide an idea, a character arc, a central image or another key element of your writing. Give your piece cohesion and structure. Your piece should have a clear beginning, middle and end, regardless of whether it’s a narrative, an argument or a reflective piece. Each part should seamlessly transition into the next, maintaining a logical flow of ideas. Make appropriate use of language, style and voice. The language and style of your writing should suit the purpose and audience. This includes choosing the most appropriate vocabulary, tone and sentence structures. In your Unit 3 drafts and assessment pieces, you will have worked hard to develop your own unique voice. You likely have a preferred form of writing (fiction or nonfiction, story, article etc.) and you should lean into that during the exam. Write with fluency and expression. Your writing should read smoothly, with a natural flow of ideas and language. This can be achieved by varying your sentence structures, giving your writing a subtle rhythm and clearly articulating your ideas. Transitions between paragraphs or sections should be logical and easy for the reader to follow.

Section C In Section C you will analyse a text in which the writer seeks to persuade a particular audience to agree with their point of view on an issue. The text will be primarily written but will also contain one or more visual elements. This task has been part of the VCE English exam for many years and as part of your preparation you may use past exam papers as sources of practice material. In some cases you will find that the task material consists of more than one written piece, but the exam specifications for 2024–2027 indicate that there will only be a single ‘unseen persuasive text’ in the English exams during this period. The following strategies will help you to address the Section C requirements and criteria. Understand the contention. What, essentially, is the writer saying? An accurate understanding of the writer’s central argument underpins your analysis. Clearly state the writer’s contention in your introduction. Read the background information carefully. This is where you will find out the intended audience and the context for the text. Your analysis will be strengthened by a consideration of how the writer’s choices of argument and language are shaped by their particular audience and context (see the final bullet point below). Examine the sequencing of the argument. Writers will arrange their material and their points of argument in a particular order so as to engage their intended audience and influence their thoughts and feelings. Look at the overall shape of the argument, then drill down into the specific points and language choices. Shifts in tone are important aspects of the structure, too. Examine language choices. Writers make deliberate choices of words to add impact to their arguments and to evoke the audience’s emotions. Identify words with strong positive or negative connotations and associations and spend some time in your analysis ‘unpacking’ their likely effects on the audience. You will not have time to analyse every use of language in the text, but discuss a representative sample of language choices. Use effective verbs. In your analysis of a persuasive text, verbs enable you to describe what the writer is doing and how they are doing it. Repeating the verbs ‘positions’ and ‘persuades’ doesn’t show your understanding of how argument and language are being used. Verbs such as ‘reinforces’, ‘emphasises’, ‘instils’, ‘elicits’ and ‘undermines’ can be used to show your understanding of how a writer is attempting to persuade. See the verbs in the activity on page 210 of English Year 12 for some other examples. Analyse how argument, language and visuals are working together. Don’t treat these as separate elements of the text, since an audience’s response will be a result of how all these elements are working in combination. Look at how language is used to present an argument, and how an image complements and reinforces particular reasons or pieces of evidence.

t: How the Marker Reads Your Essay
b: How the Marker Reads Your Essay Examiners do not read your essay the way a friendly teacher does – they read it in passes, testing it against the criteria. Knowing the passes lets you write for them.

g: How the Marker Reads Your Essay
b: The Six Passes First, the scope audit: the topic is broken into its explicit and implicit parts, including modifying words (“unrelenting cruelty”, not just “cruelty”) and both halves of a double-barrelled prompt. A dimension you never address keeps you out of the 8–10 range. Second, the summary filter: every sentence is silently sorted into retelling, explaining, or analysing how the author constructs meaning – and if retelling dominates, the essay cannot reach the upper band no matter how fluent it is. Third, the topic-sentence thread: conceptual topic sentences that build a progressive argument separate 9–10 essays from 7–8 essays that give three parallel examples of one idea. Fourth, the authorial hand: markers look for sentences whose subject is the author (“Jackson constructs…”, “Weir juxtaposes…”) – writing about characters as though they are real people is a mid-band signature. Fifth, evidence gravity: quotes that stand alone as their own sentences read mid-band; short quotes woven into your own grammar, drawn from across the whole text, read upper-band. Sixth, the gap analysis: the difference between your mark and the next band is always something specific and nameable – which is why good feedback tells you what was missing, not just what was there.

g: How the Marker Reads Your Essay
b: What the Bands Feel Like A 5 is relevant but basic: simple structure, simple vocabulary, evidence that supports plot points. A 7 is clear and detailed, uses evidence effectively, but stays at the level of what the text shows rather than how and why it was built that way. A 9 or 10 is sophisticated and perceptive: it reframes the topic conceptually, treats the text as a construction, uses precise metalanguage correctly, and integrates evidence so smoothly the quotation marks could be removed without breaking the sentence.

g: How the Marker Reads Your Essay
b: Section-Specific Traps In Section A, a contention that simply agrees or disagrees without a bigger conceptual claim caps the essay in the middle band, and ignoring the text’s social and historical values keeps the top band out of reach. In Section B, a competent story that never engages the Framework’s ideas sits mid-band, as do clichéd premises and unearned endings – while adapted echoes of your mentor texts signal studied craft. In Section C, “the readers” is a mid-band audience; the upper band names who the writer targets and what they are being positioned to think, feel and do. Naming a technique without explaining its function for that specific audience is label-picking, and it caps the analysis no matter how many techniques you spot. Track the argument’s arc and tonal shifts; treat any visual as part of the argument, not a separate exhibit.

t: Key Takeaways from the 2025 Assessment Report
p: Key Takeaways from the 2025 Assessment Report
b: Part 12 Key Takeaways from the 2025 Assessment Report What the VCAA assessors reported from the 2025 English examination, broken down by section — the marking approach, the strategies that earned top marks, the pitfalls that cost them, and a priority checklist distilled for the 2027 cohort. In this part 1 General Exam Advice 2 Section A: Analytical Response to a Text 3 Section B: Creating a Text 4 Section C: Analysis of Argument and Language 5 Priority Checklist for 2027

Part 12 General Exam Advice The 2025 examination produced near-identical averages across all three sections — 5.4, 5.4 and 5.5 out of 10 — with very few students at either extreme. The middle is crowded; the marks that separate a 5 from an 8 come from the specific skills assessors described, not from writing more. Section Average /10 What it was A 5.4 Analytical response to a text B 5.4 Creating a text (Frameworks of Ideas) C 5.5 Analysis of argument and language How assessors marked Holistic, criteria-based, benchmarked. Every section was assessed against the published criteria and expected qualities (EQs), using benchmark scripts to set standards. The three EQs are interconnected: the quality of your ideas (EQ1) sets the level of challenge for structuring and substantiating them (EQ2), and language (EQ3) is judged by how well it communicates those ideas. Everything is applied in relation to the topic. Sound ideas, apt quotations or fluent expression that do not serve the set task cannot score highly. This principle recurs through every section of the report. First-draft conditions were respected. Assessors explicitly acknowledged that exam writing is timed first-draft work; fluency was not equated with perfection. Administrative habits that mattered Shade the box for your chosen text and topic in Section A, and for your Framework and stimulus in Section B — and write the Section B title at the start of your response. Choose the topic that best lets you demonstrate your knowledge and skills, not the one you predicted. Bring a dictionary. Assessors specifically noted students with no strategy for unfamiliar words in topics — some simply substituted "and" for a term they didn't understand, which derailed their essays.

t: Section A: Analytical Response to a Text
p: Section A: Analytical Response to a Text
b: Part 12 Section A: Analytical Response to a Text The 2025 topics were deliberately narrow — specified ideas and values rather than broad prompts — and this shaped how responses needed to be structured, sequenced and evidenced. Students with topic-interpretation strategies handled both familiar and unfamiliar phrasings well. Topic types Propositional topics offered a proposition with a command term: Discuss , Do you agree? or To what extent do you agree? You may challenge the proposition where warranted, but never the topic's conceptual focus itself — a topic linking love and destruction requires discussing both, though "inseparable" can be contested. Quotation topics paired a quotation with a proposition. There was no obligatory way to use the quotation, but how you used it revealed your understanding of what it conveys in context. The verbs The verb in a topic carries the author's purpose, and flattening every verb into a generic "presents" was unwise. Assessors also warned that verbs are often nominalised or implied, and new ones appear each year. Used in 2025 New in 2025 celebrates, challenges, condemns, demonstrates, displays, explores, highlights, mocks, shows, suggests is (a cry for), depicts, glorifies, warns Implications: where the top marks lived There was a direct correlation between recognising a topic's implications and higher scores. Watch for: absolute terms ("there are no right choices"), connotation (" easy to overlook "), what a proposition is silent about, comparison ("requires more than individual effort"), an included quotation, and the verb itself. What high-scoring responses did Interpreted before writing — considered what the topic implies, not just what it states. Sequenced strategically — used opening and closing summary sentences in each paragraph to make ideas and their connections explicit, guiding the reader through the reading of the text. Substantiated with range — drew on linguistic elements, characters, structure, plot and allusion, and discussed how these interplayed; assessors noted high scorers took "a more philosophic consideration of the ideas, rather than a literal consideration". Resolved the topic — used the conclusion to actually answer the question, showing the interplay of context, audience and purpose. Used language to communicate. Sophisticated vocabulary scored only when it carried sophisticated ideas; "poorly applied polysyllabic words" were called out explicitly. What limited responses Discussing a favourite theme adjacent to the topic instead of the topic (e.g. writing about patriarchy when the topic was about truth). Addressing only half the topic — in a topic such as "individuals can be both victims and villains", writing about villainy but not victimhood. Substituting prepared material for the terms actually on the paper, or having no strategy for unfamiliar words.

Part 12 Section B: Creating a Text Nearly half the state wrote on protest, yet all four Frameworks averaged within 0.4 marks of each other — choose the Framework that suits your ideas, not the popular one. Framework % of students Average score /20 Writing about country 10% 11.2 Writing about protest 47% 10.9 Writing about personal journeys 25% 10.9 Writing about play 17% 10.8 The rules of the task The title is fixed. You cannot change or modify it; assessors ignored any additions. Choosing a title selects its Framework — no mixing and matching titles, Frameworks or stimulus sets. If your shaded box and your title disagreed, assessors followed the title. Write the title at the start and shade both the Framework and stimulus boxes. Stimulus ideas must come from your selected Framework's stimulus material, though how you use them is open. Mentor texts don't need referencing , and there is no preferred form, style, purpose or audience — responses could explain, express, reflect or argue, and could adapt or subvert any prose form. What lifted responses Using the title as the focus while exploring Framework ideas purposefully through a cohesive text. Making deliberate structural and linguistic choices that amplify ideas — the annotated high scorers moved economically between place and time, used imagery to imply location, and chose words that carried complex emotion. Establishing a voice that connects strategically with the reader — one exemplar built "a thoughtful, confiding reflective voice" from its opening lines. Trusting an adult reader to infer meaning, and guiding that inference deliberately. What limited responses Using stimulus literally (a story of children playing a board game with no other connection to the Framework or title). Rambling texts with no observable purpose; simplistic or barely-related ideas; relying on plot alone. Contorting a pre-prepared piece to fit the exam title, or writing for yourself rather than a reader. Sensationalised content, cloying sentiment and clichéd language — assessors said these "were rarely the most powerful option". Remember an unknown adult reads this for assessment.

t: Section C: Analysis of Argument and Language
p: Section C: Analysis of Argument and Language
b: Part 12 Section C: Analysis of Argument and Language The 2025 text was a letter to a community newsletter from a "local resident" proposing that a regional town replace its annual fireworks with an alternative celebration. Students found it highly accessible — which made the discriminators sharper. Background information is not decoration The publication details and the author's "local resident" persona had to be used: inferring the regional audience and its values, the author's altruistic credibility, and the unhurried "evolution, not urgency" framing enabled the most focused analyses. Read the background inferentially before writing — the analysis flows from it. The argument structure most students saw Establishing a shared value: love of the celebration in its beautiful setting. Raising previously unconsidered problems — environment, frightened pets (with a photo), noise-sensitive residents, cost — aligned with community values. Rebutting reasons to keep the status quo. Presenting the alternative as a "win-win" (with an inspiring second visual). What separated skill levels Identification is not analysis. Most students could list arguments and label techniques; far fewer could explain how the sequencing of ideas served the purpose, or what a device actually did to the intended audience. Interplay was the discriminator. The strongest responses explained how argument, written language and visuals worked together — nearly everyone noticed the frightened dog photo, but skill showed in explaining its contribution to the developing argument, not just "appeals to emotion". Strategic selection beat exhaustive coverage. Discussing every element was impossible in the time and wasn't expected; choosing the elements most central to the persuasion correlated strongly with success. Language worth recognising Assessor-noted elements included appeals to parochial pride, social justice and economic responsibility; strategic characterisation ("beloved pets", "little Fido or Fluffy", "cheaper and smarter"); escalation ("a single wayward spark ... devastating consequences"); reflection-prompting rhetorical questions; inspirational collective language ("Together we have the opportunity ... to lead the way"); and closing the door on alternatives ("a no-brainer").

Part 12 Priority Checklist for 2027 The habits below fall straight out of the 2025 report — each one addresses something assessors explicitly rewarded or penalised. Before the exam Build a topic-interpretation routine: identify the conceptual focus, the command term, the verb, and at least two implications before planning. Rehearse unfamiliar-verb strategy — and pack a dictionary. Practise writing to a fixed title in Section B without bending a pre-prepared piece to fit. For Section C practice, always start from the background information and write down audience, purpose and author positioning before analysing. In the exam Shade every box: text and topic (Section A); Framework and stimulus (Section B) — and write the Section B title first. Section A: open and close each paragraph with sentences that link your ideas to the topic; use the conclusion to resolve the question. Section B: keep the title in view as you write; make every structural and word choice serve your purpose and reader. Section C: select the few elements most central to the persuasion and explain their interplay — argument, language and visuals together. Everywhere: sophisticated language only where it communicates a sophisticated idea. Summarised from the VCAA 2025 English examination report. Read alongside the 2024 takeaways and the assessment criteria .
Assess your current study habits

Identifying strengths and weaknesses Take a few minutes to jot down what’s working well in your current study routine. What areas could use some improvement? Consider factors like time management, focus, and understanding of different subjects.

Setting realistic goals Based on your assessment, you could start by setting 2-3 specific, achievable goals for improving your study habits. Make these goals SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Write them down and place them somewhere visible as a daily reminder.

Create a personalised study schedule Now that you know where you stand, it’s time to map out a path to exam success. Think of your study schedule as a roadmap to help you navigate your way through VCE studies.

Time management tips List all your subjects and the topics you need to cover for each. Assess how much time you have until your exams. Consider prioritising subjects based on difficulty and your current performance. Using a study schedule template Remember: Be realistic with your schedule. If you’re not a morning person, a sunrise study session may not suit you. Try to work with your natural rhythms, and not against them.

t: Find a study schedule template that works for you – digital or physical, whichever works best.
b: Find a study schedule template that works for you – digital or physical, whichever works best. Block out fixed commitments like school, extracurriculars, and family time. Allocate study blocks for each subject, ensuring a mix of subjects each day. Don’t forget to schedule breaks and ’me time’ to avoid feelings of burnout.
Organise your study materials A cluttered space can contribute to a cluttered mind. Here are some strategies to effectively organise your study materials.

Gathering resources Collect all your textbooks, notes, and past papers for each subject. Organise digital resources into clearly labelled folders on your computer. Consider creating a ’study toolkit’ with essentials like highlighters, sticky notes, and index cards.

Creating a study-friendly environment Find a quiet, well-lit space where you can focus without distractions. Ensure you have a comfortable chair and desk at the right height. Keep your study area clean and organised – a tidy space can do wonders for your concentration.

t: Implement active recall and spaced repetition
b: Implement active recall and spaced repetition Below are some tried and true study techniques you might like to explore.

g: Implement active recall and spaced repetition
b: The power of self-testing After studying a topic, close your books and try to recall as much as you can. Create flashcards for key concepts and test yourself regularly. Explain concepts out loud as if you’re teaching someone else.

g: Implement active recall and spaced repetition
b: Spacing out your study sessions Avoid cramming by spreading out your study sessions over time. Review material at increasing intervals: e.g. 1 day later, 3 days later, 1 week later, etc.

t: Utilise practice exams and past papers
b: Utilise practice exams and past papers Another way to effectively prepare for exams is by practising past exams. Here are some techniques you might find helpful.

g: Utilise practice exams and past papers
b: Simulating exam conditions Find past papers or practice exams for your subjects. Set up a quiet space and time yourself as you would in a real exam. Avoid using your notes or textbooks during these practice sessions.

g: Utilise practice exams and past papers
b: Analysing your performance Mark your practice exams using the relevant marking schemes, if available. Identify areas where you lost marks and focus on improving these in your study sessions. Keep a log of common mistakes to avoid repeating them in the real exam.
Develop a healthy study-life balance It’s important to look after yourself and practice self-care during this time. Find what works best for you, or try our ideas below.

Incorporating breaks and relaxation Use techniques like the Pomodoro method: 25 minutes of focused study followed by a 5-minute break. Schedule longer breaks for activities you enjoy – maybe a quick game of basketball or a chat with friends. Practice mindfulness or meditation to help manage stress and improve focus.

Maintaining physical and mental well-being Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep per night – your brain consolidates memories and learning during sleep. Incorporate regular exercise to improve your mood and reduce stress. Eat a balanced diet with brain-boosting foods like blueberries, nuts, and fatty fish.
Collaborate with study groups Two heads are better than one, and a study group can be a powerhouse of knowledge, inspiration and motivation.

The benefits of peer learning Explaining concepts to others can help solidify your own understanding. Gain new perspectives and insights from your peers. Stay motivated and accountable with group study sessions.
Organising effective study sessions Set clear objectives for each study session. Use tools like shared Google Docs or virtual whiteboards for collaborative note-taking.
Seek help when needed Remember, asking for help isn’t a sign of weakness.
Utilising teacher support Don’t hesitate to approach your teachers with specific questions. Attend any extra help sessions offered by your school or community. Ask for feedback on your work.

Exploring additional resources Explore online tutorials or video explanations for challenging topics. Consider getting a tutor for subjects where you’re really struggling. Join online forums or study groups for your specific subjects.
Fine-tune your exam day strategy When your exams are approaching – make sure you’re feeling prepared.
Pre-exam preparation Get a good night’s sleep before the exam. Eat a nutritious breakfast to fuel your brain. Arrive at the exam venue early to avoid last-minute stress.

During the exam tactics Read through the entire paper before starting to answer questions. Manage your time wisely – allocate minutes to each section based on mark values. If you get stuck on a question, move on and come back to it later.

Part 13 · Effectively Studying For Exams Week-by-Week Revision Program Twelve weeks of structured revision mapping this site’s chapters and tools to a plan. Count back twelve weeks from the exam and start; if you have fewer weeks left, begin at the matching week number and compress the early stages. Adjust around your SACs — the order matters more than the calendar. Weeks 12–11 · Rebuild the foundations Read: your text’s Background and Context and Values chapters ( Picnic at Hanging Rock / The Lottery and Other Stories ), then What is Needed in an Essay . Do: re-watch the film / re-read the play once, casually. Skim the scene summaries or quote tables alongside. Tool: 10 minutes of Quote Flashcards daily — start building recall now, when it’s cheap. Weeks 10–9 · Master the evidence Read: the Thematic and Character Quote Banks for your text, and the Symbols chapters. Do: build a one-page theme map: each major theme, three quotes, one symbol, one technique. The Glossary supplies the technique names. Tool: flashcards daily; add the Technique Quiz twice a week. Weeks 8–7 · Learn the craft of the essay Read: Interrogating the Topic , then plan paragraphs with the Th.E.S.A.M.L. scaffold in the Essay Outline Builder . Study: one annotated exemplar per week ( SB / RE ) — click through every highlight, one colour category at a time. Tool: Essay Outline Builder — plan two essays per week without writing them. Micro-Drills for topic sentences. Weeks 6–5 · Write, mark, rewrite Do: one full timed Section A essay per week ( Practice Topics & Timer , 60 minutes). Swap with a friend and mark each other against the criteria . Read: the 2024 and 2025 assessor takeaways — especially the topic-verb guidance. Fix: run a paragraph through the Vocabulary Upgrader after each essay. Weeks 4–3 · Sections B and C Read: Creating Texts with its three scored sample pieces, and Analysing Argument including the vocabulary bank. Do: one timed Section B piece and one timed Section C analysis per week, and mark both against the criteria . Use the practice stimuli and practice articles . Weeks 2 · Full dress rehearsals Do: at least one complete three-hour exam under conditions — the Exam Generator makes a fresh paper, or use a practice exam . Fifteen minutes reading time, no phone, all three sections. Mark: every section against the criteria ; note which section costs you most and give it the spare hours this week. Week 1 · Final week Read: the Exam Checklists , the Priority Checklist for 2027 , and Exam Format one last time. Do: light passes of the quote banks and flashcards; one plan a day with the Outline Builder — no more full essays after mid-week. Sleep is revision. Pair this program with the advice in the rest of Effectively Studying For Exams — spaced repetition, study-life balance, and exam-day strategy.
