Study Tools Glossary of Techniques Every film and persuasive technique from the guide in one alphabetical reference. Ad hominem Metalanguage Attacking the person making an argument rather than the argument itself. Adjective Persuasive technique Describing words usually connected to a noun (naming word). e.g. The bright red house (bright and red = adjectives; house = noun) — Adds emphasis. Allegory Metalanguage A narrative whose characters and events stand for a parallel moral, political or historical meaning. Alliteration Persuasive technique Repeating and playing upon the same letter. e.g. A back-breaking job... — Adds emphasis and reinforces meaning, especially where an idea is repeated. Often used to create a highly emotive image. Allusion Metalanguage An indirect reference to another text, event or figure that imports its associations into the work. Anaphora Metalanguage Deliberate repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses to build rhythm and force. Anecdote Persuasive technique A short account or story of an entertaining or interesting incident. e.g. In my experience... — Usually makes reader sympathetic and receptive to the point; can set up a character, then position reader to accept or reject that individual character. Antithesis Metalanguage Setting opposing ideas in balanced phrasing to sharpen the contrast between them. Appeal to authority Metalanguage Citing experts, credentials or institutions so the audience defers to the position. Appeal to fear Metalanguage Raising threatening consequences so the audience feels the risk of not agreeing. Appeal to hip-pocket Metalanguage Framing an issue around cost and personal finances to engage self-interest. Appeal to patriotism Metalanguage Invoking national identity and pride so agreement feels loyal and dissent disloyal. Archetype Metalanguage A character type or pattern recurring across literature that carries instant associations. Archival effect Film technique Footage styled to look like old film. — The final picnic images simulate the limited frames of historic film, as if the past is a lost record. Aside Metalanguage A short remark delivered to the audience that other characters do not hear. Associations Persuasive technique Words that create meanings beyond the literal meaning of the word. e.g. attractive, alluring, pleasing, charming — Suggests or influences reader response in certain ways, often subconsciously. Implied meanings need to be identified. Attacks/praise Persuasive technique The writer attacks or praises an opponent or idea. This is really an assertion of the writer’s viewpoint. e.g. denigrating or humiliating the person, discrediting opponents as unreliable, dishonest, suggesting unsatisfactory associations — Often effective in placing the reader in a position of agreement with the writer/speaker through forceful language and insistent claims, even without evidence. Bandwagon Metalanguage Suggesting most people already agree, pressuring the audience to join the majority. Bias Persuasive technique One-sidedness in presentation of view/opinion. e.g. Eminem’s tour promoter obviously sees no danger in what Eminem says. — Can subjectively influence the reader by intentionally only presenting one side of the argument. Call to action Metalanguage A direct instruction telling the audience what to do next. Characterisation Metalanguage The methods an author uses to construct a character: dialogue, actions, appearance, others' reactions. Chiaroscuro Metalanguage Strong contrast of light and shadow in a frame, often signalling moral ambiguity or noir style. Cliché Metalanguage A worn expression whose overuse signals lazy or manipulative reasoning — or is deployed knowingly. Clichés Persuasive technique Worn out, overused expressions. e.g. Fit as a fiddle, Turn over a new leaf, Pushing the envelope — Are familiar, often colloquial, so can offer a shortcut to convey meaning. Close-up Film technique Tightly frames a face or object to reveal emotion or detail. — Stopped watches, Miranda’s face, Sara’s photograph of Miranda. Colloquial language Metalanguage Informal, conversational wording that builds rapport and an ordinary, relatable persona. Colourful words and descriptive language Persuasive technique Words that are heightened, vivid, lively, and full of interest. e.g. Hot = blistering, sultry, muggy, suffocating... — Produce a picture and/or induce an emotion. Engage reader by gaining attention and often put a new slant on familiar events and issues. Connotation Metalanguage The emotional or cultural associations a word carries beyond its literal meaning. Contention Persuasive technique The main line of argument in a text. A statement of the main idea being argued or debated. Focuses on WHAT is being argued. — Pinpoints the issue and the writer’s point of view. Helps the reader identify the issue and evaluate the techniques used to persuade them to agree. Costume Film technique Clothing used to communicate character, class and ideas. — White muslin, gloves and hats at the college; Irma’s red dress on her return; Mrs Appleyard’s black mourning clothes. Cross-cutting Film technique Cutting between two scenes happening at the same time. — Moving between the college and the Rock, or between Sara and Albert on the night of her death. Cumulative listing Metalanguage Piling up examples or details so the sheer accumulation feels like proof. Diegetic sound Film technique Sound that exists within the world of the film. — The ticking of clocks, the thrum of the Rock, cicadas and birdsong. Dissolve Film technique One image fades gradually into another, linking them. — Michael’s swan vase gives way to Miranda and then to a real swan, linking the three. Dramatic irony Metalanguage When the audience knows something a character does not, creating tension or poignancy. Emotional Appeals Persuasive technique Play on people’s emotions such as fears, insecurities, hopes, desires, and values. Can target: • A sense of jus
